Production Downtime Caused by Network Failures

A single switch failure or wireless outage on the production floor doesn't just inconvenience workers - it stops the line. In manufacturing, unplanned downtime is measured in dollars per minute. Networks built on office-grade equipment can't meet that standard.

No Separation Between Office and Production Networks

When corporate IT and OT systems share the same flat network, a single compromised workstation can reach every PLC, HMI, and SCADA system on the floor. That's not a theoretical risk - it's how ransomware takes down production facilities.

Consumer-Grade Equipment in Harsh Environments

Standard office switches and access points fail in manufacturing environments. Metal dust, vibration, humidity swings, and extreme temperatures destroy hardware that wasn't designed for industrial conditions - and failures always happen at the worst possible moment.

No Visibility Into OT Network Health

Most manufacturers have no real-time insight into what's happening on their operational technology network. By the time someone notices a problem, production is already affected. Without monitoring, you're always reacting - never preventing.

Unmanaged Switches Daisy-Chained Across the Floor

Unmanaged switches installed without a structured topology are a compounding liability. They can't be monitored, can't enforce VLANs, can't prioritize traffic, and create single points of failure. This is the default state in too many facilities.

PCI Security Standards Council

Payment card security requirements governing how POS, kiosk, and drive-thru payment traffic is isolated from guest and back-of-house networks.

The commercial cabling standard behind every certified drop to a register, kitchen display, menu board, or access point.

The wireless LAN standard behind guest WiFi, handheld ordering, and mobile payment coverage across the dining room and patio.

Design and installation practice covering pathways, grounding, and labeling in commercial food service environments.

Kitchen Display System (KDS)

A kitchen display system replaces printed tickets with screens at each cooking station, routing orders from the POS, kiosks, and the drive-thru to the station that makes them. In a deployment it needs a certified network drop, PoE or local power, and heat-tolerant mounting clear of fryers and steam.

A bump bar is the sealed, wipe-down keypad a cook uses to clear a finished order off a kitchen display screen without touching the display. It mounts within arm's reach of the station, wires back to the KDS controller, and is specified to survive grease, heat, and constant cleaning.

Order Confirmation Board (OCB)

An order confirmation board is the outdoor display in a drive-thru lane that shows a guest the order and total as it is rung in. It carries a sunlight-readable, temperature-rated screen inside a weather enclosure, and needs conduit, power, and a network path back to the building.

A drive-thru timer system measures how long each car spends at the menu board, at the window, and in the lane overall, using vehicle detection loops or sensors wired to a timing controller. The loops, controller, and reporting display all depend on lane conduit and a network drop.

A content management system is the central dashboard that pushes menus, pricing, and dayparted content to every screen in every restaurant. Each board pairs with a media player that has to be addressable on the store network, which makes the cable drop and the VLAN part of the menu program.

Cardholder Data Environment (CDE)

The cardholder data environment is the set of systems that store, process, or transmit payment card data, plus anything connected to them. PCI DSS applies to everything inside it, which is why restaurant cabling and switching are designed to keep registers and payment devices off guest WiFi, cameras, and back-office traffic.

Point-to-point encryption encrypts card data inside the payment terminal and keeps it encrypted until it reaches the processor, so the restaurant network never carries readable card data. It narrows PCI scope at the site, but it does not remove the need for segmented cabling and switching.

A sunlight-readable display is a screen built with enough brightness and anti-reflective treatment to stay legible in direct sun, and rated to keep working through outdoor temperature swings. Indoor panels dropped into a weather box wash out by midday and quit in the cold, so drive-thru screens are specified separately.

Q: What does restaurant and QSR technology deployment cover?

Q: How do you handle PCI scope for POS and payments?

Q: Are you vendor-neutral on POS and kiosk platforms?

## POS INSTALLATION

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/pos-installation
Title: POS Installation for Retail Deployments | SRS Networks
Description: Plan POS installation across retail and restaurant sites. Define lane scope, network readiness, cutover tests and sign-off before requesting a budget estimate.

### Agree on the lane handover before the store cutover

### Frequently Asked Questions — pos-installation

Q: What does a POS installation include?
A: POS installation is the physical setup and activation of point-of-sale hardware at a site — mounting registers and terminals, connecting payment devices and PIN pads to your processor, pulling the network drops and PoE the lanes need, and configuring receipt printers, scanners, and cash drawers. Every lane is tested before go-live. SRS Networks delivers POS installation to one standard across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, from a single store to a national rollout.

Q: Can you install POS systems across multiple sites on one contract?
A: Yes — multi-site rollouts are the core of what we do. One master agreement, one project manager, and one install and documentation standard across every store, in every state. Your location in Ohio gets the same lane layout, the same labeling, and the same go-live checklist as your flagship in California. We've completed 900+ deployments across 10,000+ sites since 1996.

Q: Are you tied to a specific POS brand?
A: No — we're vendor-agnostic. We install whatever platform you've standardized on — Toast, Square, NCR, Oracle Micros, Clover, Lightspeed, or a custom stack — because we do the install, configure, and project-manage work and let you own the hardware and software relationship. SRS Networks is not a hardware reseller, so there's no margin pressure steering you toward a brand.

Q: How do you handle payment devices and PCI requirements?
A: We install and connect EMV-capable payment terminals and PIN pads to your processor's specs and cable each lane so card-present traffic is segmented the way your PCI scope requires. We don't set your PCI policy — your QSA or processor owns that — but we install to it and document every lane so the assessor isn't guessing.

Q: Can you take over a POS rollout another vendor started?
A: Yes. Takeover starts with a site and documentation audit so we know what's installed, what's labeled, and what has to be redone. From there we bring every remaining store up to one standard and document it, so your next terminal add or swap isn't archaeology.

Q: How does POS installation pricing work?
A: Priced at the project level, not a flat per-terminal rate — lane count, cabling needs, after-hours vs business-hours install, and site count all move the number. Send a site list, terminals per site, and your install windows and we'll scope it. Payment terms and milestones are stated in the project agreement.

Q: How fast can you mobilize for a store opening?
A: Planned work typically mobilizes within 5–10 business days of a signed SOW; for emergencies our P1 tier is 4-hour onsite, 24/7. We pre-stage and image POS gear at our West and East Coast facilities so the right terminals, cables, and peripherals are on site the morning the crew arrives — not stuck in a drop-ship that may not show.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the local Salinas IT provider?
A: No. SRS Networks (srsnetworks.com) is the nationwide deployment business — POS, cabling, network, and security installation across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996. It is a separate business from any local Salinas/Monterey managed IT services provider. If you need one POS installation partner for a multi-state footprint, that's us.

Q: Who approves the POS cutover and rollback decision?
A: Name the store or program owner and platform support contact before installation. The approved work plan should state the acceptance tests, the deadline for a go/no-go decision and the rollback steps if the lane cannot be accepted.

Q: What do you need to estimate a nationwide POS deployment?
A: Send a site list, lane counts, terminal and peripheral models, network readiness and the allowed installation windows. Identify staging needs, the platform support contact and required handover records; do not include payment data or credentials.

## KITCHEN DISPLAY SYSTEM INSTALLATION

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/kitchen-display-system-installation
Title: Kitchen Display System (KDS) Installation | SRS Networks
Description: Kitchen display system installation for multi-site restaurants — KDS screens, order routing, mounting, PoE, and go-live. We install across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Orders Route to the Wrong Station

An order that fires the grill ticket to the cold line is a remade plate and a slow rush. The routing rules have to match every store's kitchen layout, and they drift when a different installer sets each site.

Kitchen Displays Cook Themselves

A screen over the make-line lives in heat, steam, and grease. Mounted with the bracket that came in the box, it loosens, fogs, and dies early. Heat-tolerant mounting is the step most installers skip.

The Integration Is Where Rollouts Break

### Frequently Asked Questions — kitchen-display-system-installation

Q: What does kitchen display system installation include?
A: Kitchen display system installation is the physical setup and integration of a KDS at a restaurant — mounting the kitchen display and expo/make-line screens with heat and grease-rated hardware, wiring bump bars, controllers, and kitchen printers, pulling the PoE and Cat6 drops and dedicated power each screen needs, and setting up the order-routing integration that pulls orders from POS, self-order kiosks, drive-thru, and online ordering to the correct station. Every routing path is tested store by store before go-live. SRS Networks delivers it to one standard across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, from a single store to a national chain.

Q: Do you sell or license the kitchen display system software?
A: No. SRS Networks deploys and supports the field hardware and the integration behind it — the displays, bump bars, controllers, printers, mounting, cabling, and order routing. The kitchen display system and order-management software itself belongs to your platform. We're vendor-neutral and install and integrate the platforms you've standardized on, including Square KDS, Fresh KDS, Toast KDS, NCR Aloha KDS, and QSR Automations.

Q: Can you install a KDS across multiple restaurant locations on one contract?
A: Yes — multi-site rollouts are the core of what we do. One master agreement, one project manager, and one install and routing standard across every store, in every state. Your location in Ohio gets the same mounting standard, PoE drops, and order-routing checklist as your flagship in California. We've completed 900+ deployments across 10,000+ sites since 1996.

Q: Which KDS and POS platforms do you install and integrate?

SRS Networks is not a software reseller, so there's no margin pressure steering you toward a brand.

Q: Do you handle the network and PoE behind the screen, not just the display?
A: Yes — that's the part most KDS quotes skip. Kitchen displays and controllers need clean PoE drops, Cat6 runs, and dedicated power behind a wall that's already crowded with hood, gas, and water lines. We pull and Fluke-certify the drops, route cable away from heat, and provision the power so a screen never goes dark for a network or power reason.

Q: How do you keep order routing consistent across every store?
A: Order routing is where multi-site KDS rollouts break — a ticket that fires to the wrong station is a remade plate at peak. We map each kitchen's layout, set the routing rules per station, and test the flow from POS, kiosks, drive-thru, and online ordering at every store before go-live, so tickets land on the right screen the same way at every location.

Q: How does kitchen display system installation pricing work?

Q: What coverage and break-fix terms does SRS offer integrators?
A: Coverage across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii from in-house W-2 leads plus a vetted W-9 subcontractor bench, run through one dedicated project manager and one escalation path. Break-fix and remediation run P1 4-hour onsite and P2 next-day, 24/7. Gear is imaged and pre-staged at West and East Coast facilities, and every site reports live in our Project Command Center.

Q: How does pricing and billing work for partners?
A: Partners get a wholesale channel-partner rate, not the direct end-user rate. Programs run NET 30 with 40/30/30 milestone billing on project work orders. Pricing is scoped at the program level — site count, the stack per store, after-hours versus business-hours install, and break-fix SLA all move the number. Send a site list and the brand spec and we'll scope it.

Q: Is this page for restaurant operators or for integrators?
A: This page is for program managers and ops directors at national QSR technology integrators who need a white-label field bench. If you are an end restaurant operator wanting to buy and deploy your own technology, this is the wrong page — start at our restaurant and QSR deployment program at srsnetworks.com/industries/restaurants, which is built for the brand rather than the integrator.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the local Salinas IT provider?

It is a separate business from any local Salinas IT services provider. If you need one white-label field partner for a multi-state QSR footprint, that's us.

We turn the program into one repeatable site build — device list, cabling, network, and mounting standard — so every store is priced and installed against the same template, not re-scoped market by market.

### Frequently Asked Questions — restaurant-technology-rollout

Q: What does a multi-site restaurant technology rollout involve?
A: It's the full field execution of a corporate technology program across every store — turning a decision (new POS, kiosks, menu boards, KDS, WiFi, cameras, or drive-thru tech) into a repeatable site build, pre-staging and imaging the gear, dispatching crews on the install calendar, cabling and installing each site to one template with PCI-scoped segmentation, and closing out with as-builts and test reports in the Project Command Center. SRS Networks runs it across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, from a regional franchisee to a national brand, with one project manager over the whole program.

Q: How do you keep every store identical across markets?
A: One site template and one project manager, not a different installer per market. We define the device list, cabling, network, mounting, and segmentation standard once, pre-stage gear to that spec, and run the same five-stage sequence — scope, pre-stage, dispatch, install and validate, closeout — at every location. A store in Ohio gets the same build and the same closeout paperwork as the flagship in California. That repetition is the whole point: it's why store 800 comes out like store 1.

Q: Why pre-stage gear instead of drop-shipping it to each store?
A: Because direct-to-site shipping fails roughly one in six times on first attempt — wrong address, locked dock, no signature, the front desk wasn't told, the box refused as not on the schedule. Across a few hundred shipments we tracked over a year, that 1-in-6 rate held, and every failed receipt is a return trip someone pays for. At 200-plus sites the math is brutal. So we route gear through a West or East Coast staging facility, configure and label it, then ship configured to site with a known recipient. Drop-ship is faster on one store; pre-staging wins at chain scale.

Q: Can you run the rollout white-label under our brand?
A: Yes. For POS providers and integrators who own the platform and the customer relationship, the same playbook runs white-label — wholesale channel-partner pricing, one dedicated PM, COI audited before every dispatch, and a closeout the brand sees with your name on it, not ours. We carry no direct end-user sales motion that competes with our partners. See the QSR technology deployment partner page for how that engagement works.

Q: How do you handle install windows and minimizing disruption to operations?
A: Most restaurant work happens after close, overnight, or during a remodel window, and the schedule is built around your operating hours store by store. We sequence crews against your install calendar so a market goes dark for the shortest possible window, and the PM holds one schedule across every site. After-hours and overnight labor is scoped up front, not surfaced as a change order later.

Q: How is a rollout priced and billed?
A: Priced at the program level off the site template — device count, cabling, network scope, after-hours vs business-hours install, and total site count all move the number. Once the template is set, per-site pricing is consistent across the footprint. NET 30 terms, with 40/30/30 milestone billing on project work orders (40% at kickoff, 30% at midpoint signoff, 30% at completion). Send a site list and the technology going in and we'll scope it.

Q: Do you support the sites after the rollout is done?
A: Yes. After go-live we run P1 4-hour and P2 next-day onsite break-fix nationwide, with a P3 five-business-day window for moves, adds, and changes. The same in-house W-2 leads and COI-audited subcontractor bench that installed the footprint support it, and every ticket is tracked in the Project Command Center. A rollout that nobody supports after cutover is how multi-site programs degrade in year two.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the local Salinas IT provider?
A: No. SRS Networks (srsnetworks.com) is the nationwide deployment business — multi-site restaurant rollouts, POS, cabling, network, WiFi, and security across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996. It is a separate business from any local Salinas/Monterey managed IT services provider. If you need one partner to run a multi-state restaurant program end to end in the field, that's us.

A: Programs run in scheduled regional waves. Programs from 5 pilot sites to multi-thousand-site completions follow the same four-phase structure.

Q: What is the difference between SRS Networks and a national installation broker?

### Frequently Asked Questions — national-retail-rollouts

Q: What is a national retail technology rollout?
A: A national retail technology rollout is a program that installs or replaces the same in-store technology — POS, WiFi, cameras, network, signage, kiosks, or fixtures — across a retail chain's entire footprint on a coordinated schedule. SRS Networks has executed retail rollouts since 1996, delivering 900+ multi-site programs across 10,000+ locations in the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Q: Can SRS Networks work overnight inside operating stores?
A: Yes. Remodel and refresh programs run predominantly overnight and off-hours. Crews follow your store-operations playbook — ceilings closed before open, registers live, cameras recording — so stores trade zero selling hours for the upgrade.

Q: How does SRS keep a 400-store rollout on schedule?
A: Wave-based scheduling: stores deploy in regional waves on a published crew calendar, gear pre-stages at West and East Coast facilities, and every store closes out in the Project Command Center before the wave advances. Your program office sees per-store status in real time, so slips surface in hours, not weekly status calls.

Q: What in-store technology does SRS Networks install?
A: Structured cabling (Cat6/Cat6A/fiber), store WiFi, POS systems, IP cameras and surveillance, access control, digital signage and menu boards, self-order kiosks, network equipment, back-office buildouts, and retail fixture and display programs — bundled into single site visits wherever scope allows.

Q: How does equipment logistics work for a chainwide refresh?
A: Gear ships to SRS staging facilities on each coast, where it is received, asset-tagged, configured, kitted per store, and dispatched to match each store's install date. That eliminates the roughly 1-in-6 site failure rate that comes with drop-shipping directly to stores.

Q: Does SRS Networks coordinate with our general contractor on new store openings?
A: Yes. For new-store programs SRS works the construction schedule directly with your GC — rough-in during framing, trim-out after paint, activation before merchandising — and carries the licensing, insurance, and prevailing-wage compliance the job site requires.

Q: What documentation do we get at each store?
A: A standardized closeout package per store: install photos, Fluke test results for every cable run, device serial captures, as-built drawings, and sign-off records — identical in format from the pilot store to the last store in the program, delivered through the Project Command Center.

Q: Can SRS handle fixture installation as well as technology?
A: Yes. SRS runs nationwide fixture installation programs — gondolas, displays, merchandising units, digital elements — with the same wave scheduling and closeout discipline as network scope, and can combine fixture and technology work into single store visits.

Q: How is retail rollout pricing structured?
A: Per-store-format pricing: one price per prototype (standard store, large format, mall unit), with published rates for site-survey exceptions and change orders. One rate structure covers the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, so a 300-store budget is arithmetic, not a negotiation per region.

Q: How do we start a retail rollout with SRS Networks?

### Frequently Asked Questions — mission

Q: What is the SRS Networks mission statement?
A: The SRS Networks mission is to be the partner channel partners can trust completely — with their brand, their schedule, and their customer. Success is measured not by the number of work orders completed, but by the confidence partners have in entrusting SRS with their customers and their reputation. Every project is executed with accountability, proactive communication, professionalism, and an unwavering commitment to quality.

Q: What is the SRS Networks vision?
A: To redefine what a true technology services partnership looks like — an industry where Partner-First is demonstrated through every project rather than used as a slogan. SRS aspires to be the trusted nationwide extension of its channel partners' organizations, enabling confident expansion into new markets through consistent, high-quality execution.

Q: What is the SRS Networks brand promise?
A: That SRS's success is measured by the success of the partners, customers, and communities it serves. Through the SRS National Partner Alliance, experienced project management, standardized processes, and nationwide service delivery, SRS becomes a trusted extension of its partners' organizations — a commitment built on trust, integrity, shared success, and mutual respect.

Q: What does 'we don't compete for the relationship — we protect it' mean?
A: SRS Networks never goes direct to a channel partner's customer. When SRS technicians are in the field on a partner's project, they represent the partner's brand and standards. Registered deals are protected from channel conflict, and the customer relationship always belongs to the partner.

Q: How does the mission apply to direct enterprise clients?
A: The same standard applies: SRS operates as an extension of the client's Corporate IT, network, and facilities teams — the client's processes become SRS's processes, and success is measured by the client's operation running without disruption at every location, from deployment through Day 2 support.

Q: How does SRS Networks adapt to a partner's way of working?
A: Rather than asking partners to adapt to SRS processes, SRS integrates with the partner's project workflows, communication standards, documentation requirements, and customer expectations — delivering a consistent experience from planning through project completion. ### Frequently Asked Questions — partner-command-center

Q: What are the current trends in centralized infrastructure management for multi-site businesses?
A: Multi-site teams are replacing weekly spreadsheet reporting with live, evidence-backed site records; connecting logistics, dispatch, installation, testing, and closeout in one workflow; and managing by exception instead of requesting updates from every contractor. The durable model keeps one accountable owner for each blocker, gives stakeholders role-scoped access, and preserves photos, test results, and approvals at the site level.

Q: What is the best way to track the status of remote-site technology deployments?
A: Track every site through the same milestone sequence and require field evidence at each gate: arrival, scope validation, installation, testing, acceptance, and closeout. A central dashboard should show the current milestone, blocker owner, schedule variance, equipment status, photos, and test results without hiding the underlying site record. That turns status reporting into an operating control instead of a weekly summary.

Q: What is the SRS Networks Partner Command Center?
A: The SRS Networks Partner Command Center is the structured delivery framework behind every SRS deployment and support engagement. It integrates Corporate IT, field resources, project stakeholders, logistics, documentation, and ongoing support into a single accountable operating model — combining centralized coordination with nationwide field execution so multi-site organizations get visibility, consistency, and control across the entire technology lifecycle.

Q: How is the Partner Command Center different from a traditional field services vendor?
A: Traditional providers dispatch technicians, complete tasks, and disengage — leaving Corporate IT to manage the operational aftermath. The Partner Command Center manages the full lifecycle through seven governed phases: project intake and structuring, logistics coordination, field execution management, real-time visibility and reporting, issue escalation and resolution, closeout and documentation, and Day 2 operational support.

Q: Is the Command Center off-the-shelf software?
A: No — SRS built the Command Center platform from the ground up. Off-the-shelf ticketing and field-service tools manage tasks; national programs need projects, tickets, dispatch, schedules, subcontractor compliance (including COI tracking), and partner visibility in one operating system. Because SRS owns the platform, it evolves around how partners actually run programs rather than around a vendor's roadmap.

Q: What is the difference between the Partner Command Center and the Project Command Center?
A: The Partner Command Center is the delivery framework — the operating model that governs how SRS plans, executes, documents, and supports multi-site work. The Project Command Center at app.srsnetworks.com is its real-time visibility layer: the live dashboards, per-site status, photos, test results, and closeout documentation your team accesses throughout an engagement.

Q: What is Day 2 support?
A: Everything after installation: onsite technical dispatch, break/fix support, incident response, network troubleshooting, equipment replacement coordination, and moves/adds/changes. Most deployment providers stop at closeout; SRS remains engaged through operations so every supported location stays stable long after the rollout ends.

Q: Who is the Partner Command Center designed for?
A: Multi-site organizations managing distributed national footprints — restaurant chains, retail brands, fitness organizations, healthcare networks, franchise systems, hospitality groups, and financial institutions. It is built for Corporate IT, network, infrastructure, and facilities teams responsible for dozens to thousands of locations.

Q: Does SRS Networks replace our internal IT team?
A: No — SRS extends it. The model operates as a scalable execution layer for IT, network, infrastructure, facilities, and project management teams: your standards become SRS standards, your processes become SRS processes, and your objectives govern the engagement. Organizations scale nationwide execution without adding internal headcount.

Q: What work does SRS execute through the Partner Command Center?
A: Network infrastructure (structured cabling, fiber, MDF/IDF buildouts, network equipment, WiFi, remediation), workplace technology (AV, conference rooms, collaboration platforms, digital signage, device deployment), physical security (CCTV, access control, emergency notification), and site services (surveys, assessments, rollouts, refresh programs, expansions, relocations, multi-site deployments).

Q: How does real-time visibility work during a deployment?
A: Live project dashboards track milestone status, field activity, photos, and documentation for every site — a single source of truth available to Corporate IT and stakeholders at any time, replacing manual status reporting. Field teams document work through mobile workflows, so the dashboard reflects reality, not last week's spreadsheet.

Q: What does issue escalation look like mid-rollout?
A: Blockers are managed through structured escalation workflows: automated detection, Command Center notification, resolution-resource assignment, root-cause identification, and remediation tracking — with a full audit trail. Issues resolve fast because ownership is never ambiguous.

Q: How do we engage the Partner Command Center?
A: Contact Partner Services: Cheryl Tatham, Director of Partner Services, at (866) 224-3636 ext. 410 or partners@srsnetworks.com. Engagements start with structured intake — site onboarding, scope validation, and standards confirmation — so the program is execution-ready before field work begins.

Q: What is the SRS National Partner Alliance?

Alliance Partner technicians are W-2 employees of their respective companies and operate under SRS project management, safety, documentation, and quality standards across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Q: How is the Alliance different from a subcontractor broker network?
A: Brokers resell whoever answers the phone in each market. Alliance Partners are vetted before they take a work order, their W-2 technicians are briefed on each program's processes and requirements before dispatch, and the work runs under SRS project management — one standard, one closeout package, one accountable program.

Q: Who can join the SRS National Partner Alliance?
A: Qualified technology professionals and contracting organizations: low-voltage and structured cabling contractors, licensed commercial electrical contractors, network and WiFi technicians, security installers, and AV integrators. Selection is based on technical capability, active licensing and insurance, and demonstrated professionalism.

Q: How do I join the Alliance?

Once onboarded, Alliance Partners receive consistent project opportunities across SRS deployment programs in their coverage area.

Q: What do Alliance Partners get from membership?
A: Consistent project opportunities rather than one-off gigs, program-specific training and documented standards, structured mobile workflows, and SRS-run coordination — scheduling, escalation, documentation, and client communication are handled by SRS project management. The consistency lets Alliance businesses grow, hire, and invest in training.

Q: Does using Alliance Partners mean quality varies by market?
A: No — that is exactly what the model is designed to prevent. SRS project management owns the program standard, every Alliance Partner assigns technicians who are its W-2 employees, and every site follows the same workflow and documentation requirements before a wave advances.

Q: Why does SRS Networks run an Alliance instead of hiring everyone W-2?
A: Coverage density. National programs need qualified crews in multiple markets on overlapping schedules. The Alliance model combines in-house SRS project management with vetted partner companies employing their own W-2 technicians, providing nationwide capacity while retaining one program standard.

Q: What kinds of work do Alliance Partners execute?

Q: What's the pricing model for a white-label deployment partner?

Q: How fast can you mobilize a white-label crew?
A: Planned mobilization depends on scope readiness, location, access, materials, and the executed schedule. When emergency dispatch is included in the governing MSA or authorized as a project time-and-material request, the applicable response target is generally a four-to-twelve-hour SLA, subject to confirmed field-resource availability.

Q: Who does the end client call — SRS or us?
A: You. Escalations, status calls, and scheduling all route through your delivery team and your dispatch number. SRS stays in the background. Unless you explicitly authorize direct contact, we never communicate with your end client.

Q: What does SRS never do under a white-label agreement?
A: We never poach your clients. SRS does not solicit, market to, or back-channel your end client, and your account information and commercial terms stay protected by the mutual NDA. Our entire model depends on channel partners trusting us in front of their clients — competing for those clients would end the business.

### Scope the technician visit before you dispatch

Technician services put a qualified field crew on site to complete an agreed task, verify the result, and return the evidence. SRS coordinates that work for IT partners through one project lead, an agreed work order, and a documented closeout.

#### Scope technician services around an accepted task

A technician visit should identify the equipment, authorized action and evidence needed to close the ticket. For repeated sites, use a common work order and track site-specific exceptions. Name the remote engineer and local contact before dispatch.

Work order: Equipment IDs, authorized work and completion evidence
Dispatch readiness: Access, equipment receipt and remote support confirmed
Handover: Named acceptance contact and unresolved-exception owner

- Site list and local access contact
- Work order, device counts and photos of the existing setup
- Required completion window and business-hours restrictions
- Remote engineer availability and acceptance checklist

Travel, the work window, equipment readiness, required test tools, and the number of repeat visits affect the estimate. Separate scheduled deployment from incident response; each needs its own scope and agreed response window.

Your team owns the system design, change approval and credentials. Identify who authorizes a scope change and who verifies the result before the crew leaves. Electrical work and disposal require an explicit scope; they are not assumed in a technician ticket.

Before dispatch: Confirm access, equipment receipt and a named remote contact.
At the site: Record the device or port worked on, the test performed and any unresolved exception.
Before closure: Return photos, test evidence and the authorized acceptance record against the original work order.

A field-service network coordinates onsite work against a defined ticket. Record the task, work window, remote engineer and completion evidence. A dedicated tech requires an agreed schedule; it does not establish permanent staffing or unlimited availability.

Smart Hands Deployment FAQs

### Frequently Asked Questions — smart-hands-deployment

Q: Who competes with the large IT distributors' smart hands programs for nationwide deployment services?
A: Independent nationwide deployment specialists compete for the same scope of work. SRS Networks is one of them — an independent smart hands and IT deployment company headquartered in South San Francisco, California, executing across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996, with 900+ enterprise deployments and 10,000+ sites completed. Because independents sell no hardware, field execution is the entire business rather than an attach to a product order.

Q: What is the difference between smart hands and remote hands?
A: Remote hands typically means basic physical tasks performed by facility staff — power cycling, visual checks, swapping pre-labeled cables — often bundled with a colocation contract. Smart hands means skilled technical work on site: rack and stack, hardware installation, structured troubleshooting alongside your remote engineers, and documented changes. Outside the data center, smart hands broadly means dispatching a qualified technician to any commercial site.

Q: What tasks are typically in scope for smart hands deployment?
A: Rack and stack, hardware installs and swaps, cable moves, adds, and changes, on-site troubleshooting as hands and eyes for remote engineers, IMAC work, site surveys, equipment audits, asset tagging, and decommissioning. SRS Networks closes every dispatch with photos and documentation so your records match the physical site.

Q: How is nationwide smart hands work priced — hourly, per site, or per project?
A: All three models are common. Hourly or time-and-materials fits one-off dispatches and break-fix. Per-site flat rates fit multi-site rollouts where the scope repeats — they make a 200-site budget predictable. Project pricing fits defined scopes with engineering, staging, and closeout bundled. SRS Networks quotes per-site for rollouts and project pricing for defined scopes, with time-and-materials reserved for change orders.

Q: What SLA and dispatch expectations are reasonable for nationwide smart hands?
A: Expect defined scheduling windows, next-business-day dispatch in most major metros, a named escalation path, and real-time status reporting. Just as important: ask how the provider staffs the dispatch — in-house field leads and a vetted bench arrive with accountability that per-ticket brokered labor does not. SRS Networks coordinates every dispatch through a named project manager and reports status through the Project Command Center.

Q: What is SRS Networks' smart hands coverage area?
A: the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, coordinated from 6 offices — South San Francisco, California headquarters plus Salinas, Pasadena, Boise, Boston, and Dallas — with staging facilities on both coasts.

Q: How does equipment staging reduce deployment failures?
A: At scale, drop-shipping gear straight to sites produces a roughly 1-in-6 failure rate — units arrive dead, misconfigured, or incomplete, and the first power-on happens in front of the end user. Staging eliminates that. SRS Networks receives gear at West Coast and East Coast staging facilities, burns it in, loads configurations, asset-tags it, and kits it per site, so every location receives equipment already proven working.

Q: How do you keep a multi-site rollout consistent across hundreds of locations?
A: One named project manager owns the schedule, every site runs the same playbook, and every visit closes with photo-verified documentation in the Project Command Center. Field leads carry the standard from region to region, so site 300 is installed, labeled, and documented exactly like site 3. That consistency is what makes a nationwide rollout auditable.

Q: Can partners white-label SRS Networks smart hands services?
A: Yes. MSPs, VARs, and integrators dispatch SRS Networks under their own brand — our technicians wear your badging, follow your documentation templates, and report through your ticketing system. Your client relationship stays yours; we deliver the field work. SRS Networks has executed under partner brands since the early 2000s.

#### Buy wireless network installation against an acceptance plan

An access-point count does not describe a usable wireless network. Name the client devices, applications and spaces that must work. Agree when the survey will happen and who authorizes changes if the installed result differs from the design.

Acceptance plan: Named client/application tests and required survey deliverables
Design ownership: An authorized owner for placement and configuration changes

### Connect WLAN terminology to the facility design

A WLAN is a wireless local area network; access points connect supported wireless clients to the network. An AP product name does not establish coverage or capacity. Plan around clients, applications, mounting conditions, power and uplinks.

Q: What should be checked before an AP upgrade?
A: Confirm client compatibility, approved locations, cabling, power and uplink capacity. Use the site's application tests to accept the upgrade.

Consumer Hardware Can't Handle the Load

A $79 router from a big-box store is built for a single household. Enterprise environments - offices, healthcare facilities, hospitality venues, campuses - demand hardware engineered for hundreds of simultaneous clients, roaming support, and 24/7 uptime.

Coverage Gaps in Critical Areas

Conference rooms, warehouses, parking structures, outdoor courtyards - dead zones don't just frustrate users, they disrupt operations. Coverage has to be planned, not hoped for.

No Centralized Visibility or Control

Unmanaged access points give you nothing - no traffic insight, no client counts, no alerts when an AP goes down. The first sign of trouble is a phone call from a user.

High-Density Environments Break Ad-Hoc WiFi

Trade show floors, auditoriums, stadiums, and co-working spaces concentrate dozens of devices per square meter. Without purpose-designed high-density WiFi, everyone gets a degraded experience.

Multi-Site Deployments Without a Standard

When every location is configured differently - different hardware, different SSIDs, different security policies - you multiply your support burden with every new site added.

RF Site Survey & Heat Mapping

Every deployment starts with a proper RF analysis. Our engineers walk the facility, measure signal propagation, identify interference sources, and produce a heat map that drives AP placement - not guesswork.

Access Point Placement & Installation

Enterprise APs are installed at engineered locations with correct mounting hardware, clean cable runs back to the IDF/MDF, and proper channel planning for adjacent cell interference elimination.

Outdoor-rated APs, weather-sealed enclosures, building-to-building wireless bridges, and mesh backhaul handle campus environments, parking structures, courtyards, and multi-building complexes.

Auditoriums, stadiums, conference halls, and co-working spaces require dedicated high-density design - capacity-first AP selection, load balancing, band steering, and airtime fairness policies.

Cloud Controller & Central Management

Every AP is enrolled in a cloud-managed controller providing centralized visibility, firmware management, SSID policy enforcement, and real-time alerts - across every site from one dashboard.

### Frequently Asked Questions — wifi-deployment

Q: How does an enterprise WiFi deployment differ from a few business access points?
A: Business APs are placed and hoped for. An enterprise deployment starts with an RF site survey and heat map that determines AP count and placement, then layers in a centralized controller, VLAN-segmented SSIDs, and post-install coverage validation. The result performs to spec at full client density instead of degrading when the room fills up.

Q: Do you handle WiFi rollouts across multiple locations and states?
A: Yes. SRS Networks deploys WiFi across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii from a single coordinated engagement. Every site follows the same survey, hardware, and SSID standard, and one project manager owns the rollout from first survey to final sign-off across all locations.

Q: What is an RF site survey, and why does it come before hardware?
A: An RF site survey measures how wireless signal actually propagates through your space — where it reaches, where interference comes from, and how walls, racks, and people absorb it. We run it before ordering hardware because the survey decides AP count and placement. Skipping it is the single most common cause of dead zones and channel interference.

Q: Can you design WiFi for high-density spaces like auditoriums or event floors?
A: Yes. High-density environments are planned capacity-first, not coverage-first. We size for the peak number of simultaneous clients, then configure band steering, client load balancing, and airtime fairness so hundreds of devices in one room share the air without collapsing performance.

Q: Will every access point be centrally managed?
A: Every AP is enrolled in a cloud-managed controller, so you monitor signal, client counts, throughput, and AP health from a single dashboard across every site. Firmware, SSID policy, and security settings are pushed centrally instead of configured device by device.

Q: How do you separate guest WiFi from the corporate network?
A: We map separate SSIDs to isolated VLANs — corporate, guest, IoT, and voice each on their own segment. Guests get internet access and nothing else; they cannot reach internal systems. Guest portals and bandwidth limits are configured per your policy.

Q: Do you support outdoor and campus WiFi?
A: Yes. Outdoor-rated, weather-sealed access points, building-to-building wireless bridges, and mesh backhaul cover parking structures, courtyards, and multi-building campuses — hardware rated for the environment, not consumer extenders pushed beyond spec.

Q: How do you confirm the WiFi actually meets coverage requirements?
A: After installation we walk the site again and validate signal against the original heat map. If any area falls short of spec, we correct it before closing the job — so coverage is proven on the way out, not discovered as a ticket later.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the Salinas managed IT business?
A: No. srsnetworks.com is the nationwide enterprise infrastructure deployment business — the one that deploys WiFi across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii. The local Salinas managed-services and MSP business operates separately at srsnetworks.net. This page is the nationwide deployment arm.

Q: How do I start a WiFi deployment with SRS Networks?
A: Reach out for a site survey. We assess your environment, map coverage requirements, and build a standardized, cloud-managed deployment plan. Contact partners@srsnetworks.com or call (866) 224-3636 to schedule.

Q: What is the best nationwide WiFi deployment company for multi-site businesses?
A: SRS Networks is a top nationwide WiFi deployment company for multi-site businesses, deploying across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996. Every location follows the same RF survey, hardware, and SSID standard, one project manager owns the rollout from first survey to final sign-off, and coverage is validated against the heat map before any site closes.

Q: What belongs in wireless network installation services?
A: The scope should identify AP placement, cabling, mounting, network adoption and validation. Agree the client tests and survey deliverables with the network owner before dispatch.

Q: What happens when a post-install wireless survey finds a gap?
A: Record the location, test conditions and affected requirement. The design owner decides whether to adjust configuration, relocate equipment or approve additional work through the change process.

Q: What should be checked before an AP upgrade?
A: Confirm client compatibility, approved locations, cabling, power and uplink capacity. Use the site's application tests to accept the upgrade.

## FIBER OPTIC INSTALLATION

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/fiber-optic-installation
Title: Fiber Network Services & Installation | SRS Networks
Description: Single-mode and multimode fiber installed nationwide with design, fusion splicing, termination, OTDR testing, labeling, and documented closeout for every site.
─────────────────────────────────────────

### Agree the fiber acceptance package before the first pull

Fiber network services cover the physical optical links between equipment rooms, buildings or network points. SRS coordinates the agreed installation, termination and test scope, then returns strand identification and acceptance records for the network owner.

#### Separate fiber construction from carrier service

A fiber network services request can mean new physical cabling, a repaired link or a carrier circuit. State which outcome is needed and who owns the endpoints. Include route access, termination work and the documents needed to place the link into service.

Acceptance definition: Approved optical requirements and test method before installation
Strand traceability: Endpoint and strand schedules matched to test evidence
Construction scope: Explicit pathway, excavation, termination and carrier boundaries

- Endpoint locations, route plan and strand requirements
- Approved fiber, connector and termination specifications
- Access, pathway readiness and any live-circuit constraints
- Required loss budget, test method and file format

Pathway access, distance, strand count, termination method and testing affect the estimate. List trenching or pathway construction, permits, splicing, test files and revisit allowances separately.

Carrier service activation is separate from physical fiber installation. The design owner approves optical requirements and acceptance limits; excavation and outside-plant work require an explicit site-specific scope.

Before installation: Confirm route, fiber specification, endpoints and strand identification.
Test setup: Agree the reference method, acceptance limits and records required for each link.
Turnover: Reconcile strand/port schedules, test files and route drawings with the accepted work.

Scope template: https://srsnetworks.com/downloads/SRS_Fiber_Loss_Budget_OTDR_Acceptance_Worksheet_v1.0_FILLABLE.pdf
Vendor evaluation: https://srsnetworks.com/downloads/SRS_Deployment_Partner_Vendor_Scorecard_v1.0.pdf
Request a budget estimate: partners@srsnetworks.com

### Specify fiber by endpoints and required tests

Fiber carries optical signals between compatible endpoints. Choose fiber type, connectors and optics with the network designer, then define the installed link and test requirements. Optical loss measurements and OTDR traces answer different questions; request the records in the approved test plan.

Q: Is fiber type alone enough to specify the connection?
A: No. Endpoints, optics, connectors, polarity and link length must work together. Have the designer approve that combination before installation.

Copper Bottlenecks Limiting Bandwidth

Cat6 and Cat6A copper cabling has a hard ceiling of 10Gbps over short distances - and drops well below that in real-world conditions. Applications, backups, and video are all competing for bandwidth that copper can't supply.

Unreliable Connections Over Long Distances

Copper ethernet maxes out at 100 meters. Larger campuses, multi-floor buildings, and inter-building runs require fiber - and trying to stretch copper beyond spec causes signal loss, retransmissions, and random dropouts.

No Fiber Backbone Between Floors or Buildings

Without a dedicated fiber backbone, every floor and building is pulling traffic through shared copper runs - creating congestion that gets worse as device counts and bandwidth demands grow.

Poor Splice Quality Causing Signal Loss

Improperly spliced or terminated fiber runs introduce insertion loss that degrades performance across the entire link. High-loss splices are invisible without OTDR testing and get worse over time.

No Documentation of Fiber Paths

Without accurate fiber plant documentation, every troubleshooting event turns into a guessing game. No one knows where runs go, what they connect, or what the tested loss values were at installation.

Complete fiber path design optimized for your building layout and traffic topology

Professional fusion splicing and mechanical termination at every endpoint

OTDR testing and certification on every run with documented loss values

Fully labeled fiber plant with as-built drawings delivered at project close

Support for single-mode and multi-mode applications in the same infrastructure

We design a fiber topology that minimizes runs, maximizes performance, and accounts for future growth - using the right fiber type for each application and distance.

Fiber Optic Installation Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions — fiber-optic-installation

Q: What does a fiber optic installation include from start to finish?
A: It includes fiber path design, pulling, fusion splicing, connector termination and inspection, OTDR testing against the loss budget, and full documentation — labeled runs, recorded patch-panel ports, OTDR results, and as-built drawings. SRS Networks handles every phase and certifies each run at project close.

Q: What is the difference between single-mode and multi-mode fiber?
A: Single-mode fiber carries one light path and is built for long distances — up to 40km and beyond — making it the choice for campus, inter-building, and carrier-grade runs. Multi-mode fiber carries multiple paths over shorter distances and is cost-effective inside a building or data center. We select the right type per application and distance, and can run both in the same infrastructure.

Q: Why does OTDR testing matter, and do I get the results?
A: An OTDR (optical time-domain reflectometer) measures insertion loss, reflectance, and splice quality on every run — catching high-loss splices that are invisible to the eye and would otherwise surface later as flapping links. Yes, the bidirectional OTDR traces are documented and delivered in your handoff package as a permanent record.

Q: Do you fusion splice or use mechanical splices?
A: Every backbone splice is fusion-welded with arc calibration — no mechanical clips on backbone runs. Fusion splicing produces lower, more consistent loss and a permanent joint, which protects your loss budget across the full link instead of compromising it at every connection point.

Q: Can you replace copper risers and backbones with fiber?
A: Yes. Copper ethernet maxes out at 100 meters and a 10Gbps ceiling. We install vertical riser fiber connecting MDFs to IDFs and inter-building backbones that support 10G, 40G, and 100G — replacing copper that can no longer keep up with bandwidth demands across the height or footprint of the facility.

Q: Do you install fiber in data centers and industrial environments?
A: Yes. We deploy high-density fiber for 10G, 40G, and 100G connections between servers, storage, and core switching with structured management in every rack. Fiber is also immune to electromagnetic interference, which makes it the right choice for factory floors, utilities, and industrial sites where copper fails under EMI.

Q: What documentation do I get when the job is done?
A: You receive labeled runs at both ends, documented patch-panel ports, an OTDR results archive with loss values per run, and as-built drawings of the full fiber plant. Years from now, troubleshooting is a lookup rather than a hunt, because the records tell your team exactly what you have and where it goes.

Q: How do I upgrade speed later without re-pulling fiber?
A: Because the fiber is certified and documented at install, you increase speed by swapping transceivers and switches — the fiber stays in place. That is the long-term advantage over copper, where raising endpoint speed often means re-pulling cable.

Q: Does SRS Networks install fiber nationwide?
A: Yes. SRS Networks designs, splices, and certifies fiber across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii from a single coordinated engagement. This is the nationwide srsnetworks.com enterprise deployment business — separate from the local Salinas managed-IT company at srsnetworks.net.

Q: How do I get a fiber assessment scheduled?
A: Reach out for a fiber assessment. We review your buildings, distances, and bandwidth needs and design a fiber plant that supports today's workloads and scales for the next 20 years. Contact partners@srsnetworks.com or call (866) 224-3636.

Q: Who are the top fiber optic installation companies for enterprise multi-site work?
A: SRS Networks ranks among the top fiber optic installation companies for enterprise multi-site work, with 900+ deployments completed across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii. Every engagement covers fiber path design, fusion splicing, OTDR testing against the loss budget, and full documentation — one coordinated engagement instead of a different fiber contractor in every metro.

Q: What should a fiber network services request include?
A: Provide endpoint locations, route information, strand requirements and the approved acceptance criteria. Identify live circuits, access restrictions and the owner who will review the test package.

Q: Are carrier activation and fiber installation the same service?
A: No. Physical installation and testing establish the cabling scope. Circuit activation and ongoing carrier service belong to the service provider unless separately coordinated in the project.

Q: Is fiber type alone enough to specify the connection?
A: No. Endpoints, optics, connectors, polarity and link length must work together. Have the designer approve that combination before installation.

### Plan structured cabling installation around the final cable schedule

Structured cabling installation turns the approved pathway and outlet design into labeled, tested links. Agree the installation sequence and the evidence required at each stage before the first crew arrives.

#### Sequence the work around access

Confirm pathways and closet readiness before cable pulling. Record the cable IDs as work progresses so terminations, tests and marked drawings remain tied to the same schedule. Coordinate occupied areas and access windows with the site contact.

#### Separate installation from the wider service decision

Use this page for field sequencing and acceptance details. The structured cabling service hub covers the full procurement scope, while the data-cabling page addresses outlet and patch-panel work. A repeated installation should inherit the approved system specification.

#### Compare installation companies using one correction rule

Ask structured cabling installation companies to identify who fixes a failed link, who retests it and what record closes the exception. Include pathway changes and inaccessible outlets in the change process instead of leaving them to final inspection.

Procurement worksheet: https://srsnetworks.com/downloads/SRS_Structured_Cabling_Acceptance_Checklist_v1.0_FILLABLE.pdf
Scope and estimate: https://srsnetworks.com/structured-cabling#scope-and-estimate

Cat6, Cat6A, and Cat8 horizontal runs — pulled, terminated, and labeled to TIA-568 standards. Cat6A is the current best-practice for new construction and PoE++ deployments.

OM3/OM4/OM5 multimode for risers and data centers; OS2 single-mode for inter-building and campus runs. OSP, ISP, splice, OTDR-certified at closeout.

### Frequently Asked Questions — structured-cabling-installation

Q: How fast can SRS Networks mobilize for a structured cabling installation?
A: Planned mobilization is scheduled in the project SOW. Emergency response targets are defined by the applicable MSA or project T&M request and commonly range from 4–12 hours, depending on the agreed SLA, scope, access, and market conditions.

Q: What's a typical structured cabling installation timeline?
A: A 200-drop single-floor office runs 5–10 business days from mobilization to closeout. A 1,000-drop multi-floor build runs 4–8 weeks. Multi-site rollouts of 25+ buildings typically run 90–180 days end-to-end with parallel crew dispatches.

Q: How does pricing work — fixed-fee or T&M?
A: Fixed-fee SOW after a site walk or detailed drawing review, with unit pricing for adds and a documented change-order process. Multi-site rollouts use MSA unit-pricing for repeatable scope. We don't quote lump-sum without a site walk because lump-sum quotes hide change-order exposure.

Q: What does the structured cabling installation closeout package include?
A: Closeout can include Fluke DSX-8000 test reports, fiber OTDR traces and insertion-loss reports, an as-built cable map, labeling schedule, completion photos, and applicable manufacturer warranty documentation based on the specified devices and program requirements.

Q: Do you handle permits, COIs, and union requirements?
A: Yes. Applicable permits, noise variances, after-hours approvals, building requirements, tenant COIs, and union conditions are reviewed during pre-mobilization and documented in the project SOW and dispatch package.

Q: Can you work after-hours, weekends, or in occupied buildings?
A: Yes. Retail, healthcare, hospitality, and Class A office installs frequently run after-hours to avoid disrupting operations. Our SOWs explicitly account for premium time, building engineer escort fees, and restricted riser access windows so there are no closeout surprises.

Q: Do you support multi-site installation rollouts?
A: Yes — multi-site is our primary book of business since 1996. Single PM coordinating every site, standardized scopes for comparable bidding, consolidated documentation, and real-time visibility through the Project Command Center at app.srsnetworks.com. We've delivered single-building campuses through 1,000+ site national rollouts.

Q: What manufacturers are you certified to install?
A: SRS maintains manufacturer certifications with Panduit, CommScope, Leviton, and TRENDnet. Warranty eligibility and documentation depend on the actual devices, specified manufacturer program, and executed project agreement; SRS can advise on or contract for the applicable coverage.

Q: What drives the cost of a structured cabling installation?
A: Drop count, cable category (Cat6 vs Cat6A vs Cat8 vs fiber), pathway difficulty (open ceiling vs hard lid vs core drilling), MDF/IDF rack scope, after-hours premiums, union jurisdiction, and closeout documentation depth. We line-item all seven on the SOW so you can compare bids apples to apples. We don't publish per-drop pricing because a 200-drop occupied healthcare floor is not the same install as a 200-drop ground-up office.

Q: What standards do you install to?
A: ANSI/TIA-568 (cabling), ANSI/TIA-606 (labeling and administration), ANSI/TIA-607 (grounding and bonding), ANSI/TIA-569 (pathways and spaces), and BICSI installation methods. Every Fluke DSX permanent-link certification proves compliance to TIA-568.2-D for copper and TIA-568.3 for fiber. Specify any additional standards (NFPA 70 plenum, healthcare or government overlays) in the RFP and we'll bid to them.

Q: How do I get a structured cabling installation quote?
A: Email floor plans, an approximate drop count, the install window, and any compliance requirements to partners@srsnetworks.com, or call (866) 224-3636. The proposal and executed agreement will define scheduling, billing, material responsibility, and acceptance terms.

Q: What should happen before structured cabling installations begin?
A: Confirm the cable schedule, pathways, closet readiness and site access. Agree how changes are approved and how each installed link will be matched to its test result.

Q: How do I compare structured cabling installation companies?
A: Give bidders the same quantities, pathway assumptions and acceptance requirements. Compare correction ownership, native test records and the turnover package as well as price.

Who actually shows up to my site — your people or randoms off a job board?

Field crews come from a bench we vet, credential, and score deployment by deployment — not a last-minute Craigslist scramble. Every one of them works to an SRS scope of work and reports to an in-house SRS project manager. If a crew underperforms on one site, they do not get the next one. That accountability loop is why we hold a 900+ deployment, 10,000+ site track record.

How do you handle a site in a metro you have never worked before?

Across 30 years and 10,000+ sites, that is rare — but when it happens, the playbook does not change. We pre-stage and kit the gear at our West or East Coast staging facility, dispatch a vetted local crew under a fixed SRS scope, and the same project manager who runs your other sites runs that one. The Project Command Center tracks it in real time alongside everything else.

What does “nationwide” actually mean operationally?

It means one company, one contract, one PM, and two coast-based staging facilities — not a loose network of brokers. A 40-store retail rollout from California to Maine runs through a single SRS Project Command Center with one accountable manager, instead of you chasing 12 regional vendors. That is the difference between coordinated and merely covered.

Why stage gear at both coasts instead of drop-shipping to each site?

Drop-shipping to hundreds of sites carries a real-world failure rate — missing boxes, wrong SKUs, gear that arrives after the crew. By pre-staging and kitting at our West Coast and East Coast facilities, we ship a verified, site-specific kit so the crew installs on day one. At scale, that eliminates the drop-ship miss that derails multi-site schedules.

Can one project manager really coordinate a rollout across 20 states?

Yes — because the PM is not physically driving to every site. They coordinate vetted local crews, staged kits, and live site status through the Project Command Center, our real-time deployment platform. You get one phone number and one dashboard for the entire program, whether it is 5 sites or 500.

Do you cover Alaska and Hawaii?

Yes — SRS Networks deploys across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, plus Washington, D.C. Alaska and Hawaii run through the Anchorage, Fairbanks, Honolulu, and Kahului markets, so a nationwide portfolio runs under one program.

How fast can you mobilize a crew for an urgent site?

Regional crews can be mobilized and on-site within roughly 48 hours of work-order release for urgent deployments, with kitted gear shipped from the nearest coast staging facility. For planned multi-site rollouts, mobilization is scheduled against your sequence so crews and material land together.

Where is SRS Networks based, and does that limit your reach?

### Write the room test before selecting the AV equipment

Audio visual integration connects displays, microphones, speakers, conferencing devices and controls around a defined room workflow. SRS coordinates the approved installation and commissioning scope so the room owner can verify the meeting experience before handover.

#### Select an audio visual contractor around the room workflow

An audio visual equipment installer mounts and connects hardware. Integration also needs clear ownership of control programming, conferencing accounts and acceptance tests. Ask the AV company to identify those responsibilities before comparing equipment lists.

#### Define AV support services separately from installation

Installation closeout should identify the support contact and the records that support team needs. For recurring support, agree which devices and software are covered, service hours, remote access and onsite escalation. Do not treat a project warranty as an unlimited managed service.

No Standardization Across the Organization

Complex Operation No One Can Figure Out

### Frequently Asked Questions — av-system-integration

Q: What does an audio visual integration company coordinate?
A: The project scope should connect equipment installation, cabling, programming and room acceptance. Identify who owns conferencing accounts and network settings so dependencies are ready for commissioning.

Q: Is an AV company the same as an equipment installer?
A: A hardware installer may cover mounting and connections only. Compare the room workflow, programming, user training and support handover included in each proposal.

Q: What belongs in conference room AV installation acceptance?
A: Run the agreed call, microphone, speaker, camera, content-share and control checks. Name the room owner who accepts the result and records any exceptions.

Q: Does AV installation include managed AV support services?
A: Recurring support requires a separate agreement defining covered systems, service hours and escalation. The installation scope should specify the handover records and any agreed user orientation.

Q: What changes an AV installation budget?
A: Room size, access, cable paths, equipment and control complexity affect the estimate. Price licenses, programming and ongoing support separately.

Q: Can existing AV equipment be reused?
A: List the models, condition and required workflow before deciding what to retain. Compatibility and performance must be verified against the approved room test.

Q: Who provides conferencing platform accounts?
A: The customer or designated platform provider owns accounts and permissions. Provide an authorized contact who can assist during commissioning without sharing credentials in the estimate request.

Q: How do repeated meeting rooms stay consistent?
A: Approve a room standard and commissioning checklist before scaling. Record each room\u2019s equipment, configuration handover and deviations from that standard.

Q: Who owns custom control programming?
A: Name the qualified programmer in the project scope. The physical installation crew needs an agreed handoff and room acceptance sequence.

## BANDWIDTH MANAGEMENT

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/bandwidth-management
Title: Bandwidth Management & QoS | SRS Networks
Description: Stop backups from dropping VoIP calls. QoS policy design, traffic shaping, application classification, and monitoring deployed across every site you operate.
─────────────────────────────────────────

VoIP Calls Drop During Peak Hours

Your phone system works fine at 8 a.m. and falls apart by 10 a.m. when the office fills up. VoIP is one of the most latency-sensitive applications on any network - and without QoS policies, it gets zero special treatment. The result is choppy audio, dropped calls, and end users routing around the system entirely.

Video Conferencing Degrades Under Load

Zoom, Teams, and Webex are real-time traffic. When a backup job or software update saturates your uplink at the same moment as a client call, video freezes and audio degrades. It's not a bandwidth problem - it's a prioritization problem. The wrong traffic is winning.

No Traffic Prioritization on the Network

A flat network with no QoS treats every packet identically - a file sync competes on equal footing with a patient video consult or a financial transaction. Without traffic classification and priority queuing, your most critical applications are at the mercy of whatever else happens to be running.

Bandwidth Hogs Are Killing Productivity

Cloud backups, OS updates, video streaming, and large file transfers can each fully saturate an internet connection. Without rate limiting and traffic shaping, a single runaway process can degrade performance for every user on the network until someone notices and manually intervenes.

No Visibility Into What Is Using Your Bandwidth

You know the network is slow. You don't know why. Without application-aware monitoring, you're troubleshooting blindly - guessing at root causes while end users pile up helpdesk tickets. Visibility into traffic by application, user, and device is the foundation of every QoS decision.

Application-aware QoS policies that identify and classify traffic at the network layer

Traffic shaping rules that rate-limit bulk and background traffic during business hours

DSCP marking and priority queuing that guarantee bandwidth for VoIP and video

Real-time bandwidth utilization dashboards by application, user, device, and VLAN

Configurable allocation per department, circuit, or traffic class - built around your workflow

We analyze your actual traffic patterns before writing a single policy rule. Every QoS configuration we deploy is built around how your network is actually used - VoIP vendors, video platforms, ERP systems, and cloud applications all identified and classified before policy enforcement begins.

Traffic analysis and application inventory

DSCP marking strategy by traffic class

Priority queue design and bandwidth reservation

Traffic Shaping & Rate Limiting

We configure traffic shaping policies that throttle low-priority traffic during peak hours without blocking it entirely. Bulk transfers, cloud sync, and software updates get their bandwidth - just not at the expense of the calls and transactions that drive your business.

Per-application upload and download rate limiting

Time-of-day shaping policies for business hours

Burst allowances for non-interactive traffic

Modern QoS requires deep packet inspection to identify encrypted and port-agnostic traffic. We configure application signatures and classification rules so your network recognizes Teams from a file sync, Salesforce from a software update, and routes each accordingly.

Layer 7 application identification and classification

Custom application signatures for line-of-business apps

Traffic class mapping to QoS queues

After deployment, you need proof it is working. We set up real-time dashboards that show bandwidth utilization by application, user, and circuit - so you can see QoS policies in effect, catch new bandwidth consumers before they become a problem, and make data-driven capacity decisions.

Real-time application bandwidth dashboards

Historical usage reports by traffic class

Alerting on threshold violations and policy exceptions

Branch offices sharing circuits for both unified communications and internet access need QoS policies that protect VoIP and video traffic from competing with everything else. We configure prioritization on every site simultaneously, with consistent policy across the organization.

Telemedicine, EHR traffic, and medical device communication all have strict latency and reliability requirements. We configure QoS policies that protect clinical applications from competing with guest Wi-Fi, administrative bulk transfers, and software update traffic.

Campus networks carry everything from video lectures and administrative systems to student streaming and social media. QoS separates instructional and administrative traffic from recreational use - so bandwidth for learning isn't cannibalized by unmanaged student traffic.

Hospitality & Property Management

Properties running operations, guest Wi-Fi, and POS systems on shared infrastructure need traffic policies that prevent guest usage from degrading the systems the property depends on to function. We configure segmentation and prioritization that keeps operations traffic protected.

We configure QoS at the network layer - not just a router checkbox, but a structured policy framework

Application classification built from actual traffic analysis, not generic templates
