### Frequently Asked Questions — it-rollout-pricing-models

Q: How are multi-site IT rollouts priced in 2026?
A: Under six models: per-site fixed unit pricing (a rate card by site archetype — the national-rollout standard), unit-rate schedules (per drop, per AP, per camera, per terminal), time and materials (discovery and remediation work only), not-to-exceed hybrids (T&M with a cap), milestone-based pricing (construction-linked projects), and national MSA rate structures (one rate card across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii). Most national programs of 25+ sites run on per-site fixed pricing, at 15-30% below single-site rates.

Q: What is per-site fixed unit pricing?
A: A rate card that assigns one fixed price per site archetype — for example, small retail/QSR at $7,500-$16,500 per site or branch offices at $9,500-$22,000, covering install labor and materials with network hardware excluded. The vendor carries site-level execution risk, and the buyer can budget a 100-site program by multiplying the rate by the site count.

Q: When does a unit-rate schedule beat per-site fixed pricing?
A: When per-site scope varies too much to standardize. A unit-rate schedule prices each unit of work — Cat6 drops at $175-295, Cat6A at $220-390, WiFi AP installs at $450-$900, IP cameras at $450-$1,100 installed, POS terminals at $350-$850 — and the invoice is units times rate. It fits refresh programs where one site needs 4 drops and the next needs 40.

Q: When is time and materials the right model?
A: Only for discovery and remediation work — cleaning up undocumented cabling, assessing unknown site conditions, or emergency fixes where scope cannot be defined up front. T&M puts all cost risk on the buyer, so a disciplined vendor moves the work to fixed or unit-rate pricing the moment scope becomes definable.

Q: What is a not-to-exceed (NTE) contract?
A: A hybrid: work bills as time and materials, but total cost is capped at an agreed ceiling. The buyer gets T&M flexibility with a worst-case number for budgeting, and the vendor carries the overrun risk above the cap. NTE fits remediation-heavy scopes where surveys have bounded the unknowns but not eliminated them.

Q: What is a national MSA rate structure?
A: A master service agreement with one rate card that holds across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii — per-site archetype rates plus published adders for tier-1 metros (+25-40%), prevailing-wage sites (+30-50%), and after-hours work (+25-50%). This is how SRS Networks prices national accounts: every regional cost variable becomes a published adder instead of a change-order negotiation.

Q: Who carries the cost risk under each pricing model?
A: Per-site fixed and milestone-based put execution risk on the vendor. Unit-rate splits it — the vendor owns the rate, the buyer owns the quantity. Time and materials puts nearly all risk on the buyer. Not-to-exceed shares it: buyer pays actuals up to the cap, vendor absorbs overruns above it. The model choice is really a decision about who is better positioned to control each risk.

Q: What red flags signal bad rollout pricing?
A: Four show up constantly: no published rate card (every site becomes a negotiation), unpriced revisit truck rolls (each one costs $450-$950, and industry first-visit completion runs only 85-92%), vague mobilization or travel line items, and missing after-hours terms on a program that will inevitably need overnight work at a +25-50% premium. If the pricing model does not name these, they surface later as change orders.

Q: How does SRS Networks structure a national rate card?
A: Per-site fixed rates by archetype under a national MSA, with published adders for tier-1 metros, prevailing wage, after-hours, and rush dispatch (+50-100%), plus program management at 8-12% of program cost. Every program starts with a 3-5 site pilot wave that validates the rate card against real site conditions before national waves launch. Rates are built from SRS Networks 2026 field data across 900+ multi-site deployments.

Q: Which costs affect the field estimate?
A: Mounting access, work windows, pathways, travel, device quantities and readiness gaps affect field labor. Platform licenses, calibration and application integration should be quoted separately by their assigned owners.

Q: How should a pilot become a multi-site deployment?

Messy, Unmanaged Cable Runs

Cables draped across ceiling tiles, bundled with zip ties at random intervals, running through walls with no documentation. Messy cabling isn't just ugly - it makes every future move, add, or change a troubleshooting nightmare.

No Labeling or Documentation

When nothing is labeled and no as-built drawings exist, every trace takes time. Technicians spend hours identifying which cable goes where before any actual work can begin. Downtime goes up; productivity goes down.

Code Violations and Inspection Failures

Low-voltage wiring has specific code requirements for conduit fill, bend radius, plenum-rated cable in air-handling spaces, and separation from high-voltage runs. Unlicensed or careless installs fail inspections and create liability.

Wrong Cable Types for the Application

Running Cat5e where Cat6A is required. Using non-plenum cable above a drop ceiling. Installing coax where fiber belongs. Using the wrong cable doesn't just hurt performance - it often means ripping it all out and starting over.

No Testing or Certification

Cables installed without Fluke or similar certification testing leave hidden faults undiscovered until they cause intermittent network drops, slow throughput, or security camera outages - usually at the worst possible time.

## MDF IDF BUILDOUT

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/mdf-idf-buildout
Title: MDF & IDF Room Buildout: Rack, Power, Cabling | SRS Networks
Description: Telecom rooms built right the first time — rack and cabinet install, cable management, power distribution, labeling, and documentation for every closet you own.
─────────────────────────────────────────

### Define MDF and IDF in the network-room context

In telecommunications, MDF means main distribution frame and IDF means intermediate distribution frame. The terms can also identify the rooms or cabinets housing distribution equipment. Unqualified acronym searches may have other meanings; this page addresses network infrastructure.

Q: How should an MDF-to-IDF connection be documented?
A: Identify endpoints, backbone links, terminations and required tests. Keep labels consistent with marked drawings and native test files.

Tangled Cables That Make Troubleshooting Impossible

When cables aren't labeled, managed, or documented, every outage becomes a forensics project. Tracing a mystery cable through a bundle of 50 to find a failing run can take hours - and the problem usually comes back because nothing was fixed at the root.

Equipment Overheating from Poor Airflow

Switches, patch panels, and UPS units generate heat. A closet without blanking panels, proper cable routing, or airflow planning runs hot - and equipment that runs hot fails early. Most telecom closet failures start with a thermal problem that was ignored.

Racks Built Without a Plan

Equipment mounted wherever it fits, cable trays absent or overflowing, half-populated racks with no room for growth. A rack that wasn't built with a plan is a rack that has to be completely rebuilt the next time something changes - costing far more than building it right the first time.

Power Distribution That Puts Equipment at Risk

Daisy-chained power strips, circuits shared between unrelated equipment, and no UPS protection leave your active gear vulnerable to surges, brownouts, and unexpected outages. In a properly built telecom room, every piece of active equipment is on protected, dedicated power.

No Room to Grow and No Capacity Planning

Telecom closets that weren't designed with expansion in mind hit their limits fast. When the rack is full, the patch panel is out of ports, and the circuit is maxed out, the only option is a costly emergency rebuild that could have been avoided with proper planning upfront.

Rack and cabinet installation built to TIA-568 standards with proper spacing and airflow

### Frequently Asked Questions — moves-adds-changes

Q: What do MAC, IMAC, and IMACD stand for?
A: MAC stands for moves, adds, and changes: the recurring physical-layer and device work an installed base generates after go-live. IMAC puts install at the front (install, move, add, change), and IMACD adds dispose at the end (install, move, add, change, dispose) to cover retiring the gear that comes out. Vendors use the three terms for the same ticket types; the practical difference is whether disposal is in the contract.

Q: How is a MAC ticket priced?
A: From the unit-rate schedule signed with the MSA, not negotiated ticket by ticket: a per-move rate, a per-drop rate, a per-device rate for swaps and adds, and a per-visit rate for disposal pickups. Site variables such as after-hours windows, escorts, and prevailing wage are flagged on the site record before dispatch so they do not arrive as change orders. NET 30 is standard, and we take no margin on hardware.

Q: What response time do you commit to on a MAC ticket?
A: Three tiers, stated as hours. P1: 4-hour onsite response, 24/7. P2: next business day onsite. P3: within five business days. Under about 50 miles in a dense metro a local shop will beat those numbers on drive time; across a multi-state installed base, dispatch latency matters more than drive time, and the ticket is already assigned while a local vendor is still being found.

Q: Do you update the as-builts after each ticket?
A: Yes, the same day the ticket closes. The port schedule, device inventory with serial numbers, and drawings held in the Project Command Center are updated from the tech's closeout photos and test results, so the next ticket at that site is scoped against the current plant rather than the original install. The record is yours to keep and exports by API into your PSA or CMDB.

Q: Can our MSP submit tickets under its own brand?
A: Yes. Techs work under your brand, closeout lands on your template, and your client sees a co-branded portal or a weekly export in your format. Non-solicitation of your end client is written into the MSA, and we do not resell hardware, software, or managed services, so there is nothing for us to pitch your client after the visit. Direct inquiries from your client route back to you every time.

Q: Do you handle disposal of the equipment that comes out?
A: Yes, as a disposal line on the ticket or as a scheduled pickup across a wave of sites. Retired switches, phones, PCs, and cameras leave the site with a serial-number inventory and a chain-of-custody record, then hand off to our IT asset disposal process. Data-bearing devices are logged separately so the sanitization record can be matched back to the ticket.

Q: How do you know the site layout before the tech arrives?
A: From the as-builts on file: closet photos, the port-to-panel schedule, the device inventory, and the drawings, all held per site in the Project Command Center. Sites we installed already have them. Sites we did not install get a documentation baseline visit first, and that record becomes the reference for every ticket that follows.

Q: Is there a minimum ticket volume?
A: No contractual minimum, and no registration fee for channel partners. The economics are the minimum: coordination overhead is roughly fixed per program, so below about 25 sites in one metro a local shop is cheaper and we will say so. The model pays back when the sites are spread across states or the ticket volume needs the same closeout record everywhere.

Q: Do you cover Alaska and Hawaii?
A: Yes. The 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, under one MSA and one rate structure. Alaska and Hawaii run through the Anchorage, Fairbanks, Honolulu, and Kahului markets on the same ticket flow and the same project manager as a mainland site; the only difference is materials lead time, shown as its own line on the schedule. Work is coordinated from South San Francisco HQ and offices in Salinas, Pasadena, Boise, Boston, and Dallas.

Q: Who actually shows up for the ticket?
A: An in-house W-2 SRS lead or a vetted W-9 sub from the bench, under 24-month agreements with a 150-mile non-compete, working to our runbook and labeling scheme. Every COI is audited in the Project Command Center against the site's limits, additional-insured language, and expiration before a truck rolls. A sub who cannot hold the standard at one site does not get the next one.

Q: What does a MAC ticket closeout include?
A: Photos of the work and the rack, the test result on any new or re-terminated link, the updated port schedule and device inventory, the labeling applied, and the site contact's signoff. It is delivered in the same format on every ticket at every site, in the Project Command Center, and it is the same closeout discipline used on the 900+ multi-site programs SRS has run since 1996.

Title: MPLS Network Solutions | SRS Networks

─────────────────────────────────────────

Unreliable Internet-Based Site Connectivity

Routing critical inter-office traffic over commodity internet means you're at the mercy of public congestion, packet loss, and unpredictable latency. It works until the moment it matters - and then it doesn't.

No Guaranteed Bandwidth Between Locations

Without committed information rate guarantees, your WAN traffic competes with everything else on the internet. During peak hours, ERP replication and VoIP degrade first - and there's nothing you can do about it.

Complex Carrier Contracts with No Technical Oversight

Carrier contracts are designed for procurement teams, not engineers. Most organizations sign multi-year MPLS agreements without anyone who understands what they're actually buying - or whether it's configured correctly.

Even when MPLS is in place, QoS misconfiguration means your class-of-service markings don't map correctly to carrier CoS labels. Voice and video traffic gets treated like bulk data - and the network performs accordingly.

No Clear Path Off Legacy MPLS

SD-WAN conversations stall because there's no structured migration plan. Cutting over without proper planning risks outages, misrouted traffic, and a worse user experience than the MPLS infrastructure you were trying to escape.

## MULTI BUILDING CONNECTIVITY

Each building operates as its own disconnected island. Staff moving between structures lose connectivity, shared resources are unavailable across buildings, and IT is stuck managing multiple independent systems with no common baseline.

Expensive Per-Building ISP Connections

Running a separate ISP circuit into every building multiplies your monthly bandwidth spend without multiplying performance. You're paying for redundancy you don't need when a shared campus backbone could serve every structure.

Without a unified network backbone, there's no single pane of glass. Switches, APs, and routers in each building are managed independently - which means more administrative overhead and more visibility blind spots.

Consumer or prosumer wireless bridges connecting buildings introduce latency, interference, and single points of failure. When the link drops, entire buildings lose connectivity and there's no redundant path to fall back on.

Inconsistent Performance Across Structures

Network quality varies dramatically from building to building. End users in outlying structures get a degraded experience compared to those in the main building - and there's no way to benchmark or enforce a consistent standard.

### Frequently Asked Questions — multi-site-it-deployment-cost

Q: How much does a multi-site IT deployment cost per site in 2026?
A: 2026 planning ranges on 25+ site programs: small retail/QSR $7,500-$16,500 per site, large-format retail $18,000-$48,000, restaurant full tech stack $12,000-$32,000, branch office $9,500-$22,000, medical clinic $14,000-$34,000, warehouse/distribution center $35,000-$120,000, and standard offices at $250-$450 per user. Ranges cover install labor and materials with network hardware excluded, and carry ±30% variance for site conditions.

Q: What is included in a per-site deployment price?
A: Per-site ranges cover install labor and install materials — cabling, mounting, termination, rack work, testing, and closeout documentation. Network hardware (switches, APs, cameras, POS terminals) is excluded unless stated. Program-level costs are layered separately: site surveys at $150-$1,200 per site, program management at 8-12% of program cost, staging and freight at 3-6% of hardware value, and a 10-15% contingency.

Q: How much cheaper is a multi-site program than single-site pricing?
A: Multi-site programs run 15-30% below single-site pricing at 25 or more sites, because mobilization, project management, and staging costs amortize across the program. Within a single site, volume also helps: 5-15% below list above 200 drops, and 10-20% at 1,000+ drops.

Q: What is the 25-site economic floor?
A: Roughly 25 sites is where a national deployment partner becomes cheaper than stitching together local contractors. Below that floor, per-site coordination overhead eats the margin a national partner would otherwise save you — which is why SRS Networks tells buyers under roughly 25 sites to hire a local shop instead.

Q: How much should we budget for program management?
A: Plan on 8-12% of total program cost for program management on a multi-site rollout — scheduling, site coordination, escalation handling, and closeout tracking across every location. On top of that, carry a 10-15% budget contingency for site-condition surprises inside the ±30% variance band.

Q: Do site surveys cost extra, and are they worth it?
A: Yes — remote surveys run $150-$400 per site and on-site surveys run $450-$1,200 (up to $1,500 in tier-1 metros). They are usually worth it: a single skipped survey that triggers one revisit truck roll ($450-$950) plus re-mobilization already exceeds the survey cost, and surveys prevent change orders inside the ±30% variance band.

Q: How do region and schedule change per-site cost?
A: Tier-1 metros (NYC, SF, Boston, Chicago) run 25-40% above national ranges, prevailing-wage projects add 30-50%, after-hours or overnight work adds 25-50%, and rush or emergency dispatch carries a 50-100% premium. A national rate card should publish each of these as an explicit adder, not bury them in change orders.

Q: Is network hardware included in deployment pricing?
A: No — the per-site ranges cover install labor and materials only; network hardware is priced separately. With dual-coast pre-staging, freight and logistics typically run 3-6% of hardware value, versus a roughly 1-in-6 site-visit failure rate (missing, wrong, or damaged gear) when hardware drop-ships direct to site. Datacom products purchased through SRS carry a 5-year bumper-to-bumper warranty.

Q: What failure costs should a rollout budget anticipate?
A: The big ones: revisit truck rolls at $450-$950 each (industry first-visit completion runs 85-92%; SRS targets 98%+ via dual-coast pre-staging), failed-COI stop-work incidents at $5K-$40K, and drop-ship failures hitting roughly 1 in 6 site visits without staging. A 10-15% contingency exists to absorb what remains.

Q: How does SRS Networks price a national deployment?
A: Per-site fixed unit pricing on a rate card by site archetype, structured under a national MSA — one rate structure across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii with published adders for tier-1 metros, prevailing wage, and after-hours work. Programs start with a 3-5 site pilot wave to validate the rate card before national waves. Ranges come from SRS Networks 2026 field data across 900+ multi-site deployments.

### Frequently Asked Questions — multi-site-rollout-budgeting-guide

Q: How do I budget a multi-site technology rollout in 2026?
A: Price the per-site install first from a rate card by site archetype, then layer program costs: site surveys at $150-$400 per site remote or $450-$1,200 on-site, staging and logistics at 3-6% of hardware value, program management at 8-12% of total program cost, and a 10-15% contingency. Network hardware is budgeted as its own line. Run a 3-5 site pilot wave before committing national waves.

Q: What percentage should program management add to a rollout budget?
A: 8-12% of total program cost. That line covers scheduling, dispatch, escalation, vendor and site coordination, and closeout tracking across every wave. Budgets that skip it do not avoid the cost — they absorb it as overrun, missed windows, and revisit truck rolls at $450-$950 each.

Q: How much contingency should a multi-site rollout budget carry?
A: Carry 10-15% of program cost as contingency. Per-site ranges carry ±30% variance for site conditions, region, and scope, so some sites will land above the rate-card midpoint no matter how well you plan. Draw contingency only on approved change orders and return it if unspent — it is insurance, not a slush line.

Q: What does a 100-site retail network refresh cost in 2026?
A: Roughly $2.0M-$2.4M as a total funded program. The math: 100 sites at the $12,000 small-retail install midpoint is $1.2M of labor and materials; add on-site surveys (about $60,000 at $600 per site), a hardware allowance, staging at 3-6% of hardware value, program management at 8-12%, and a 10-15% contingency, and the program lands at $2.0M-$2.4M depending on contingency draw.

Q: Should we run a pilot wave before the national rollout?
A: Yes — deploy 3-5 sites before committing national waves. The pilot validates scope assumptions, install timing, closeout documentation, and the per-site number itself against real site conditions. Pilot actuals are what let you lock a per-site fixed rate card with confidence before regional waves begin.

Q: How much should site surveys add to the budget?
A: Remote surveys run $150-$400 per site; on-site surveys run $450-$1,200 per site, up to $1,500 in tier-1 metros. Surveys are how you shrink the ±30% site-condition variance band before the rate card locks instead of paying for surprises as change orders after it.

Q: What should we budget for staging, freight, and logistics?
A: 3-6% of hardware value with pre-staging at coastal facilities. Without staging, roughly 1 in 6 drop-shipped site visits hits missing, wrong, or damaged gear — and each failed visit triggers a $450-$950 revisit truck roll. Staged logistics is one of the cheapest lines in the budget relative to what it prevents.

Q: What do revisit truck rolls cost if a site fails the first visit?
A: $450-$950 per revisit, plus the schedule slip. Industry first-visit completion runs 85-92%, which means an unmanaged 100-site program should expect 8-15 revisits. SRS targets 98%+ first-visit completion through dual-coast pre-staging and per-site work packages, which is why the revisit line stays small on SRS programs.

Q: When should we lock the per-site rate card?
A: After the 3-5 site pilot wave and before regional waves begin. Pilot actuals prove or correct the per-site number; locking the card at that point means every remaining site prices off a fixed rate by archetype — no per-site renegotiation, no quote drift, and a budget finance can forecast to the end of the program.

Q: Is a national rollout budget worth building below 25 sites?
A: Usually not. Roughly 25 sites is the national-rollout economic floor — below it, per-site coordination overhead eats the margin a national partner brings, and SRS tells buyers to hire a good local contractor instead. At 25+ sites the math flips: multi-site programs run 15-30% below single-site pricing, and the full line-item structure starts paying for itself.

## MULTI TENANT NETWORKING

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/multi-tenant-networking
Title: Multi-Tenant Network Design | SRS Networks
Description: VLAN-isolated networks for office buildings, MDUs, and co-working floors — per-tenant bandwidth control and one portal for the property team to see it all.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Tenants Sharing a Flat Network

When every tenant lands on the same unmanaged network, business traffic, guest devices, and personal use all compete on equal footing. There is no isolation, no control, and no way to enforce any policy that actually sticks.

No Traffic Isolation Between Businesses

Tenant A can see Tenant B's devices. In a legal office, a medical practice, or a financial firm, that is a compliance exposure. Flat shared networks are a liability masquerading as a convenience.

Bandwidth Hogging by One Tenant

One tenant runs a video production studio and saturates the entire shared uplink. Every other tenant suffers. Without per-tenant bandwidth allocation, there is no fair use - just whoever uses the most wins.

Security Liability Across Tenants

A compromised device on one tenant's network can propagate laterally to every other tenant on the same broadcast domain. Property owners and operators inherit that liability whether they built the network or not.

No Per-Tenant Monitoring or Visibility

When a tenant reports a problem, you have no data. No per-tenant traffic logs, no utilization baselines, no way to diagnose issues beyond walking the floor. Management without visibility is just guessing.

We design the full logical architecture before a single cable is run. Network topology, VLAN structure, uplink capacity, and management access are all planned around the property's tenant mix and long-term occupancy model.

### Frequently Asked Questions — national-vs-regional-deployment-vendor-cost

Q: Is one national vendor cheaper than multiple regional contractors?
A: It depends on site count, and the honest answer cuts both ways. Below roughly 25 sites, regional contractors usually cost less — local shops carry no program overhead and their market rates win. Above roughly 25 sites the math flips: multi-site programs run 15-30% below single-site pricing, one MSA rate card replaces dozens of market quotes, and vendor-management overhead stops multiplying with every added contractor.

Q: What is the 25-site economic floor?
A: Roughly 25 sites is the point where a national deployment partner starts making economic sense. Below it, per-site coordination overhead eats the margin a national vendor needs to run the program, so the buyer ends up paying for structure the job does not need. SRS Networks tells buyers below the floor to hire a local shop — and answers the question that way in its own RFP responses.

Q: How much cheaper is multi-site program pricing than single-site pricing?
A: Multi-site programs at 25+ sites run 15-30% below single-site pricing in 2026, because mobilization, project management, and staging are amortized across the whole program instead of loaded onto each site. Single-site volume discounts are smaller: 5-15% below list above 200 drops on one site, and 10-20% at 1,000+ drops.

Q: What does managing multiple regional vendors actually cost?
A: Every added vendor multiplies overhead: a contract to negotiate, COIs to track (auditing runs about $40 per site, and a failed-COI stop-work costs $5,000-40,000), separate invoicing to reconcile, and a different workmanship standard to QA. That cost rarely appears on any quote — it shows up as internal staff time, which is why stitched-vendor programs look cheaper on paper than they run in practice.

Q: Why does rate consistency matter on a national program?
A: Because regional market rates swing hard: tier-1 metros like NYC, SF, Boston, and Chicago run 25-40% above national, and prevailing-wage sites add another 30-50%. Stitch ten regional contractors together and you get ten rate structures moving independently. A national MSA rate card fixes per-site pricing by site archetype across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, so the budget you approve in January is the budget you close in December.

Q: When do regional contractors beat a national partner?
A: Below the 25-site economic floor, in a single dense market, and for ongoing hands-on local support. If all your sites sit in one metro, a good regional shop mobilizes faster and cheaper than any national program structure — SRS Networks says so directly and declines work below the floor rather than pricing structure the job does not need.

Q: Does a national partner just mark up local labor?
A: Program management on a professionally run national rollout costs 8-12% of program cost, and you pay for coordination either way — as a visible line item with a national partner, or as internal staff time managing contracts, COIs, invoices, and QA across regional vendors. The difference is that a national partner prices it, targets 98%+ first-visit completion, and owns the misses; self-managed coordination is unpriced and open-ended.

Q: How does hardware staging change the national vs regional comparison?
A: Staging is where the models diverge most. Drop-shipping hardware direct to sites — the default in a stitched regional model — fails on roughly 1 in 6 site visits with missing, wrong, or damaged gear, and each failure is a $450-950 revisit. Routing hardware through staging costs 3-6% of hardware value. SRS Networks pre-stages every national program at its West Coast and East Coast facilities and targets 98%+ first-visit completion.

Q: How does SRS Networks price national deployment programs?
A: One national MSA rate structure: a fixed per-site rate card by site archetype that holds across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, with survey, staging, program management (8-12%), and revisit pricing stated up front. Multi-site programs at 25+ sites price 15-30% below single-site rates, and SRS recommends carrying a 10-15% contingency. Rate cards and wave schedules come from field data across 900+ multi-site deployments since 1996.

### Turn the deployment service into an accepted site program

Technology deployment services coordinate the physical installation and activation of equipment across business locations. A rollout scope connects site readiness, staged materials, field work and acceptance records so each location can be handed over on the same terms.

#### What a deployment service must hand over

A dispatched technician is one part of a deployment. Ask for a site-specific work order, equipment custody record, approved test plan and an escalation route. When a building differs from the pilot, record the change before repeating it across the next wave.

#### Separate installation from operation

Decide who prepares device configurations, approves network changes and supports the application after handover. A successful hardware installation does not prove that every business workflow has been accepted; the application owner must participate in the agreed checks.

Repeatable scope: A sample site work order with exclusions and readiness requirements.
Exception control: A documented hold, approval and return-visit process.
Acceptance record: A sample closeout package tied to a device and location.

- Approved equipment list and staging responsibility
- Operating hours, access contacts and cutover windows

This scope covers physical technology deployment. Application development, software release pipelines, platform subscriptions and ongoing support require separate ownership and agreement.

Your project manager owns the fix and tells you before anyone on site does, with a plan attached. ## NETWORK ACCESS CONTROL

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/network-access-control
Title: Network Access Control (NAC) | SRS Networks
Description: Enterprise network access control solutions. 802.1X authentication, RADIUS deployment, endpoint compliance, and guest access management by SRS Networks.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Any Device Can Plug In and Connect

Without port-based access control, any laptop, personal phone, or rogue device that hits an open jack or connects to your wireless gets network access. You have no say in it.

No Visibility Into What's Connected

Most networks have zero device inventory at the port level. You don't know if it's a corporate laptop, a contractor's tablet, a printer, or something that doesn't belong there.

Rogue Devices Are a Real Threat

An unauthorized device that lands on your corporate segment - intentional or not - can scan the network, move laterally, and exfiltrate data before anyone notices. NAC stops that.

Guest Traffic Mixed with Corporate

If your guest Wi-Fi isn't isolated, visitors are on the same segment as your file servers and internal apps. One compromised guest device is a direct path into your environment.

Compliance Failures from Uncontrolled Access

HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and SOC 2 all require demonstrable network access controls. Without NAC, you can't prove which devices accessed sensitive segments - and that means audit failures.

Red-Line in the Field, Daily

The crew lead marks deviations the day they happen — a drop that moved, a pathway rerouted around a duct, a sleeve added, a run that came in longer than designed. Each red-line carries a date and the technician who made it, so the final drafting has an audit trail instead of a guess.

Rough-In Verification Before Close-Up

Before ceilings and drywall close, we photograph and verify pathway, support spacing, penetrations, and firestop. This is the only window that exists for it. Once the building closes, anything undocumented above the grid stays undocumented until somebody cuts a hole.

Terminate, Label, and Build the Map

The port-to-outlet map is built as the terminations happen, not from the design schedule. Outlet, cable, panel port, rack, and room are recorded together at the moment the link is landed, and labels go on to the TIA-606-B scheme already registered in step one.

Certify and Bind Results to the Record

Copper is certified on a Fluke DSX in permanent link configuration and fiber gets Tier 1 loss testing plus Tier 2 OTDR traces where the spec calls for it. Results are exported with label IDs intact and joined to the port map so every row in the record carries its own evidence.

Draft Red-Lines Into Final CAD

A drafter incorporates the field red-lines into the CAD set and we QA the drawings against the test data and the photo record. If a link exists in the drawing but not in the test file, or the reverse, it gets resolved before the package leaves us. That reconciliation is where most as-builts fail.

Issue and Walk the Closeout Package

You receive the full package — PDF, DWG, CSV, tester exports, photos, warranty certificate — and we walk your team through it on a call or on site. Punch items are closed against the record, and your network group knows how to read the map before the contractor leaves the property.

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-as-built-documentation

Q: What is included in a network as-built documentation package?
A: A complete package has eight parts: floor plans showing drop locations, outlet IDs, pathway routing and firestop penetrations as installed; front and rear rack elevations at true RU positions; a port-to-outlet map with one row per link; a backbone and riser schematic with strand counts and splice points; the ANSI/TIA-606-B labeling schedule and issued-identifier register; per-link certification test results; a bill of materials with part numbers and the warranty registration; and a photo record of rough-in, pathway, grounding, and finished racks. If any one of those is missing, the package will not survive the first move, add, or change your team tries to make from it.

Q: What is the difference between as-built documentation and the original design drawings?
A: Design drawings show what was planned before anyone opened a ceiling. As-builts show what is actually in the building after the work is done. On a real project those two sets always differ, because drops move around casework, pathways reroute around mechanical, run lengths come in longer than estimated, and rack layouts change once the equipment physically arrives. A package that is just the issued-for-construction set with a new title block is not an as-built, and it is the single most common substitution buyers accept without noticing.

Q: What file formats do you deliver the as-built package in?
A: PDF binder for distribution, native DWG or CAD files for the floor plans, rack elevations, and backbone one-line, CSV for the port-to-outlet map, and the original Fluke project files and OTDR traces rather than screenshots of them. You also get the photo archive named to the same identifiers used in the drawings. Documentation you cannot edit is documentation you will pay someone to recreate, so we hand over the editable and importable files, not just a flattened set.

Q: How does the red-line to final drawing workflow actually run?
A: We baseline the issued-for-construction set at mobilization and register the outlet, rack, panel, and telecom room identifiers we will use. From there the crew lead red-lines deviations the day they happen, with a date and the technician's name attached. Before ceilings and drywall close we photograph and verify pathway, support spacing, and penetrations, because that window never reopens. At the end a drafter incorporates the red-lines into the CAD set, and we reconcile the drawings against the certification data and the photo record before anything ships.

Q: Are cable certification test results part of the as-built record?
A: Yes, and they are bound to it rather than filed beside it. Copper links are certified on a Fluke DSX in permanent link configuration and fiber gets Tier 1 insertion loss testing plus Tier 2 OTDR traces where the specification calls for it. Results are exported with label IDs intact and joined to the port map, so any row in the record traces to its own pass result and margin value. A summary that says all links passed, with no per-link records behind it, is a claim rather than evidence and will not satisfy a manufacturer warranty submission.

Q: Can you produce as-built documentation for a network somebody else installed?
A: Yes. That work starts as a field survey rather than a red-line exercise: we trace and identify the existing plant, apply a TIA-606-B labeling scheme, certify the links so the record has test data behind it, and draft the drawings and port map from what we find. It is slower and more expensive than documenting during a build, which is exactly why it is worth insisting on a real as-built the first time. For a full inventory of an inherited environment, our IT infrastructure audit covers the wider network alongside the cable plant.

Q: What is a port-to-outlet map and why do network teams care so much about it?
A: It is the table that says which faceplate in which room lands on which patch panel port in which rack. One row per horizontal link, carrying outlet ID, room and floor, cable ID, panel and port, rack, telecom room, media type, length, and test status. It is the artifact your team touches every single time they add a device, chase a fault, or plan a switch refresh. When it is built from the design schedule instead of from the terminations, the errors do not surface at handover — they surface months later when someone patches the wrong port and takes a floor down.

Q: When during a project do we receive the as-built package?
A: The package is issued at closeout, but it is produced throughout the build rather than assembled afterward. While the job is running, your team can watch the record fill in through the Project Command Center instead of waiting until demobilization to find out what you are getting. At handover we walk your network group through the drawings, the map, and the test data on a call or on site, and punch items get closed against the record. That way the people who will operate the infrastructure understand how to read it before the crew leaves the property.

Q: Do you deliver the same as-built format across a multi-site rollout?
A: Yes, and that consistency is most of the value at scale. One identifier scheme, one drawing standard, one CSV column structure, and one folder layout applied identically to every site on the program, coordinated out of a single project manager rather than left to whichever crew happened to work that location. On a single building documentation quality is a preference. Across ninety sites it decides whether you have a network your team can operate or ninety separate mysteries.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the local Salinas IT provider?
A: No. SRS Networks (srsnetworks.com) is the nationwide enterprise infrastructure deployment business, delivering structured cabling, certified fiber, and as-built documentation across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996, with offices in Salinas, South San Francisco, Pasadena, Boise, Boston, and Dallas plus West and East Coast staging facilities. It is a separate company from any local Salinas or Monterey managed IT services provider. If you need one contractor to deploy and document infrastructure across a multi-site footprint, that is us.

## NETWORK BID COMPARISON TEMPLATE

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/network-bid-comparison-template
Title: Network Installation Bid Comparison Template | SRS Networks
Description: Download a network bid comparison template for leveling scope, exclusions, unit rates, schedule, testing, documentation, risk, and normalized project price.
─────────────────────────────────────────

A network bid comparison should normalize base scope, exclusions, allowances, unit rates, schedule, field coverage, testing, documentation, commercial terms, and price. Never compare the submitted totals until every bidder is leveled to the same scope. The apparent low bid often moves after omitted lifts, surveys, testing, travel, or project management are restored.

Bid-leveling scorecard

Scope

Included, excluded, allowance, or unclear

0–25

Execution

Crew model, coverage, waves, and escalation

0–20

Evidence

Testing, photos, as-builts, and signoff

0–20

Commercial

Total, units, terms, and validity

0–20

Risk

COIs, dependencies, site rules, and exceptions

0–15

Turn narratives into yes or no

Map every requirement to included, excluded, allowance, or unclear. Do not let a polished proposal substitute for a line-by-line compliance response.

Price the exceptions

Add a reasonable value for each excluded requirement before comparing totals. An exclusion has a cost even when the bidder leaves the number blank.

Record the award logic

Keep evaluator scores, clarifications, normalized totals, and the final rationale together. That record matters when the first change request arrives.

Download Fillable PDF

154 interactive fields for price leveling, scoring and award rationale.

https://srsnetworks.com/downloads/SRS_Network_Bid_Comparison_Template_v1.0_FILLABLE.pdf

When this is not the right approach

When all bidders use a fixed master-service rate card and the site scope is identical, a full scorecard is unnecessary. Compare availability, exceptions, and estimated hours.

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-bid-comparison-template

Q: Can I download the network bid comparison template?
A: Yes. The page provides a free, ungated print-ready PDF and a fillable PDF with interactive form fields. No email address or account is required.

Q: What is the short answer on network bid comparison template?
A: A network bid comparison should normalize base scope, exclusions, allowances, unit rates, schedule, field coverage, testing, documentation, commercial terms, and price. Never compare the submitted totals until every bidder is leveled to the same scope. The apparent low bid often moves after omitted lifts, surveys, testing, travel, or project management are restored.

Q: What information should be collected before starting network bid comparison template?

Network cabling company FAQs

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-cabling-companies

Q: How should I compare network cabling companies?
A: Compare companies against the same requirements matrix: survey assumptions, included scope, field-delivery model, insurance controls, materials, testing, labels, documentation, schedule ownership, escalation, exclusions, unit rates, billing milestones, and warranty terms. Verify claims with current artifacts and references.

Q: What evidence should a cabling company provide before award?
A: Ask for a redacted closeout package, native sample test results, the proposed test-equipment list and calibration status, an escalation workflow, a field-resource verification process, relevant references, current insurance evidence, and a line-by-line scope compliance response.

Q: Is the lowest network cabling bid usually the best value?
A: Not necessarily. First restore omitted surveys, lifts, travel, after-hours access, testing, project management, documentation, revisits, and material assumptions to a normalized total. A low submitted price can become expensive when exclusions are discovered after award.

Q: When should I use a nationwide rather than local cabling company?
A: A nationwide company is most useful when several markets or repeated sites need one scope standard, one escalation owner, consistent testing and closeout, centralized reporting, and coordinated scheduling. One small local project may be better served by a qualified local commercial contractor.

Q: What multi-site controls matter most?
A: Look for controlled site intake, readiness checks, repeatable material kits, named project and field leadership, exception escalation, live status reporting, quality review, failed-test correction, material reconciliation, punch ownership, and a consistent closeout package for every location.

Q: How does SRS Networks compare?
A: SRS Networks is headquartered in South San Francisco and has completed 900+ deployments across 10,000+ sites. SRS combines in-house W-2 field leads with a vetted subcontractor bench, dual-coast staging, and centralized project reporting across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Q: Does SRS provide ongoing managed IT after cabling installation?
A: No. This service covers project-based physical infrastructure deployment and closeout. Ongoing help desk, managed IT, and application administration remain with the client or its technology partner unless a separate written project scope explicitly states otherwise.

Q: How should warranties and commercial terms be compared?
A: Compare the written manufacturer coverage, installer obligations, exclusions, correction process, billing milestones, payment terms, proposal validity, change authorization, and unit rates. SRS terms depend on the executed MSA and project authorization; warranty coverage depends on the selected products and written agreement.

Q: How should I use a network cabling directory?
A: Use it to assemble a shortlist, then verify each firm's fit for your site list and work window. Request comparable scope and sample turnover evidence before making an award.

Q: What evidence should network cabling companies provide before award?
A: Ask for a redacted cable schedule, test file, marked drawing and correction process. Confirm the named project and field owners and how excluded work is handled.

Failed Audits With No Roadmap to Remediate

Compliance Gaps You Don't Know Exist

Most organizations have compliance gaps they simply haven't discovered yet. Misconfigured firewalls, improper network segmentation, missing encryption on data in transit, undocumented system access - the gaps that auditors find first are often the ones nobody was looking for.

No Documentation to Support Your Compliance Posture

Inconsistent Security Controls Across Systems

When security configurations differ between departments, locations, or systems, you create unpredictable compliance exposure. One misconfigured switch, one unpatched device, or one undocumented exception can undermine an otherwise compliant environment.

Regulatory Penalties and Contractual Risk

HIPAA fines, PCI-DSS assessments, and contract requirements tied to SOC 2 reports are not hypothetical risks - they have real dollar values attached. Organizations that operate without a current compliance audit are carrying liability they may not even be aware of.

Cables Left in Ceilings and Walls

No Documentation of What Was Removed

Without a formal decommission record, there's no chain of custody and no asset reconciliation. Finance can't close out the equipment, IT doesn't know what left the building, and compliance has nothing to show an auditor.

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-documentation-services

Q: What do I actually receive at the end of a network documentation engagement?
A: Six artifacts per site: as-built floor plans with every drop keyed to its jack ID, port maps correlating switch port to patch panel position to faceplate ID, rack elevations at 1U granularity front and rear, cable schedules carrying cable ID and origin and destination and length, an IDF and MDF record sheet per room, and a system-ready export. Drawings come as DWG and PDF, tabular records as XLSX and CSV. Every file carries a revision number, a date, and a change log entry. The labels themselves are installed in the field as part of the same engagement, so the record and the rack read the same way.

Q: We have 200 sites and almost no records. How do you document an estate that size without shutting anything down?
A: Nothing we do requires downtime. We start from the network rather than the building, pulling LLDP and CDP neighbor tables, interface descriptions, MAC address tables, and ARP data per site to build the logical map, which costs you nothing operationally. Field technicians then verify it in person, confirming panel and port counts, photographing racks, and toning only the runs the data could not prove. Sites are sequenced in waves so your team is never coordinating more than a handful at a time, and a typical estate of that size runs as a rolling program rather than a single event.

Q: How is this different from network consulting or an IT infrastructure audit?
A: They answer different questions. Network consulting tells you what to do next and delivers a decision. An IT infrastructure audit tells you what is wrong and delivers a punch list of findings and remediation scope. Network documentation tells you what you have, port by port, and delivers a record your team operates from every day. Buyers frequently ask for an audit when the real gap is that nobody can find a drop, and that is a documentation problem, not an assessment problem.

Q: What labeling standard do you use, and do you install the labels or just design the scheme?
A: We label to ANSI/TIA-606-B and we install. The scheme is sized to the estate using the standard's administration classes, from Class 1 for a single telecom room up to Class 4 for a multi-campus footprint, and it covers cables, termination hardware, pathways, spaces, and grounding busbars rather than just ports. Labels are printed on thermal-transfer stock with self-laminating vinyl wraps for interior cable and heat-shrink for outside plant, so they survive handling and do not curl off a jacket in eighteen months. Handing over a naming convention and expecting site staff to apply it is how twelve different schemes get invented across forty sites.

Q: How do you keep the documentation current after the project closes?
A: Through a recurring moves-adds-changes program tied to your change process. When a port is repatched, a switch is swapped, or a drop is added, the update lands in the document set within an agreed SLA window and the revision and change log are updated with it. Without that, documentation is accurate on the day it ships and drifting by month three, which is why so many organizations are on their second or third documentation project. The maintenance program is usually the cheapest line on the engagement and the one that determines whether the first line was worth spending.

Q: Can you document infrastructure that another vendor installed?
A: That is most of what we document. Inherited plant is the normal case: the original installer is out of business, the drawings were never delivered, or four acquisitions each brought their own conventions. We treat the field as the source of truth and verify everything rather than trusting legacy paperwork. Where we genuinely cannot prove a path, we flag it as unverified instead of guessing, because three honest unknowns are far more useful to your team than thirty confident errors.

Q: What file formats do you deliver, and can the output load into our DCIM or CMDB?
A: Drawings ship as DWG and PDF, and tabular records as XLSX and CSV. For the system import we map field names and value formats to the schema your platform expects, whether that is a NetBox rack and device model, a Device42 import template, or a ServiceNow CMDB class, so ingestion is a load rather than a manual re-keying project. Tell us the target system at scoping and we shape the export to it. If you have no system yet, the delivered files stand on their own and remain usable in Excel and any DWG viewer.

Q: Do you document fiber backbone and outside plant, or only horizontal copper?
A: Both. Backbone documentation covers riser paths, conduit and innerduct occupancy, strand assignments per pair, splice points and enclosure locations, and the OTDR and insertion-loss records for each certified run. Outside plant adds handhole and vault locations, route drawings, and heat-shrink labeling that survives the environment. Backbone is usually the least documented part of an estate and the most expensive to get wrong, since a single undocumented strand assignment can turn a routine cutover into an outage.

Q: How long does documenting a site take, and how is it priced?
A: A single-IDF site with a few hundred drops is typically one technician day for the field survey plus publication time. A multi-IDF campus runs longer and is scoped per room. Pricing is at the project level driven by site count, drop and port counts, IDF count, how much usable legacy record exists, and whether labeling installation and a maintenance program are in scope. We quote after a walkthrough or a review of your site list and floor plans, generally within three to five business days of receiving them.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the local Salinas IT provider?
A: No. SRS Networks at srsnetworks.com is the nationwide enterprise infrastructure deployment business, delivering network documentation, structured cabling, and multi-site deployment across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996 from offices in Salinas, South San Francisco, Pasadena, Boise, Boston, and Dallas. It is a separate company from any local Salinas or Monterey managed IT services provider. If you need one documentation standard applied identically across a national footprint, that is the work we do.

Field Technicians Configuring On-Site

### Normalize scope before comparing per-site prices

Network installation cost depends on actual site requirements. Separate equipment, cabling, access, labor and commissioning. Compare identical quantities, work windows and exclusions; a small-office example is not an enterprise program budget.

Q: Which assumptions belong beside an estimate?
A: Record device counts, cable quantities, readiness, work windows and acceptance work. Identify travel and revisit assumptions separately.

2,500-5,000 sq ft · 8-16 drops · 2-4 APs

Cat6 drops to POS lanes, back office, and pickup screens, plus AP mounting and provisioning and a clean backboard or wall-mount rack. Adding a typical retail camera package of 8-16 cameras runs another $6,000-$16,000 installed.

15,000-60,000 sq ft · 24-60 drops · 8-20 APs

Sales floor, stockroom, and receiving coverage push both drop counts and AP counts up. Longer home runs and lift work move sites toward the top of the range.

The densest small-footprint archetype. POS installs run $350-$850 per terminal, and a typical QSR site with 3-6 terminals lands at $2,500-$7,500 for POS work alone before kitchen display, menu boards, and drive-thru cabling.

Branch office / bank branch

2,000-6,000 sq ft · 12-24 drops

Teller lines, platform desks, and ATM/ITM connections. Security requirements — escorted access, after-hours windows — are the usual reason a branch lands above the midpoint.

3,000-10,000 sq ft · 20-40 drops

Exam rooms, nurse stations, and imaging pull drop counts higher than square footage suggests. Occupied-space work and infection-control protocols add labor hours.

Warehouse / distribution center

50,000-300,000 sq ft · high-density WiFi + IDFs

The number is driven by WiFi density and backbone, not drop count. AP installs run $450-$900 each at height, and a fiber backbone from the MDF to 2-4 IDFs runs $8,000-$25,000 per building.

Per-user basis · cabling, switching, WiFi, rack

Offices price cleanest per user. Alternate framing: $1.50-$4.50 per sq ft for structured cabling only, or $3.00-$8.00 per sq ft for full network infrastructure. Full office math is on the office cost page below.

Tier-1 metros (NYC, SF, Boston, Chicago) run 25-40% above national ranges. Prevailing-wage scopes add another 30-50%.

After-hours and overnight work adds 25-50% (1.25x-1.5x labor). Rush or emergency dispatch adds 50-100%.

Drops, APs, cameras, and terminals per site are the core unit counts. A 40-drop clinic and a 12-drop branch are different jobs even at the same square footage.

Without pre-staging, roughly 1 in 6 site visits hits missing, wrong, or damaged gear. Staged freight runs 3-6% of hardware value and protects the schedule.

Multi-site programs at 25+ sites run 15-30% below single-site pricing because mobilization, staging, and management amortize across sites.

Ceiling type, pathway, riser access, and occupied-space constraints drive the ±30% variance band. Surveys ($150-$400 remote, $450-$1,200 on-site) tighten it.

Roughly 25 sites is where a national deployment partner starts beating local contractors — multi-site pricing runs 15-30% below single-site rates. Below that floor, per-site coordination overhead eats the margin, and SRS tells buyers to hire a local shop.

At 100 sites the rate card is locked by archetype, gear pre-stages at West and East Coast facilities, and waves sequence by region. Per-site cost stabilizes because surprises get engineered out, not priced in.

At 500+ sites, pricing moves to a national MSA rate structure — one rate card across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii, so site 400 prices the same way site 4 did. This is how SRS prices national accounts.

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-installation-cost-per-site

Q: What does network installation cost per site in 2026?
A: In 2026, network installation runs $7,500-$16,500 per site for small retail/QSR, $18,000-$48,000 for large-format retail, $12,000-$32,000 for a restaurant's full tech stack, $9,500-$22,000 for a branch office, $14,000-$34,000 for a medical clinic, and $35,000-$120,000 for a warehouse or distribution center. Standard offices run $250-$450 per user. Ranges cover install labor and materials on 25+ site programs, with ±30% site-condition variance; network hardware is excluded.

Q: What is included in a per-site network installation price?
A: Install labor and install materials: cable drops, AP mounting and provisioning, rack or backboard work, POS lane and camera cabling where scoped, testing, labeling, and closeout documentation. Network hardware — switches, APs, controllers — is excluded unless stated. Site surveys, staging and freight, program management, and contingency are budgeted as separate program-level lines.

Q: Is network hardware included in these per-site ranges?
A: No. The per-site ranges cover install labor and install materials only. Hardware is scoped separately because stacks vary — for example, enterprise WiFi AP hardware runs $400-$1,200 per AP on top of the $450-$900 per-AP install. Budget hardware as its own line, plus 3-6% of hardware value for staging, freight, and logistics.

Q: How much does a small retail or QSR site cost to install?
A: $7,500-$16,500 per site in 2026 for a typical 2,500-5,000 sq ft location with 8-16 drops and 2-4 APs, covering install labor and materials on a 25+ site program. Adding a typical retail camera package of 8-16 cameras runs another $6,000-$16,000 installed, and POS installs add $350-$850 per terminal.

Q: How much does a warehouse network installation cost?
A: $35,000-$120,000 per building in 2026 for a 50,000-300,000 sq ft warehouse or distribution center. The number is driven by high-density WiFi and backbone rather than drop count: AP installs run $450-$900 each (much of it at height), and a fiber backbone from the MDF to 2-4 IDFs runs $8,000-$25,000 per building.

Q: How is office network installation priced?
A: Offices price cleanest per user: $250-$450 per user in 2026 for network installation. Alternate framings: $1.50-$4.50 per sq ft for structured cabling only, or $3.00-$8.00 per sq ft for full network infrastructure (cabling, switching, WiFi, rack). A 2,000-6,000 sq ft branch office with 12-24 drops runs $9,500-$22,000 per site.

Q: Do per-site costs go down on multi-site programs?
A: Yes. Multi-site programs run 15-30% below single-site pricing at 25+ sites because mobilization, staging, and program management amortize across the portfolio. Single-site volume helps too: 200+ drops on one site prices 5-15% below list, and 1,000+ drops prices 10-20% below. Ask for a multi-site rate card, not a one-site quote.

Q: What pushes a site to the top of its price range?
A: Tier-1 metros (NYC, SF, Boston, Chicago) run 25-40% above national ranges and prevailing wage adds 30-50%. After-hours or overnight work adds 25-50%, and rush or emergency dispatch adds 50-100%. Hard-lid ceilings, difficult pathways, and escorted access do the rest — that is the ±30% site-condition variance band.

Q: Why does SRS recommend a local contractor below 25 sites?
A: Because roughly 25 sites is the national-rollout economic floor. Below it, per-site coordination overhead eats the margin a national partner brings, and a good local shop will usually beat national pricing on jobs below that floor. At 25+ sites the math flips: multi-site programs run 15-30% below single-site pricing.

Q: How accurate are these 2026 per-site ranges?
A: They are 2026 national planning ranges from SRS Networks field data across 900+ multi-site deployments — not survey data or industry averages. Carry ±30% variance for site conditions, region, and scope, and tighten it with site surveys: $150-$400 per site remote or $450-$1,200 on-site before the rate card locks.

Q: Which assumptions belong beside an estimate?
A: Record device counts, cable quantities, readiness, work windows and acceptance work. Identify travel and revisit assumptions separately.

## NETWORK LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/network-lifecycle-management
Title: Network Lifecycle Management | SRS Networks
Description: Track every device to its end-of-life date. Managed firmware schedules, planned refresh windows, 5-year roadmaps, and budget forecasting instead of surprises.
─────────────────────────────────────────

End-of-Life Equipment Still Running in Production

Switches, firewalls, and access points that have passed their vendor end-of-life date don't receive security patches. They're running in production with known vulnerabilities that can't be fixed - not because nobody cares, but because nobody tracked the lifecycle.

No Firmware Update Schedule

Firmware doesn't update itself. Without a managed schedule, critical security patches and stability fixes go unapplied for months - or years. By the time something breaks, the device may be three major versions behind with a laundry list of known issues.

Reactive Replacements After Failures

When equipment fails without warning, the response is emergency procurement - paying premium prices, accepting longer lead times, and deploying hastily under pressure. Equipment that was managed on a lifecycle never reaches that point.

Without a roadmap, the network evolves by accident. New requirements get bolted onto aging infrastructure that was never designed for them. Capacity runs out, compatibility issues compound, and the gap between current state and where the business needs to be widens every year.

Budget Surprises from Emergency Hardware Purchases

A failed core switch mid-year isn't in the budget. Neither is the expedited shipping, after-hours labor, and emergency consulting that comes with it. Organizations without lifecycle planning consistently overspend on IT hardware - they just don't realize it until it hits.

Proactive hardware refresh planning with recommended replacement windows before end-of-life

Managed firmware and security patch schedules applied across the entire network fleet

Five-year technology roadmaps aligned to business growth, compliance, and operational requirements

Lifecycle documentation for every device - model, firmware version, purchase date, and EOL date

Budget forecasting for planned upgrades so hardware spend is never a surprise

Healthcare organizations operate under HIPAA and face regulatory scrutiny on network security. End-of-life devices with unpatched vulnerabilities aren't just a technical risk - they're a compliance liability. SRS keeps healthcare networks current and documented for audit readiness.

## NETWORK LOAD BALANCING

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/network-load-balancing
Title: Network Load Balancing | SRS Networks
Description: Run both ISP circuits active/active and distribute server traffic with health checks, automatic failover, SSL offloading, and traffic shaping for critical apps.
─────────────────────────────────────────

A Single Server Failure Brings Everything Down

When traffic routes to one server and that server fails, the application goes down with it. There's no automatic rerouting, no failover - just a dead service and a support call at 2am.

Bandwidth Bottlenecks During Peak Hours

With a single ISP link, peak-usage periods saturate the pipe. There's no way to shift traffic to a secondary circuit or distribute load across multiple providers when one link maxes out.

No Intelligent Traffic Distribution

Without load balancing, requests pile up on whichever server happens to be in rotation - regardless of its current load, health status, or response time. Users experience slow, inconsistent performance.

No Health Monitoring or Automatic Failover

IT teams find out about server or link failures when users complain. There are no health probes, no automated failover policies, and no recovery logic - just manual intervention after the damage is done.

Multi-ISP Environments With No WAN Intelligence

Organizations with two or more ISP connections often use them in active/passive mode - wasting the secondary link's capacity until there's a failure. There's no dynamic routing or cost-based policy.

WAN link load balancing across multiple ISP connections for true active/active throughput

Band-Aid Fixes That Miss the Root Cause

No Proactive Optimization Process

Overcrowded Racks Nobody Can Work In

Equipment piled on top of equipment, cables draped across shelves, and zero vertical organization. The moment something fails, a technician spends 45 minutes tracing wires before they can even diagnose the problem.

Cable Tangles That Block Airflow

A bundle of unmanaged cables stuffed behind equipment isn't just ugly - it's a cooling failure in slow motion. Blocked airflow raises temperatures, shortens hardware lifespan, and can cause thermal shutdowns at the worst possible time.

No Hot/Cold Aisle Planning

Equipment producing heat in the same direction it's intaking air is a design problem, not just a placement problem. Without proper airflow planning, cooling systems work harder and equipment still runs hot.

Zero Labeling or Documentation

When nothing is labeled, every troubleshooting event becomes an investigation. Which port goes where? Which UPS feeds which circuit? Without documentation, your infrastructure is only understandable by the person who built it.

No Path for Future Expansion

Racks built without a growth plan run out of usable space fast. Adding a new switch or server means reorganizing everything - or worse, bolting equipment wherever it fits and compounding the existing mess.

Title: Network Redundancy Solutions | SRS Networks

─────────────────────────────────────────

Single Internet Connection with No Failover

One ISP connection means one point of failure. When that circuit goes down - fiber cut, carrier outage, CPE failure - the entire organization loses internet access until the provider restores service.

No Hardware Redundancy in the Network Core

A single core switch or router is a single point of failure for every device downstream. One hardware failure takes down an entire floor, building, or campus with no automatic recovery path.

Manual Failover That Requires IT Intervention

Networks designed to fail over manually don't fail over when it matters most - nights, weekends, and holidays when no one is watching. Recovery time is measured in hours, not seconds.

Extended Outages from Cascading Single Failures

When one failure triggers additional failures - a downed ISP circuit overloading backup links, or a failed switch cascading to connected devices - outages become prolonged and difficult to isolate.

No SLA Protection Without Redundant Architecture

Uptime commitments and SLA guarantees require redundant infrastructure to back them up. A single-path network architecture cannot support five-nines availability regardless of what the ISP contract says.

Dual ISP connectivity with BGP or policy-based automatic path switching - no IT intervention required

End-of-Life Hardware Still in Production

Security Vulnerabilities from Outdated Firmware

Flat Networks With No Isolation

Everything on one segment means one compromised device can reach everything else - workstations, servers, printers, cameras, and critical systems. There's no boundary to stop lateral movement.

Without segmentation, attackers who breach one endpoint have direct access to your entire network. Ransomware and credential-harvesting tools exploit flat networks by design.

Compliance Failures (PCI, HIPAA)

PCI DSS requires cardholder data environments to be isolated. HIPAA mandates controls around PHI access. Flat networks consistently fail both. Auditors flag it every time.

IoT Devices on Production Networks

Smart thermostats, IP cameras, badge readers, and manufacturing sensors sitting on the same segment as your servers are attack vectors waiting to be used. IoT firmware is rarely patched.

No Visibility Into East-West Traffic

North-south traffic gets logged. East-west traffic - device to device inside your network - usually doesn't. Attackers exploit this blind spot to move laterally for weeks before detection.

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-site-survey-checklist

Q: What should a network site survey include?
A: Seven categories: building access and permitting jurisdiction, MDF and IDF closet conditions, pathway and structural obstructions, power and cooling capacity, the wireless and RF environment, existing network and low-voltage systems, and schedule and labor constraints. Wireless-only surveys are the industry default and the reason pathway, power, and closet problems get discovered on install day instead of during planning.

Q: How much does a network site survey cost?
A: In 2026, remote surveys run $150–$400 per site and on-site surveys run $450–$1,200. Compare that to a single revisit truck roll at $450–$950: one avoided return trip pays for the survey. On multi-site programs the survey also converts unknown buildings into a repeatable per-site unit, which is what makes honest wave planning possible.

Q: When is a remote survey good enough?
A: When the site follows a known prototype format, existing documentation is trustworthy, and there is a competent on-site contact who can photograph closets, pathway, and ceiling conditions on request. Older buildings, warehouse RF environments, unknown pathway, occupied space, and union or landlord constraints all argue for on-site — as does any site where the install itself will run five figures.

Q: Why survey warehouse wireless at full racking instead of empty?
A: Because steel racking and full pallet positions absorb and reflect RF in ways an empty building never shows. Coverage designed in a bare warehouse routinely develops dead aisles once inventory arrives, which surfaces as scanner and forklift-terminal failures after go-live. If the building cannot be surveyed at load, the design must at minimum be modeled against the actual racking plan.

Q: What gets missed most often in site surveys?
A: Closet grounding and bonding, remaining pathway capacity, PoE budget for planned devices, and the identity of the person with authority to unlock doors and approve field changes. Wireless gets surveyed because tools and vendors exist for it; these four get skipped because they are unglamorous — and each one can stop a crew on install morning.

Q: Who should be present during an on-site survey?
A: Someone with building access authority and someone who knows the operational constraints — often facilities plus IT. On leased or GC-controlled sites, the landlord contact or superintendent matters too, since vendor onboarding and riser access rules surface there. The single most valuable participant is whoever can answer what must stay live during the work.

Q: Does a site survey replace a network assessment?
A: No — they answer different questions. A site survey documents physical conditions to price and plan an installation. A network assessment evaluates the health, performance, and design of the network already running. A refresh project usually wants both: the assessment says what should change, the survey says what it will take to change it in this building.

Q: How long does a site survey take?
A: A typical single-tenant office or retail site runs two to four hours on-site; a large warehouse or multi-closet building runs a full day, longer if RF validation at load is included. Remote surveys turn around in a day or two once photos and documentation arrive. On multi-site programs, surveys are batched geographically so travel is amortized across several buildings.

Q: Can SRS Networks survey sites we will have someone else install?
A: Yes. Surveys are sold as standalone work, and the deliverable is vendor-neutral — completed checklist per building, photographs, closet and pathway documentation, and a scope narrative any qualified contractor can bid from. Buyers running a competitive bid often prefer this, because it produces bids that are actually comparable.

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-site-survey-cost

Q: How much does a network site survey cost in 2026?
A: A remote site survey costs $150–$400 per site in 2026; an on-site survey costs $450–$1,200 per site, rising to $1,500 in tier-1 metros like NYC, San Francisco, Boston, and Chicago. Ranges carry ±30% variance for site conditions, region, and scope.

Q: What does a network site survey actually cover?
A: Cable pathways and ceiling type, IDF/MDF locations and rack space, power availability at the demarc and closets, mounting surfaces, and access constraints — locked rooms, landlord rules, escort requirements, lift needs. The deliverable is photos, measurements, and a scope confirmation the installation crew can execute against without guesswork.

Q: What is the difference between a remote and an on-site survey?
A: A remote survey ($150–$400 per site) works from floor plans, photos, and a structured call with someone at the site. An on-site survey ($450–$1,200) puts a technician in the building to physically verify pathways, power, and closet conditions. Remote works for repeatable prototype sites; on-site is worth it for warehouses, older buildings, and any site where the floor plan is stale.

Q: Is it worth surveying every site on a 100-site rollout?
A: Run the math honestly. Industry first-visit completion is 85–92%, so 100 unsurveyed sites produce roughly 8–15 failed first visits at $450–$950 per revisit — $3,600–$14,250 in revisits alone. Surveying all 100 sites remotely costs $15,000–$40,000. On pure revisit math, surveys don't always pay at that count. They pay through what they prevent: change orders inside the ±30% variance band, which routinely dwarf revisit costs on real programs.

Q: What does a failed first visit actually cost?
A: A revisit truck roll runs $450–$950 — and that is before re-mobilization fees, schedule slip across the wave, and idle-crew time. One skipped survey that triggers one revisit already exceeds the cost of the survey that would have prevented it.

Q: How do site surveys reduce change orders?
A: Per-site install pricing carries ±30% variance for site conditions. A survey collapses that variance before contracts are signed: hard-lid ceilings, missing conduit, full racks, and power shortfalls get priced into the rate card instead of arriving mid-program as change orders. On multi-site programs, change-order prevention is where survey ROI actually lives.

Q: Does SRS Networks require surveys before a national rollout?
A: SRS runs a pilot wave of 3–5 sites before committing national waves, and surveys are how that pilot locks the per-site rate card. On repeatable footprints we often survey remotely at $150–$400 per site and reserve on-site surveys ($450–$1,200) for outlier buildings. The goal is a rate card that survives contact with the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Q: What first-visit completion rate should I expect?
A: Industry average is 85–92% — meaning 8–15% of site visits fail and trigger a $450–$950 revisit. SRS Networks targets 98%+ first-visit completion by combining site surveys with dual-coast pre-staging, which eliminates the roughly 1-in-6 drop-ship failure rate that unstaged programs hit.

Q: What about wireless-specific site surveys?
A: Wireless surveys follow the same cost structure — $150–$400 remote predictive, $450–$1,200 on-site — but add RF design: AP placement, channel planning, and coverage validation. SRS delivers them through its wireless site survey and heat-mapping services as part of enterprise WiFi deployments.

### Specify ports, power and optics before configuration

Switch configuration needs a port schedule, approved VLAN and uplink design, and rollback plan. Layer 2 switching and Layer 3 routing describe different functions. SFP and QSFP identify module families, not universal compatibility.

Q: How should PoE be planned?
A: Check each device's power requirement, port capability and total switch power budget against OEM documentation. Do not assume all ports can supply their maximum simultaneously.

150 Branches, 150 Different Configs

Every site was configured by whoever happened to be onsite that week. Different VLAN IDs for the same traffic, different native VLAN on the trunk, different SNMP strings. Nothing is reproducible and nothing is troubleshootable from the NOC.

PoE Budget Guessed, Not Calculated

Port count got counted, watts did not. Wi-Fi 6E APs pulling 30W+, PTZ cameras with heaters at 60W, and desk phones all land on one switch, the PSU tops out, and low-priority ports start dropping power mid-day.

Uplinks and Trunks That Fight Each Other

Native VLAN mismatch on a trunk, an allowed-VLAN list nobody pruned, spanning-tree root sitting on an access switch in a closet. It works until a link flaps, and then the whole site is unreachable.

A Firmware Zoo Across the Fleet
