Network Switch Configuration FAQs

### Frequently Asked Questions — network-switch-configuration

Q: What does network switch configuration include?
A: It covers the full switch build, not just the IP address: hostname and management addressing, the VLAN map, 802.1Q trunk and allowed-VLAN policy, spanning-tree mode and root placement, PoE budgeting and per-port priority, stacking, LACP uplinks, and hardened management access with SSHv2, SNMPv3, TACACS+ or RADIUS, NTP, and syslog. We write that as one golden template per switch role and apply it identically at every site. Closeout includes the config archive and an as-built port map.

Q: We have 150 branches all configured differently. Can you standardize them?
A: That is the most common project we take on. We start by pulling the running config off every reachable switch and diffing them so the actual drift is visible on one page, which is usually the first time anyone has seen how far apart the sites are. From there we write a single template with a small variable block for site-specific values and lock everything else. Sites get converted on a rolling schedule during your maintenance windows so the fleet lands on one standard without a flag-day cutover.

Q: How do you calculate the PoE budget for a switch?
A: In watts against the real device list, never from port count. We classify every powered device by standard, 15.4W for 802.3af phones and older APs, 30W for 802.3at Wi-Fi 6 and 6E radios and fixed cameras, and 60W or 90W for 802.3bt Wi-Fi 7, PTZ cameras with heaters, and PoE lighting. That total drives the power supply choice, including redundancy, and we hold headroom back for the next camera or AP refresh. Per-port PoE priority is set so a spike sheds a spare port instead of an access point.

Q: Do you configure the switches before they ship to our sites?
A: Yes. Hardware lands at our West or East Coast staging facility instead of the sites. Each switch is unboxed, upgraded to the one approved image for its model family, loaded with its site-specific config, powered on, and bench-verified. Stacks are cabled and their master priority set, serial numbers are recorded against site IDs, and the chassis is labeled with the site code before it ships back out with its optics and site kit. The crew that opens the box in the closet has nothing left to figure out.

Q: Which switch platforms do you work on?
A: We configure and deploy the enterprise access and distribution platforms our clients standardize on, including Cisco Catalyst and Meraki, Aruba and HPE, Juniper EX, Extreme, Ubiquiti, and FortiSwitch. We work to your standard rather than pushing a brand, and if you have not chosen one yet we will scope the port count, PoE budget, uplink speed, and stacking requirement so the purchase matches the deployment. Procurement can run through us or through your existing reseller.

Q: How do you handle stacking and uplink design?
A: Stacks are cabled in a closed ring rather than a chain so a single stack cable failure does not split the stack, and master priority is set deliberately instead of left to election order. Members are pre-provisioned and brought to matching software before they ever join, since a version mismatch is the usual reason a member refuses to come up. Uplinks are built as LACP port-channels with speed, duplex, and MTU matched on both ends, and we specify SFP+ or 25G optics versus DAC based on the actual run length.

Q: What validation do you run before the crew leaves the site?
A: A documented pass, not a glance at the link lights. We check interface errors and duplex on every active port, confirm LLDP neighbors match the design, verify port-channel state on the uplinks, confirm the spanning-tree root is at the core and not in the closet, and measure actual PoE draw against the budgeted number. The config is then archived and the as-built port map is handed over. If anything fails the check, it is fixed on that visit rather than becoming a return trip.

Q: Can you standardize firmware across an existing fleet?
A: Yes, and it is usually overdue. Most fleets we inherit are running three or four software trains across the same model family because each switch shipped with whatever was on it, which causes stack join failures and features that behave differently site to site. We pick one approved image per model family, validate it against your feature set, load it during staging for new hardware, and schedule remote or onsite upgrades for existing gear. After that, a security advisory is one decision instead of 150 individual investigations.

Q: How is a switch configuration project priced and scheduled?
A: At the project level, driven by site count, switches per site, whether it is a refresh or a greenfield build, staging scope, and how much after-hours labor the maintenance windows require. Template design is a one-time engineering effort that gets amortized across the whole fleet, which is why per-site cost drops sharply as site count grows. From a received site list and device inventory we typically return a firm number in 3 to 5 business days, and a 150-site rolling deployment usually runs 8 to 16 weeks depending on window availability.

Q: Do you also install the racks, cabling, and access points at the same visit?
A: Yes. Switch configuration is normally one line on a larger scope that includes rack and closet buildout, structured cabling, patch panel termination, access point mounting, and certified testing. Sending one crew to do all of it is cheaper and faster than sequencing three vendors through the same closet, and it removes the finger-pointing when something does not come up. One project manager owns the site from kickoff through closeout across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Q: How should PoE be planned?
A: Check each device's power requirement, port capability and total switch power budget against OEM documentation. Do not assume all ports can supply their maximum simultaneously.

## NEW CONSTRUCTION IT

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/new-construction-it

IT Brought In After Construction Ends

When IT isn't at the table during design, the building is finished before anyone realizes the network room is in the wrong location, the conduit is the wrong size, and the pathways don't go where the cable needs to go.

No Pathways Planned for Cable Runs

Ceilings are closed, walls are drywalled, and there are no sleeves, conduit, or pathways roughed in. Retrofitting cable infrastructure after construction is complete costs two to three times more than doing it right during the build.

Wrong Conduit Sizes and Locations

Electrical contractors install conduit without understanding low-voltage bend radius requirements, fill ratios, or pathway separation rules. The result is conduit that can't be used - or worse, causes signal interference.

No Coordination with the General Contractor

Without a low-voltage trade partner at the GC's coordination meetings, IT infrastructure gets planned around rather than planned in. Critical decisions get made without the right input - and you pay to undo them later.

Expensive Retrofits After Certificate of Occupancy

Patching in IT infrastructure after a building is occupied means cutting walls, patching drywall, disrupting tenants, and paying premium labor rates. Work that costs $15K during construction can cost $60K as a retrofit.

### Frequently Asked Questions — office-network-installation-cost

Q: How much does an office network installation cost per user in 2026?
A: A standard office runs $250-450 per user in 2026 — install labor and install materials, network hardware excluded. A 50-person office lands at $12,500-22,500 for installation. These are national planning ranges from SRS Networks field data across 900+ multi-site deployments, with ±30% variance for site conditions, region, and scope.

Q: What does office network installation cost per square foot?
A: Structured cabling alone runs $1.50-4.50 per square foot in 2026. Full network infrastructure — cabling plus switching, WiFi, and rack build — runs $3.00-8.00 per square foot. A 5,000 sq ft tenant improvement budgets $7,500-22,500 for cabling only, or $15,000-40,000 for the full infrastructure buildout.

Q: What does a branch office network installation cost?
A: A branch office or bank branch of 2,000-6,000 square feet with 12-24 drops runs $9,500-22,000 per site on 2026 national planning ranges — install labor and materials, network hardware excluded. On branch programs of 25+ sites, per-site pricing runs 15-30% below single-site rates.

Q: What is included in the per-user office network number?
A: The $250-450 per-user range covers cable drops serving each workstation, terminations at both ends, patch panels, labeling, certification testing, WiFi access point installation, and rack dressing. Network hardware — switches, access points, firewall — is excluded. Broken out per drop, Cat6 runs $175-295 and Cat6A runs $220-390 installed and certified.

Q: Is new construction cheaper than retrofitting an occupied office?
A: Yes, meaningfully. New construction and tenant improvements price toward the bottom of the $1.50-4.50 and $3.00-8.00 per-square-foot ranges: open ceilings, no furniture, coordinated trades. Retrofitting an occupied office pushes toward the top — hard-lid ceilings, working around live operations, and after-hours work at a 25-50% premium all add labor.

Q: How do regional labor markets change office network pricing?
A: Tier-1 metros — NYC, San Francisco, Boston, Chicago — run 25-40% above national ranges, and prevailing-wage projects add another 30-50%. The material-to-labor split on copper installations runs roughly 35-45% material to 55-65% labor, which is why the wage class moves the total more than any material choice does.

Q: Does the price come down for larger offices?
A: Yes. Above 200 drops on one site, per-drop pricing runs 5-15% below list; at 1,000+ drops it runs 10-20% below. On multi-site office and branch programs of 25+ locations, per-site pricing runs 15-30% below single-site rates because mobilization, staging, and program management are amortized across the program.

Q: When does an office need a fiber backbone, and what does it cost?
A: A building backbone — MDF to 2-4 IDFs on 12-strand OM4 — runs $8,000-25,000 per building on 2026 national ranges. A single-floor office served by one closet usually does not need one; multi-floor offices and larger footprints with distributed IDFs do. Component-level fiber pricing lives on the SRS structured cabling cost-per-drop guide.

Q: How should we budget the network for a tenant improvement?
A: Budget $3.00-8.00 per square foot for full network infrastructure inside the TI, then layer program-level costs: a site survey at $150-400 remote or $450-1,200 on-site, program management at 8-12% on multi-site programs, and a 10-15% contingency. Lock the cabling scope before the ceiling grid closes — open-ceiling pricing is the cheapest you will ever get.

Q: Does SRS Networks handle single offices, or only multi-site programs?
A: SRS is engineered for multi-site programs — the economic floor is roughly 25 sites, and below it we will tell you plainly that a local shop is the cheaper call, because per-site coordination overhead eats the value of a national partner. The exception is large single-site projects such as multi-floor buildouts with hundreds of drops, where scale on one site works the same way.

## OUTDOOR WIRELESS SOLUTIONS

─────────────────────────────────────────

Dead Zones the Moment You Step Outside

Indoor access points stop at the exterior wall. Parking structures, loading docks, courtyards, and building entrances are left completely uncovered - forcing staff and visitors to disconnect the moment operations move outside.

Consumer-Grade Outdoor APs Failing in the Field

Big-box outdoor APs are not built to survive sustained heat, driving rain, freeze-thaw cycles, or years of continuous operation. They fail unpredictably, create support emergencies, and need to be replaced far too often.

Parking Structures With Zero Connectivity

Multi-deck concrete parking structures block virtually all indoor signal. License plate recognition, mobile payment terminals, security cameras, and staff devices all go dark the moment they enter a parking garage.

Interference Tanking Outdoor Throughput

Outdoor RF environments are noisier than indoor ones - neighboring networks, IoT devices, point-to-point links, and adjacent channels all compete for spectrum. Without proper RF planning and channel coordination, performance degrades fast.

No Backhaul Between Remote or Distributed Facilities

Satellite buildings, remote storage yards, construction sites, and overflow facilities sit off the network entirely. Trenching fiber isn't always feasible - but leaving those locations disconnected is an operational problem that compounds.

## OUTSIDE PLANT CABLING

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/outside-plant-cabling

No Inter-Building Connectivity Plan

Organizations add buildings, portables, or outbuildings over time without any plan for how to connect them. The result is a patchwork of workarounds - wireless bridges, consumer routers, and temporary runs that never get replaced.

Weather Exposure Destroying Cabling

Cable that wasn't designed for outdoor environments degrades fast. UV exposure, temperature swings, moisture ingress, and physical abrasion destroy indoor-rated cable pulled through conduit or draped across buildings.

When underground cable gets cut by a landscaping crew or fails, nobody knows where it runs, what depth it's at, or where the manholes are. Repairs turn into full excavation projects because nobody ever documented the route.

OSP work requires coordinating with utilities, permitting offices, excavation crews, and inspection authorities. Without a contractor who manages all of it, projects stall for weeks waiting on approvals or miss utility locates entirely.

Damaged or Improperly Installed Runs

Fiber spliced without proper hardware, direct-buried cable without adequate depth, conduit without pull boxes at appropriate intervals - field errors in OSP work create maintenance nightmares that don't show up until years later.

## PATCH PANEL MANAGEMENT

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/patch-panel-management
Title: Patch Panel Installation & Management | SRS Networks
Description: Patch fields you can actually trace. Certified punch-down termination, both-end labeling, color-coded patch cords, and port-map documentation at closeout.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Unlabeled or Mislabeled Ports

When patch panel ports have no labels - or worse, wrong ones - every move, add, or change becomes a guessing game. Technicians waste time tracing circuits by hand instead of making the change and moving on.

Tangled Patch Cables Nobody Can Follow

Loose patch cords draped over equipment, bundled without order, and routed across everything in the rack create a situation where pulling one cable could disconnect something critical. It only gets worse over time.

If nobody knows which port on the patch panel maps to which drop in the building, you can't troubleshoot remotely, you can't hand off to a new technician, and you can't scale without rebuilding from scratch. Documentation isn't a nice-to-have - it's the foundation.

Slow Troubleshooting During Outages

An outage that should take ten minutes to resolve stretches into hours when nobody can trace the affected circuit. Disorganized patch panels turn every network event into a manual investigation under time pressure.

Unlabeled cables in a crowded panel get pulled by mistake. Someone is trying to disconnect one circuit and yanks another. Without proper labeling and cable management, accidental disconnections are a recurring problem - not a one-off.

## POE LIGHTING SYSTEMS

High Electrical Costs from Traditional Lighting

Legacy fluorescent and incandescent fixtures consume far more power than necessary - and without any granular control, they run on schedules that don't reflect actual occupancy. You're paying for light in empty rooms around the clock.

No Granular Control Over Individual Fixtures

Traditional lighting infrastructure gives you a light switch - on or off, nothing in between. There's no per-zone dimming, no occupancy-based automation, and no ability to adjust based on daylight levels or time of day.

Separate Siloed Systems for Every Building Function

Lighting, HVAC, access control, environmental sensors - all running on separate, disconnected infrastructure with separate vendors, separate dashboards, and no shared data. Managing a smart building with dumb systems is an exercise in frustration.

Expensive Electrical Runs for Every New Fixture

Traditional lighting requires licensed electricians, conduit, and high-voltage wiring for every fixture. Adding, moving, or relocating lights is a construction project. That cost and complexity prevents buildings from adapting to changing layouts.

No Occupancy or Environmental Data

Without sensors integrated into your building infrastructure, you have no insight into how spaces are actually used. You can't optimize HVAC zones, measure occupancy for real estate decisions, or prove ROI on your building upgrades.

### Frequently Asked Questions — pos-installation-cost

Q: How much does POS installation cost per terminal in 2026?
A: POS installation runs $350-850 per terminal or lane in 2026, hardware excluded. That range covers unboxing and staging, mounting, cable connections, peripheral setup for printers, cash drawers, and card readers, network configuration, and live test transactions. These are national planning ranges from SRS Networks field data across 900+ multi-site deployments, with ±30% variance for site conditions.

Q: What does POS installation cost for a typical QSR site?
A: A typical QSR site runs 3-6 terminals, which puts installation at $2,500-7,500 per site, hardware excluded. A restaurant deploying the full technology stack — POS plus kitchen display systems, digital menu boards, drive-thru equipment, WiFi, and cameras — lands at $12,000-32,000 per site on 2026 national planning ranges.

Q: Does POS installation cost include the hardware?
A: No. The $350-850 per-terminal range covers installation labor and installation materials only. Terminals, printers, cash drawers, and card readers are priced separately — usually purchased through the POS vendor or supplied by the chain. SRS Networks is vendor-neutral: we deploy Toast, Square, NCR, Oracle Micros, and Clover systems and resell none of them.

Q: How much does an overnight POS cutover cost?
A: Overnight and after-hours POS work carries a 25-50% premium — 1.25x-1.5x standard labor — on top of the $350-850 per-terminal installation range. Chains pay it because closing lanes during business hours costs more in lost transactions than the premium, which is why most chainwide POS refreshes run as overnight cutovers with morning go-live verification.

Q: How does POS installation pricing change on a multi-site rollout?
A: Multi-site programs of 25+ sites run 15-30% below single-site pricing because mobilization, project management, and staging are amortized across the program. Below roughly 25 sites, per-site coordination overhead eats that advantage — SRS Networks tells buyers below that floor to hire a local shop instead.

Q: What network cabling does a POS installation need, and what does it cost?
A: Each POS lane typically needs at least one Cat6 drop, which runs $175-295 installed and certified on 2026 national ranges. Kitchen display systems, printers, and back-office equipment add more drops. Full per-drop pricing for Cat6, Cat6A, and fiber lives on the SRS Networks structured cabling cost-per-drop guide.

Q: What hidden costs should we budget for on a POS rollout?
A: The big four: revisit truck rolls at $450-950 each when a site cannot be finished on the first visit, drop-ship failures — roughly 1 in 6 site visits hits missing, wrong, or damaged gear without pre-staging — the 25-50% after-hours premium, and rush dispatch at +50-100%. Carry a 10-15% program contingency and budget program management at 8-12% of total program cost.

Q: Which POS systems does SRS Networks install?
A: SRS Networks is vendor-neutral. We deploy Toast, Square, NCR, Oracle Micros, Clover, and other major platforms — and we resell none of them, so the deployment plan is never tied to a hardware margin. SRS has deployed technology for multi-site organizations across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996.

Q: How does SRS Networks avoid failed first visits on POS rollouts?
A: Industry first-visit completion runs 85-92%; SRS targets 98%+ by pre-staging every site's gear at West Coast and East Coast staging facilities — configured, tested, and kitted per site before it ships. Without staging, roughly 1 in 6 site visits hits missing, wrong, or damaged gear. Staged freight and logistics run 3-6% of hardware value.

Q: Should we run a pilot before a chainwide POS refresh?
A: Yes. Deploy a pilot wave of 3-5 sites before committing national waves. The pilot validates the install runbook, the overnight cutover timing, and the per-site rate card, so the numbers you take to finance are field-verified rather than estimated. It is how SRS Networks structures every national POS program.

Which service, which panel, which circuits, and what question the program is meant to answer. Measurement points are written into the scope before anything is installed, because moving them halfway through destroys the comparison.

### Frequently Asked Questions — power-performance-verification

Q: What is SRS Power Performance Verification?
A: It is a two-session electrical measurement program. A licensed electrical partner records a baseline log on the facility before equipment is installed, the equipment goes in, and a matching log is recorded afterward using the same measurement points, instrument specification, and window length. The deliverable is a side-by-side comparison of energy consumption, peak demand, power factor, harmonic distortion, voltage stability, and current draw.

Q: Why does the methodology have to match between sessions?
A: Because otherwise the comparison is meaningless. If the baseline runs 24 hours on a Tuesday at the main service and the follow-up runs 48 hours on a weekend at a sub-panel, the difference between the two numbers reflects the change in method, not the change in the facility. Measurement points, window length, and instrument capability are fixed in the scope before the first visit for exactly this reason.

Q: Does SRS interpret the results or certify the savings?
A: No. SRS delivers the measurement and the documented comparison. The engineering interpretation belongs to the product manufacturer or to your own engineers — the parties who designed or specified what is being evaluated. We do not certify energy savings, and we do not have a financial interest in the outcome, which is the reason the measurement carries weight in the first place.

Q: What if the data shows no improvement?
A: The report goes out unchanged. We are paid to measure, not to find a result, and a verification program that only ever confirms the vendor is not a verification program. Knowing that a product did not move the numbers at a pilot site is worth considerably more than discovering it after a 200-site rollout.

Q: Which parameters actually get compared?
A: Six that the instrument records directly: energy consumption in kWh, peak demand in kW, power factor, total harmonic distortion, voltage stability including sags and swells, and current draw per phase. Claims about equipment efficiency, heat generation, and equipment life expectancy are projections drawn from those numbers rather than measurements, and the report labels them that way. Where heat matters to the case, temperature data loggers can be added so it becomes measured too.

Q: How long does a full verification take end to end?
A: Each session is typically a 24-hour logging window with an install visit and a removal visit, so roughly two days of site presence per session. The elapsed time between sessions is driven by the installation and commissioning schedule of the equipment being evaluated, not by us. We schedule the post-installation window after commissioning is complete so the recording captures steady-state operation.

Q: Can you run this across a whole portfolio?
A: That is the intended shape. One methodology specification, one instrument capability standard, one report format, one project manager, and per-site tracking through the Project Command Center, so results compare across the portfolio instead of arriving as unrelated PDFs. Portfolio programs usually start with a pilot group before the full site list is committed.

Q: How is it priced?
A: As a fixed fee per site covering both sessions — install visit, logging window, removal visit, and reporting at each end. Fixed-fee pricing is deliberate: a two-visit program billed hourly turns into an argument about truck time somewhere around site thirty. Fees vary with facility size, service complexity, single versus three phase, and travel to the market.

Q: Can I use another facility's anchor layout?
A: Use it only as planning context. The platform designer must approve the layout for the actual geometry, obstructions and tracking requirement.

Q: What does SRS need to scope the physical work?
A: Send the site list, states, drawings, device schedule and approved installation instructions. Include access windows and the contact who owns platform commissioning so responsibilities can be agreed before dispatch.

Q: Which costs affect the field estimate?
A: Mounting access, work windows, pathways, travel, device quantities and readiness gaps affect field labor. Platform licenses, calibration and application integration should be quoted separately by their assigned owners.

Q: How should a pilot become a multi-site deployment?
A: Accept the pilot against the agreed physical and platform tests before repeating it. Carry forward the approved checklist, record site-specific differences and confirm readiness before each later visit.

Q: What does the scope workbook include?
A: It records site readiness, device locations, responsibility owners, acceptance checks and cost categories. Complete it with the platform designer and facility owner, then use it to request comparable field estimates.

Choppy VoIP Calls Nobody Can Explain

Slow ERP and CRM During Peak Hours

No Traffic Prioritization in Place

Bandwidth Consumed by Non-Business Traffic

Software updates, cloud backups, and personal video streaming consume the same pipe as your core business applications. Without shaping policies, the important traffic always loses.

## QUESTIONS TO ASK A CABLING CONTRACTOR

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/questions-to-ask-a-cabling-contractor
Title: 20 Questions to Ask a Cabling Contractor | SRS Networks
Description: The 20 questions to ask a cabling contractor before you sign — and the red-flag answers that should end the conversation. From 900+ deployments since 1996.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Who exactly will be in my building — your employees or subcontractors?

Either answer can be right. What matters is whether the contractor knows, and what governs the people who show up: agreements, supervision, background process.

“We'll figure out staffing after award.”

Can I see your COI right now, with limits?

Insurance is verified before work, not after. On enforced jobsites a failed COI check is a multi-day stop-work order — a $5K–$40K margin event on a rollout.

“Certificate available upon award.”

What BICSI or manufacturer credentials do your installers and your designer hold?

Credentials predict whether the plant will pass certification and qualify for warranty registration. A named RCDD or BICSI Technician on the design is the strong answer.

No specific credential or person named.

Where are you licensed for low-voltage work, and who holds the license?

Low-voltage licensing is state-by-state and enforcement is real. Multi-state projects need a contractor who can list its licenses, not gesture at them.

“We work everywhere” with no license list.

What does your site survey cover, and what does it cost?

Surveys run $150–$400 remote or $450–$1,200 on-site in 2026, and they are what keeps the quote from being a guess. The survey scope tells you how the contractor thinks.

“We don't need a survey for this.”

How do you handle occupied space and after-hours windows?

After-hours work carries a real +25–50% premium. A contractor who prices it up front is planning the job; one who is silent about it is planning a change order.

No premium disclosed for an occupied building.

Who is my single point of contact, and what does that cost?

Program management runs 8–12% of program cost when priced honestly. A named PM with a reporting cadence is what keeps a multi-closet job off your desk.

“The crew lead will handle coordination.”

How are change orders priced?

Unit pricing in the original quote — per drop, per AP, per camera — is your protection after award. Without it, every add is negotiated from scratch at 2–3x.

No unit rates; “we'll quote adds as they come up.”

Materials & install quality (9–12)

Exactly what cable and components are you quoting?

Category, jacket rating, manufacturer, jack and panel models. Substitutions between quote and install are where margins get quietly recovered.

“Or equivalent” with no submittal offered.

What labeling scheme will you use?

A room-faceplate-port scheme, stated up front, is the difference between a documented plant and a guessing game for every future tech.

No scheme; “we label everything clearly.”

What pathway are you using, and is fire-stopping included?

Pathway and penetration fire-stopping are real scope with real code exposure. “Existing pathway” claimed sight-unseen means nobody has looked above the ceiling.

Pathway unaddressed, fire-stopping excluded silently.

What does your warranty actually cover, and who backs it?

Installer workmanship coverage and manufacturer plant warranties are different products. SRS, for example, carries a 5-year bumper-to-bumper warranty on datacom products it installs — provided they were purchased through SRS as part of the bid. Ask any contractor for the same specificity.

“Manufacturer warranty” with no terms, or no workmanship coverage at all.

What test standard do you certify against, and what deliverable do I receive?

The strong answer names the instrument and the artifact: Fluke certification, PDF report per drop. This single answer predicts install quality better than any reference call.

“We test everything” with no standard named.

Do I get as-builts and a cable map at closeout?

As-builts are what your next contractor, your IT team, and your integrator will work from for a decade. They are deliverables, not favors.

As-builts cost extra, or aren't offered.

Do you photo-document the work?

Per-drop or per-zone photos settle disputes in minutes and prove what is above the ceiling without a lift. Standard practice for contractors who expect scrutiny.

“We can if you want” — meaning it isn't their habit.

Can I see a sample closeout package from a similar job?

The fastest possible audit: a real (redacted) closeout package shows you exactly what you will receive. Contractors with good documentation are proud to show it.

What are your payment terms and billing structure?

NET 30 with milestone billing — SRS runs 40/30/30 on project work orders — ties payment to verified progress. Terms tell you how the contractor finances itself.

A large deposit due before mobilization.

What happens if a drop fails certification?

Failed drops are the installer's to remediate inside the quoted price. That is what certification is for.

Remediation billed as time and materials.

What references do you have at this scope in the last 24 months?

Recent, similar-scope references — same site count, same building type. Old or mismatched references are a different company's track record.

References offered only from years ago or smaller jobs.

When are you NOT the right contractor for a job like this?

The honesty test. Every real contractor has a boundary — too small, too far, wrong trade mix — and can name it. The answer tells you whether the sales motion or the operations team is talking.

“We're a great fit for everything.”

Straight answers on vetting contractors

### Frequently Asked Questions — questions-to-ask-a-cabling-contractor

Q: What is the single most important question to ask a cabling contractor?
A: What test standard do you certify against, and what deliverable do I receive? The strong answer names both the instrument and the artifact — Fluke certification with a PDF report per drop, plus as-builts at closeout. That one answer predicts install quality better than any reference call, because contractors who certify their work build so it passes.

Q: How many of these questions matter for a small job?
A: Four cover the real risk on a small single-site project: the COI with limits, the test standard and deliverable, the warranty terms, and recent similar-scope references. A good local shop that clears those four is the right hire at that scale. The full 20 earn their time when the project has multiple closets, occupied space, an enforced GC, or a site count.

Q: Is W-2 or subcontractor labor the right answer?
A: Either can be right — the red flag is a contractor who can't tell you which, or whose subs operate without agreements. The strong pattern is a defined structure: SRS runs in-house W-2 leads as the backbone with a vetted W-9 subcontractor bench, every sub under a 24-month agreement with a 150-mile non-compete and a COI audited before dispatch. Ask any contractor to describe their equivalent.

Q: What insurance should a cabling contractor show before award?
A: A current COI showing general liability, workers' compensation, and auto coverage at limits that meet the site's requirements — provided with the bid, not promised after award. On enforced jobsites a failed COI check means a multi-day stop-work order, which in our experience costs $5K–$40K in margin on a rollout. Collect the certificate before you sign.

Q: Is BICSI certification legally required?
A: No — low-voltage licensing is the legal requirement and varies by state. BICSI credentials are the industry's competency signal: they predict standards-compliant pathway, termination, and testing work, and many manufacturer warranty programs require certified installers. Treat a named BICSI credential as strong evidence, and no named credential as a question mark.

Q: What if a contractor answers well but won't provide unit pricing?
A: Walk. Unit pricing — per drop, per AP, per camera — in the original quote is your only protection on change orders. A contractor who withholds it retains the ability to price every mid-project add from scratch, without competitive pressure, which typically lands at 2–3x the bid-equivalent rate. Good answers elsewhere don't offset that.

Q: Should I ask these questions before or after collecting quotes?
A: Before, ideally inside a written RFP — putting the questions in the spec forces every bidder to answer in writing and makes the responses comparable. The SRS structured cabling RFP checklist covers the spec side, and the bid-comparison guide covers scoring what comes back. Asking after quotes arrive still works; it just costs a round of clarifications.

Q: How does SRS Networks answer these 20 questions?
A: In writing, with the quote: COI attached, W-2 leads and vetted bench described, licensing listed, Fluke PDF per drop committed, as-builts and photo documentation standard, sample closeout package on request, NET 30 terms with 40/30/30 milestone billing, and unit pricing for adds. Question 20 gets a real answer too: under roughly 25 sites, a local shop is usually your better deal — and we say so.

Cable Nests Nobody Can Touch

Unlabeled Cables Nobody Can Trace

Safety Hazards from Improper Mounting

Equipment that isn't properly secured - or is pulling on cables under its own weight - is a safety hazard. Overloaded shelves, unsupported patch panels, and tension on connectors cause failures and injuries.

No Way to Add New Equipment Without Re-Cabling

A messy rack that barely accommodates today's gear is impossible to expand. Every new device means another hour of untangling just to find a free port. Growth becomes painful instead of straightforward.

─────────────────────────────────────────

Receiving and shipping doors

Portal frame or mounted antennas, reader within cable-length of the antennas, PoE or local power, conduit down the door jamb, and a network drop back to the closet

Overhead / choke-point reader

Aisle entries, staging boundaries, production gates

Ceiling or structure mount at height, PoE drop, antenna aiming that reads the pass-through without reading the neighbor

Cycle counting, spot verification

Wireless coverage that holds at the read location — this is a WiFi design problem, not a reader problem

Tool cribs, cages, high-value storage

1. Site survey before hardware

Read zones, mounting heights, existing WiFi channels, metal and racking geometry, and the actual traffic pattern through each door. RFID that was designed on a floor plan reads pallets in the next aisle.

2. Pathway, power, and drops

Conduit at the jamb, homerun Cat6/Cat6A to each reader, fire-stopping at penetrations, and a PoE budget that accounts for readers plus everything already on the switch. Every drop terminated, tested, and labeled.

3. Mount, aim, and terminate

Portal frames and antennas installed to the design's heights and angles, cable dressed and secured, readers landed on documented switch ports. Aiming is where read rates are won or lost.

Test reads through each portal with real tagged product at real forklift speed, tuning power and angle until the zone reads what it should and ignores what it shouldn't. Results documented per portal.

5. Handoff to your platform

Readers land configured to your software vendor's spec, with port maps, mounting records, and read-rate results. Their engineers commission the application against a documented install instead of a discovery walk.

### Frequently Asked Questions — rfid-installation

Q: What does RFID installation actually involve?
A: The physical work behind a read: surveying read zones and mounting locations, running conduit and certified network drops to each reader, budgeting PoE on the closet switch, mounting portal frames and antennas at the designed heights and angles, aiming the antennas, and validating read rates with real tagged product moving at real speed. The software, tags, and read strategy come from your RFID platform vendor.

Q: What does a dock-door RFID portal need from the building?
A: A portal frame or mounted antennas at the door, a reader within cable-length of those antennas, PoE or local power, conduit down the door jamb that survives a forklift strike, and a homerun network drop back to the closet. Add a switch port with PoE headroom that accounts for everything already on that switch — adding eight readers to a fully loaded switch is a common and avoidable failure.

Q: Why do RFID pilots read well but rollouts underperform?
A: A pilot is installed by the people who designed it, in the building they designed it for, with someone watching read counts all week. The rollout goes into sixty buildings with different door heights, ceiling structures, and racking, installed by whoever was available, and nobody validates reads until a cycle count disagrees three months later. Consistent mounting heights, antenna aiming, and documented read-rate validation per portal are what close that gap.

Q: Does SRS Networks sell RFID software, readers, or tags?
A: No. SRS installs infrastructure and stays vendor-neutral — we work to whatever platform you selected and land the hardware configured to your vendor's specification. Tag selection, encoding scheme, middleware, and application logic belong to your RFID vendor. That separation is deliberate: it means our install recommendations are not steering you toward a product line.

Q: How do you validate that a portal reads correctly?
A: By testing with real tagged product moving through the zone at real forklift speed, then tuning read power and antenna angle until the portal reads what should pass and ignores what shouldn't — the adjacent lane, the staging pile behind it. Results are documented per portal so there is a baseline if read performance is disputed later.

Q: Can you install RFID in an operating warehouse?
A: Yes — dock-door and choke-point work is usually scheduled into off-shift or between-shift windows so receiving and shipping aren't interrupted. Conveyor and print-and-apply installs have to be coordinated with the line integrator's commissioning window, since the line is down for both. Give us the operational calendar and the wave plan is built around it.

Q: What is the difference between RFID installation and RTLS deployment?
A: RFID typically reads tags at fixed choke points — a pallet passes a dock-door portal and gets recorded. RTLS tracks position continuously using anchor grids, usually BLE or UWB. The physical trade is largely the same (mounting at height, PoE, cabling, surveys), but anchor density and placement discipline are much higher for RTLS. SRS installs both.

Q: Do you work directly for end users or for RFID vendors?
A: Both. Operators hire SRS directly to install infrastructure for a platform they have already chosen. RFID and RTLS platform vendors use SRS as a white-label national field arm, installing under their brand at their customers' sites — a channel engagement covered on the RTLS deployment partner page. There is no channel conflict either way, because SRS sells no competing software.

Q: How does hardware logistics work across a multi-site RFID rollout?
A: Readers and antennas route through our West or East Coast staging facility, get configured and labeled per site, and ship to a named recipient. Roughly one in six direct-to-site shipments fails on first delivery — wrong dock, no signature, receiving never told — and each failure is a return trip against a schedule. Under about five sites, drop-ship is genuinely fine and cheaper.

## RFID VS BLE VS UWB TRACKING

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/rfid-vs-ble-vs-uwb-tracking
Title: RFID vs BLE vs UWB Tracking for Warehouses | SRS
Description: Compare passive RFID, BLE, and UWB tracking by accuracy, tag cost, battery needs, reader density, physical infrastructure, and warehouse use case.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Passive RFID is suited to read events at controlled points. BLE includes signal-strength proximity systems and angle-of-arrival positioning systems, which require different locator layouts. UWB positioning also varies by architecture, including wired and wireless infrastructure. Compare the selected products against required events, update rates, installation constraints, and a representative pilot rather than assuming a universal accuracy or cost ranking.

RFID, BLE, and UWB decision matrix

Passive RFID

High-volume portal and choke-point events

Reader fields require antenna design and tuning

BLE

RSSI proximity or angle-of-arrival positioning

Selected locator geometry, orientation, tag maintenance, and backhaul

UWB

Precise real-time positioning

Model-specific geometry, synchronization, commissioning, and power/backhaul

Pallet movement favors RFID

A dock or conveyor creates a controlled event point. Passive tags need no battery, while antenna placement and RF containment decide read accuracy.

Distinguish BLE proximity from direction finding

RSSI uses received signal strength; angle-of-arrival systems use directional measurements and a positioning engine. Locator orientation and coordinates matter. Specify the selected method before setting installation or acceptance requirements.

Precise motion favors UWB

Validate the chosen UWB system with real materials, movement, obstructions, and update rates. Wired and wireless designs have different field requirements. Location tracking alone is not a safety-rated collision-prevention system; safety-control design needs its own qualified owner.

Quuppa BLE angle-of-arrival positioning

Direction finding differs from RSSI proximity; vendor claims are not SRS performance guarantees.

https://www.quuppa.com/blogs-articles/quuppa-and-inplay-enable-bluetooth-angle-of-arrival-positioning-with-the-in100-nanobeacon/

KINEXON RTLS architectures

Compare the selected wired or wireless product configuration before estimating field scope.

https://kinexon.com/products/kinexon-rtls-products

When this is not the right approach

Do not select a technology from an accuracy chart alone. Pilot the real tags, materials, speeds, geometry, interference, and software workflow before setting a facility-wide standard.

## RFP EVALUATION CRITERIA

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/rfp-evaluation-criteria
Title: Cabling Bid and Proposal Evaluation Guide | SRS
Description: Evaluate cabling bids and proposals with published weights for scope, delivery, field coverage, documentation, risk, commercial terms, and leveled price.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Good RFP evaluation criteria score scope compliance, delivery method, field coverage, schedule, documentation, risk controls, commercial terms, and price. Price should be important but not dominant; a low bid with missing testing, weak site coverage, or undefined change rates is usually the most expensive response after award. Publish the weights so bidders know what evidence matters.

Recommended 100-point scoring matrix

Scope compliance

25 points

Line-by-line response and exceptions

Delivery plan

20 points

Staffing, waves, escalation, and closeout

Relevant proof

15 points

Comparable anonymized programs and references

Price and terms

20 points

Leveled total, unit rates, and exclusions

Risk and documentation

20 points

COIs, testing, reporting, and acceptance

Score exceptions before price

A bidder that excludes surveys, lifts, testing, or project management has not offered a cheaper version of the same work. It has offered less work.

Use anchored scoring

Define what a zero, midpoint, and full score mean for every criterion. Anchors reduce evaluator drift and make the award record defensible.

Run consensus after independent scoring

Evaluators should score alone first, then discuss large variances. Group scoring from the start lets the loudest voice set the result.

When this is not the right approach

A weighted matrix adds little value when the project is small, the scope is fixed, and every bidder is already prequalified. In that case, level exclusions and award on schedule plus price.

Q: What should the final deliverables include?

Q: How should buyers compare vendors for this work?
A: Compare line-by-line scope compliance before comparing price. Score the field-delivery plan, named responsibility, schedule, testing, documentation, escalation, COI and licensing evidence where required, commercial exceptions, unit rates, and normalized total.

Q: Does SRS Networks cover multi-site programs?
A: Yes. SRS Networks coordinates infrastructure deployment across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii using in-house W-2 field leads, a vetted subcontractor bench, six offices, dual-coast staging, and the Project Command Center for status and closeout visibility.

Q: When is SRS Networks not the right fit?
A: A weighted matrix adds little value when the project is small, the scope is fixed, and every bidder is already prequalified. In that case, level exclusions and award on schedule plus price.

A: No certification should be inferred from product or technology experience. SRS publishes a manufacturer authorization, company credential, license, or individual certification only after its active status has been verified and when it applies to the project.

## RFP MISTAKES THAT CAUSE CHANGE ORDERS

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/rfp-mistakes-that-cause-change-orders
Title: RFP Mistakes That Cause Network Change Orders | SRS Networks
Description: Prevent network-project change orders caused by missing surveys, pathways, access rules, quantities, testing, cutover ownership, unit rates, and acceptance criteria.
─────────────────────────────────────────

The network RFP mistakes that cause the most change orders are missing site surveys, uncertain quantities, undefined pathways, unstated access windows, unclear trade boundaries, absent test standards, no cutover owner, missing unit rates, and subjective acceptance. Each omission forces the bidder to make an assumption. The cheapest assumption wins the bid; the real condition becomes a change after award.

Nine omissions and their change-order mechanism

No survey

Clear pathway and normal access

Blocked route or lift requirement

No unit rates

Changes priced later

Any added drop or revisit

No trade boundary

Another contractor owns adjacent work

Power, patching, or firestopping gap

No acceptance test

Installer defines completion

Buyer requests evidence after demobilization

Unknown is not the same as excluded

Identify unknowns, assign an allowance, and state how they will be reconciled. Leaving the line out guarantees inconsistent bidder assumptions.

Access belongs in the scope

Badging, escorts, union rules, loading docks, ceiling restrictions, and after-hours windows change labor. Put them in the site matrix.

Changes need prepriced units

Carry labor classes, adds, moves, lifts, travel, and revisit rates in the award. Negotiating them during an outage removes the buyer's bargaining position.

When this is not the right approach

No RFP can eliminate changes when existing conditions are concealed or design decisions continue after award. Use surveys and a controlled allowance instead of pretending the uncertainty is gone.

### Frequently Asked Questions — rtls-deployment-partner

Q: What does an RTLS deployment partner actually install?
A: The physical layer a tracking platform runs on: RFID readers and dock-door portals, RTLS anchors and gateways mounted at height, the Cat6/Cat6A cable plant behind them, PoE switching sized for the added load, and site-readiness records for the platform designer. The platform vendor's engineers keep commissioning and configuration; the deployment partner keeps ladders, conduit, and certified drops.

Q: Do you deploy under our brand?
A: Yes. The engagement is white-label: crews present under your program, your client relationship stays yours, and the software and monitoring margin stays yours. SRS has run this model for MSPs, VARs, and national integrators since 1996 — the tracking-platform channel uses the same agreement structure and the same Project Command Center visibility.

Q: Who is physically on site — employees or subcontractors?
A: In-house W-2 leads run the work, backed by a vetted W-9 subcontractor network for geographic reach. Every sub operates under a 24-month agreement with a 150-mile non-compete, and every COI is audited in Project Command Center before dispatch — so your client's GC never issues a stop-work order over an insurance gap.

Q: Which tracking technologies do you deploy?
A: We scope physical installation for the approved tracking design. The platform, device models, required training, power and backhaul determine the work; the named delivery team and platform owner must confirm those requirements before dispatch.

Q: Do you compete with our software or services?
A: No, structurally. SRS sells no tracking software, no monitoring service, and no hardware — we install, configure to your spec, and project-manage. There is no product line for your account team to collide with, which is the point of using a deployment specialist instead of an integrator that also sells a competing platform.

Q: How does hardware logistics work on a national rollout?
A: Through our West and East Coast staging facilities. Readers, anchors, and switches arrive at the nearer facility, get configured and labeled per site, and ship to site with a named recipient. Roughly 1 in 6 direct-to-site shipments fails on first delivery — wrong dock, no signature, nobody told receiving — and pre-staging is what keeps a 60-site schedule intact.

Q: What documentation does each site close out with?
A: As-builts, a labeling schedule, Fluke test reports for every drop, mounting-height and placement records against your design rules, and photo documentation — all tracked in Project Command Center where your team and your client can see per-site status live. Your commissioning engineers start from a documented site, not a discovery walk.

Q: What are the commercial terms?
A: NET 30 payment terms with 40/30/30 milestone billing on project work orders — 40% at kickoff, 30% at midpoint signoff, 30% at completion signoff. One SOW covers the program; per-site work orders ride under it. W-9, COI, MSA, and NDA templates are available on request from partners@srsnetworks.com.

Q: What is the minimum engagement size?
A: The economics work at multi-site scale. Below roughly 25 sites, program coordination overhead eats the margin and we will usually advise running your pilot with a local shop — then bringing us the fleet rollout. If the pilot site is the template for a 40-facility program, involving us at the pilot is worth it so the install standard is set once.

## SAMPLE NETWORK CABLING RFP

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/sample-network-cabling-rfp
Title: Sample Network Cabling RFP, Annotated (Free) | SRS Networks
Description: A complete filled-in structured cabling RFP with an annotation under every clause explaining what it prevents. Free, ungated, 12 clauses, no email required.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Clause 5 — Testing and certification

Every drop shall be certified with a Fluke DSX-series tester to the permanent-link standard for Category 6A. Vendor shall deliver a PDF test report per drop, exported from the tester, plus a summary sheet showing pass/fail by drop ID. Any failing drop shall be remediated and retested at vendor cost prior to acceptance.

The single most load-bearing clause in the document. It names the instrument, the standard, the deliverable format, and who pays for failures. Without it, “tested” can mean a continuity check.

Clause 6 — Deliverables at closeout

(a) Fluke certification reports, PDF, per drop. (b) As-built drawings. (c) Labeling schedule mapping faceplate ID to patch-panel port. (d) Photo documentation. (e) Manufacturer warranty registration. Final payment is contingent on delivery of items (a) through (e).

Ties final payment to documentation. This is the only reliable mechanism for actually receiving as-builts — every other approach depends on goodwill after the money is gone.

Clause 10 — Pricing format

Pricing shall be submitted on the Attachment C schedule: per-drop unit rate by category; per-site mobilization; pathway and firestop as separate lines; project management as a stated line item or percentage; after-hours premium as a percentage. Lump-sum-only responses will be considered non-responsive.

Unit rates in the bid are the buyer's only leverage on change orders after award. Declaring lump-sum-only bids non-responsive is what makes bidders actually comply.

### Frequently Asked Questions — sample-network-cabling-rfp

Q: What does a network cabling RFP need to contain?
A: Twelve clauses: introduction and background, scope of work, site inventory, technical specification, testing and certification, closeout deliverables, labeling scheme, schedule and work hours, vendor qualifications, pricing format, evaluation criteria, and submission instructions. Nearly every clause exists to convert something normally discovered after award — an exclusion, a premium, a missing document — into something priced during competition.

Q: Is the sample based on a real client project?
A: No. The buyer, sites, dates, addresses, and contacts are fictional placeholders in brackets — no real organization, client, or location appears anywhere in the document. SRS does not publish client names, site details, or identifying information under any circumstances. The technical clauses, standards, and evaluation weights are real and reusable as written.

Q: What is the most important clause in a cabling RFP?
A: The testing and certification clause. It should name the instrument and standard (Fluke DSX-series, permanent-link, for the category specified), the deliverable format (a PDF report per drop), and who pays for remediation when a drop fails. Without that specificity, “tested” can legitimately mean a continuity check — which verifies the cable conducts and nothing else.

Q: How do I make sure I actually receive as-builts at closeout?
A: Tie final payment to the documentation. The sample's clause 6 lists the closeout package — certification reports, as-builts, labeling schedule, photos, warranty registration — and states that final payment is contingent on delivering all of it. Every other approach depends on vendor goodwill after the money has been paid, which is not a mechanism.

Q: Why does the sample reject lump-sum-only pricing?
A: Because unit rates in the original bid are the buyer's only leverage on change orders after award. Without per-drop, per-site, and adds pricing locked in, every mid-project addition gets priced from scratch with no competitive pressure — typically at a substantial premium. Declaring lump-sum-only responses non-responsive is what makes bidders actually itemize.

Q: Should I include a site inventory attachment?
A: Yes — it is worth more than the rest of the document combined. Address, square footage, ceiling type, closet location, occupied status, and permitted work hours per site is what converts a guess into a price. Calling out the two or three hardest sites by exception also prevents an averaged bid that under-prices them and over-prices everything else.

Q: Can I edit the sample or delete clauses?
A: Yes, it is published for unlimited use. Deleting clauses that do not apply is encouraged — a shorter RFP that is fully answerable produces better responses than a long one padded with boilerplate nobody scores. Read the annotation first, though: it names the specific failure each clause prevents, so you can tell what deleting it costs you.

Q: Is this template free, and do I have to give an email address?
A: Free, and no. The download is a direct PDF link with no form and no email capture. Gating it would defeat the purpose — a gated document cannot be cited by an AI answer engine, cannot be forwarded to a colleague, and mostly collects addresses from people who wanted a document rather than a vendor.

Q: Will SRS Networks review my RFP before I issue it?
A: Yes, free, and without requiring that we bid on it. Send your version to partners@srsnetworks.com and a senior project manager will flag scope gaps, missing certification language, and clauses bidders typically exploit on multi-site cabling work. A well-scoped RFP is cheaper for every bidder to answer, including us — that is the entire reason this is published ungated.

Q: What exactly does SRS deliver on a SARA or Stanley Healthcare project?

Q: Why does RTLS need a different Wi-Fi design than regular corporate Wi-Fi?
A: Stanley/Securitas Healthcare RTLS (AeroScout, Hugs, Roam Alert) locates tags by triangulating signal strength across multiple access points. A network designed for laptop coverage will leave gaps in stairwells, courtyards, and dense rooms — exactly where wander-management and infant-protection accuracy matter most. We do a tag-aware site survey, set the AP density accordingly, and validate coverage tag-by-tag.

Q: Do you handle the integration with SARA itself, or just the network?
A: Network, cabling, wireless, PoE edge, and endpoint installation — that's our scope. SARA platform configuration, alerting protocols, escalation paths, and the discovery process with Status Solutions stay with the authorized integrator. We hand them documented as-builts and working endpoints; they bring up the platform on top of it.

Q: Can you do a national rollout across multiple sites?
A: Yes. Multi-site is what we do. SRS Networks has deployed across 10,000+ sites in the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996. One PM, one client portal (Project Command Center), W-2 leads in every region, and a vetted subcontractor bench where it makes sense — so a 30-site senior-living rollout or a 200-site K-12 mass notification project runs to one schedule and one standard.

Q: Which industries do you most commonly deploy SARA + Stanley Healthcare infrastructure for?

Q: Do you handle the mass notification endpoints — IP speakers, digital signage, desktop alerting endpoints?

Desktop alerting endpoints rely on the corporate network we segment for life-safety priority. Every endpoint is documented and labeled at handoff.

Q: Why W-2 leads instead of subcontractors?
A: Life-safety and RTLS work has zero tolerance for the kind of inconsistency you get when a different two-person crew shows up every week. We use a vetted subcontractor bench for surge capacity and remote regions, but every project has an SRS W-2 lead on it.

### Frequently Asked Questions — sd-wan-deployment

Q: We already chose our SD-WAN vendor. Do you deploy it, or do we have to buy through you?
A: You deploy it through us regardless of where the hardware came from. We are the field execution team, not the resale channel, so the platform decision stays yours. We stage and install VeloCloud, Meraki MX, Fortinet Secure SD-WAN, Cato, Prisma SD-WAN, Aruba EdgeConnect, Versa, and Catalyst SD-WAN edges the same way: claimed to your orchestrator or tenant, configured from your template, installed to your design, validated against your policy.

Q: Why stage the appliances instead of drop-shipping them from the vendor to each site?
A: Because drop-shipping is where multi-site rollouts fail. At scale roughly one in six shipments arrives damaged, wrong, opened, or cannot be located when the tech shows up, and every one of those is a wasted truck roll plus a schedule slip. We land the gear at our West or East Coast staging facility instead, serialize each unit to a site ID, license and claim it, match firmware, activate the SIM, burn it in on the bench, and ship a complete kit that includes mounting hardware, optics, antenna, and a site-specific install sheet.

Q: How many sites can you deploy at once, and how long does a 200-site rollout take?
A: We run rollouts from 20 sites to several hundred and have completed 900+ deployments across 10,000+ sites since 1996. Throughput on a 200-site program is driven almost entirely by circuit readiness and how many cutover windows your business can absorb per week, not by crew availability. A typical 200-site estate runs 12 to 20 weeks from kickoff, with the survey pass front-loaded and installs clustered regionally. We give you a site-by-site calendar after the survey, not a guess before it.

Q: Who deals with the carriers on new circuits?
A: We do, per site, if you want us to. We place or take over the order, hold the ticket, track the FOC date, confirm the handoff type and delivered speed, and test the circuit before cutover night rather than discovering a dead demarc with a tech standing at the rack. Carriers slip. When a site slips we re-sequence it into a later cluster and move the crew to a ready site, so the schedule absorbs the delay instead of burning a dispatch.

Q: How do you schedule cutovers across sites in different time zones with different hours?
A: Each site gets a window built around its own operating hours, not around our crew calendar. Retail typically cuts pre-open, clinics after the last patient, distribution centers at shift changeover, and 24/7 facilities during their lowest-volume block. We cluster sites regionally so a crew covers several locations in one trip, and the whole calendar lives in the Project Command Center so your team can see what is scheduled where without asking for a status spreadsheet.

Q: What actually gets tested at turn-up before your tech leaves the site?
A: We confirm the tunnels to your hubs or cloud gateways establish, confirm the routing and QoS policy actually pushed from the controller instead of assuming it did, and verify DHCP, DNS, and VLAN behavior at the edge. Then we test the applications that matter at that specific site — POS to the payment processor, EMR load, phone registration, ERP client. Finally we pull the primary transport on purpose to force a failover, confirm sessions survive on the secondary or LTE path, and fail back. A site whose failover has never been exercised is a site whose failover does not work yet.

Q: What happens if the site has problems after your crew leaves?
A: The legacy edge stays racked and reversible through an agreed soak period, and the rollback runbook for that site is written before the cutover rather than improvised at 3am. If the overlay misbehaves on night four, your NOC or ours has a documented path back to the previous state without waiting on a dispatch. Once the soak passes clean, we return, pull the old hardware, and hand it to your reverse-logistics process or run it through our network decommissioning workflow.

Q: Do you do the site surveys, or do we send you our own data?
A: Either works, but we strongly recommend a survey pass. We document the demarc type and location, the existing router or firewall, available rack or wall space, power and outlet reach, the cable path from demarc to rack, and the LTE or 5G signal read at the exact mounting point rather than at the front counter. The output is a readiness sheet per site that flags the locations needing electrical, mounting, or cabling remediation before a network tech is worth sending. If you already have current survey data in a usable format, we will validate a sample and work from yours.

Q: What documentation do we get per site at closeout?
A: Serials mapped to site ID, circuit IDs and carrier account references, WAN addressing, SIM or ICCID identifiers, firmware and config version, throughput and forced-failover test results, and photos of the finished install. It rolls up into an estate-level record so a year from now your team can answer what is deployed where, on what circuit, at what version, without a discovery project. Every site status also updates live in the Project Command Center during the rollout.

Q: How is SD-WAN deployment priced?
A: Per site, with the estate size and the scope per location driving the number. The variables are survey scope, staging and kitting per unit, whether new cabling or electrical work is needed at the edge, after-hours versus business-hours labor, whether we are holding carrier circuits, and whether decommission and reverse logistics are in scope. We quote after the site list and a survey sample, typically within 5 business days, and the price holds per site across the estate so your finance team is not re-approving every wave.

Overcrowded Closets with No Organization

Equipment stacked on shelves, wall-mounted without rack enclosures, and buried under years of added devices. No one knows what everything does or where any cable goes.

Poor Cooling Causing Equipment Failures

Switches, firewalls, and servers generate significant heat. Without dedicated cooling, ambient temperature climbs until equipment throttles, locks up, or fails permanently.

Tangled Cables with No Labeling

Insufficient Power and No UPS

Network equipment running on shared branch circuits with no battery backup. A single power event takes down the entire network - and there's no protection against surges or brownouts.

No Physical Security for Network Equipment

An unlocked closet shared with HVAC equipment, cleaning supplies, or building maintenance is not a secure infrastructure space. Physical access to network equipment is a significant security risk.

### Frequently Asked Questions — sip-trunking

Q: What is SIP trunking, and how is it different from a VoIP phone system?
A: SIP trunking is the carrier layer — the IP connection that carries calls between your PBX and the public telephone network, replacing PRI or analog trunks. A VoIP phone system is everything above that line: the PBX platform, handsets, softphones, auto attendants, and call routing. They are bought and deployed separately, and you can migrate the trunk without touching the phone system if your PBX supports SIP. We do both, but this page covers the trunk work specifically.

Q: How many SIP channels do we need to replace our existing PRIs?
A: Almost never the same number. A PRI sells in fixed 23-channel blocks, so a branch that peaks at nine simultaneous calls still pays for 23. We pull call detail records from your PBX, model the busy hour per site, and size concurrent call paths against actual traffic. Because SIP channels can be pooled across the whole estate rather than stranded per location, most multi-site migrations end up buying meaningfully fewer paths than the sum of the PRI channels they replace.

Q: How much bandwidth does each SIP call consume?
A: Budget roughly 87 kbps per concurrent call in each direction on G.711 with 20 ms packetization, once RTP, UDP, IP, and Ethernet overhead are counted. G.729a compresses that to about 31 kbps per call at some cost to audio quality, and Opus varies with the bit rate negotiated. Multiply per-call bandwidth by the concurrent call paths that site will use, then reserve it in a priority queue at the WAN edge rather than assuming the circuit has headroom.

Q: Do we keep our existing phone numbers?
A: Yes. Local number portability lets you carry main lines, DID ranges, and toll-free numbers to the new carrier. The failures come from process, not policy: a port request that does not match the losing carrier's Customer Service Record gets rejected, and a billing telephone number ported before its associated DIDs can strand the rest of the range. We pull the CSR first, sequence DIDs ahead of the BTN, and clear any account-level port freeze or PIN before filing.

Q: How long does number porting take across dozens of locations?
A: A simple port on a single site typically confirms in one to two weeks from a clean LSR submission. Complex ports — large DID ranges, multiple losing carriers, or accounts with contract disputes — run three to six weeks and reject more often. On a multi-site estate we do not port everything at once. We run a pilot site first, learn that carrier's rejection patterns, then move in regional waves with the FOC date for every site tracked individually.

Q: Do we need a session border controller, or can we point the PBX at the carrier?
A: For a multi-site business, deploy the SBC. It gives you the security boundary that a firewall alone does not: topology hiding, TLS and SRTP termination, access lists restricted to the carrier's signaling IPs, and rate limiting against the SIP scanning traffic that hits any public endpoint within hours. It also handles transcoding and the header rewrites carriers expect. We deploy on Ribbon, AudioCodes, or Cisco CUBE depending on call volume and what your team already supports.

Q: How does 911 work at each location on SIP trunking?
A: Every location needs its own registered dispatchable location, not one address on the account. RAY BAUM'S Act requires the PSAP to receive a street address plus floor, suite, or similar detail, and Kari's Law requires direct 911 dialing without an access prefix plus on-site notification when a call is placed. We register an emergency response location per site, validate each address against the MSAG before cutover, and place live test calls to confirm the PSAP sees the correct address.

Q: What happens to fax machines, elevator phones, and fire alarm lines?
A: These are the items that derail otherwise clean migrations, so we inventory them on day one. Fax can often move to T.38 or stay on G.711 pass-through, but high-volume or legacy machines sometimes justify keeping one analog line. Elevator emergency phones and fire alarm communicators frequently carry code or AHJ requirements for a supervised path, and a plain ATA does not always satisfy them. We identify each one, confirm the requirement with the authority having jurisdiction, and either keep a POTS line or deploy a listed replacement.

Q: What happens to inbound calls if a site's internet circuit fails?
A: That is a routing design decision, and it should be made before cutover rather than discovered during an outage. We configure the carrier to detect trunk loss — typically through SIP OPTIONS keepalive failure — and automatically reroute inbound calls to a secondary destination: a backup circuit, an LTE or 5G path, a mobile number list, or another site's queue. Outbound survivability at the site depends on the gateway configuration. Either way, calls land somewhere a person answers instead of ringing into a dead trunk.

Q: Can we keep our existing PBX, and do you work with our carrier?
A: Usually yes on both. If your PBX supports SIP trunking natively or through a gateway, we migrate the trunk and leave the phone system in place — that is often the cheapest path and the smallest change for your users. We are carrier-agnostic: deploy on the SIP provider you already selected, or we can run a selection process and interop-test the finalists. If the PBX is genuinely end-of-life, we will tell you, and the platform replacement is scoped separately.

Q: Is SRS Networks the same company as the local Salinas IT provider?
A: No. SRS Networks (srsnetworks.com) is the nationwide enterprise infrastructure deployment business — SIP trunking migrations, voice and data cabling, and network deployment across the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii since 1996, with offices in Salinas, South San Francisco, Pasadena, Boise, Boston, and Dallas. It is a separate company from any local Salinas or Monterey managed IT services provider. If you need one partner to migrate voice trunks across a multi-site footprint, that is us.

### Frequently Asked Questions — smart-building-integration

Q: What do building IoT installation services include?
A: The agreed scope can include device mounting, power and data connections, gateway setup support, device inventory and witnessed connectivity checks. Platform configuration and specialist commissioning must be specified separately.

Q: Does connecting a sensor prove its readings are accurate?
A: No. A successful connection proves the agreed communication path. Sensor accuracy and calibration require the device or controls specialist's acceptance process.

Q: Who should approve the IoT network connection?
A: The site's IT owner should approve network placement, permitted traffic and credential handling before devices are connected. Facilities and the platform provider should confirm how the data will be used.

Q: What information is needed for an IoT installation estimate?
A: Provide the device schedule, intended locations, mounting and power requirements, network design, platform owner and operating-hour constraints. Identify any calibration or controls work separately.

Q: Can existing building cabling be reused?
A: Survey the proposed links and confirm their suitability against the device and project requirements. Reuse depends on the actual endpoints, condition, capacity and acceptance results.

Q: Does the installation include the IoT platform subscription?
A: Include platform licensing and recurring service responsibilities explicitly in the agreement. They should not be assumed to be included in a device installation price.

Q: What should the building receive at handover?
A: Request device locations and identifiers, connection records, the approved acceptance results and a list of open issues with owners. Keep platform and facilities contacts with those records.

Q: Are life-safety sensors covered by a general IoT scope?
A: Life-safety systems need their own approved design, qualified delivery team and acceptance requirements. A general building-network scope does not establish those capabilities.

Structured cabling company FAQs

### Frequently Asked Questions — structured-cabling-company

Q: What does a structured cabling company do?
A: A structured cabling company builds the physical layer that carries data, voice, wireless, security, and building-system traffic. Work commonly includes pathways, copper and fiber cable, terminations, racks, patch panels, labels, performance testing, punch correction, and as-built records.

Q: How should I compare structured cabling companies?
A: Compare the defined scope and acceptance evidence, not only the bottom-line bid. Check survey assumptions, material responsibility, crew qualifications, insurance, schedule ownership, test method, labeling standard, exclusions, change-order rules, closeout files, warranty conditions, and who owns punch correction.

Q: What is the difference between structured cabling and electrical wiring?
A: Structured cabling is the low-voltage communications infrastructure used for network, voice, wireless, security, and related systems. Electrical wiring distributes power and is governed by a different trade scope, code path, and licensing framework; project documents must define where the two trades coordinate at racks, grounding, pathways, and powered devices.

Q: Should every installed cable be certification tested?
A: The test requirement should match the system design and contract. For category-rated permanent links, certification with calibrated equipment provides evidence of performance headroom that continuity, wiremap, or a live ping cannot; fiber acceptance should likewise define the required loss or OTDR testing and limits.

Q: What documentation should a structured cabling company deliver?
A: Require test-result files, a port-to-panel schedule, marked or as-built drawings, the final label scheme, completion photos, resolved punch records, and warranty documents. The identifiers in those files must match the faceplates, patch panels, racks, and rooms visible onsite.

Q: Can SRS Networks handle multi-site structured cabling?
A: Yes. SRS has completed 900+ deployments across 10,000+ sites and serves the 48 contiguous states, Alaska, and Hawaii. One project manager holds the field standard, schedule, exceptions, test format, and closeout requirements across markets.

Q: How are warranties handled on installed datacom products?
A: Warranty coverage depends on the actual devices, manufacturer terms, specified program, and executed project agreement. SRS can advise on available manufacturer coverage or contractually provide the applicable warranty terms for the selected products.

Q: When should I hire a local structured cabling company instead?
A: Hire a qualified local contractor for a very small, single-metro job when immediate drive time and low mobilization overhead matter more than centralized program control. SRS is the stronger fit for planned commercial work, repeat sites, multiple markets, channel delivery, and projects requiring consistent testing and documentation.
