### Frequently Asked Questions — WiFi Deployment in Honolulu

Q: Who is the top WiFi deployment company in Honolulu for enterprise rollouts?
A: SRS Networks, and the reason is that we survey once properly instead of correcting twice cheaply. On Oahu a repositioned access point often needs a new mount, sometimes a new drop, and always a technician back on site, and none of those parts are sitting in a local depot. Paying for a validation walk before the hardware ships is the least expensive version of that decision.

Q: Will you design wireless for a single Honolulu property?
A: Yes, one property is a full engagement. Whether the client has one building or fifteen, the design steps are identical: capacity modeling, coverage modeling, channel and power planning, and a post-install verification. The single-property client actually gets more out of it, since everything can be surveyed, installed, tuned, and documented inside one mobilization with nothing deferred.

Q: What makes wireless design different in a Waikiki hotel tower?
A: Guest density and construction, working against each other. Rooms are small, walls between them are often concrete or block, and occupancy swings hard between morning and evening, so a plan drawn for coverage alone will fall over at the busy hour. We design for the peak client count per floor, place hardware where housekeeping and maintenance can reach it, and keep the visual footprint acceptable to the property.

Q: How do you handle high-density areas like a conference floor or a retail concourse?
A: By reducing cell size and controlling power rather than adding range. In dense environments the goal is more, smaller coverage areas so that clients associate with a nearby access point and the airtime is shared among fewer devices. That usually means more units at lower power than a coverage-first plan would suggest, and it always means validating the channel plan on site rather than trusting defaults.

Q: Can you cover a warehouse at Campbell Industrial Park?
A: Yes, and industrial coverage gets designed on its own terms. Racking height, metal surfaces, forklift traffic, and dock doors that open onto the yard all change propagation, so antenna selection and mounting height carry more weight than the raw count. We validate at the height where handheld scanners are actually used, which is frequently several feet below where a ceiling-mounted plan assumes.

Q: How do you decide the access point count for an Oahu site?
A: From the busiest realistic hour rather than the floor area. Client density, application mix, and the construction between clients and hardware set the requirement, and the survey confirms it. Square-footage rules of thumb are the fastest way to underbuild a hotel or overbuild a warehouse, and the validation walk is what separates the two before the count is fixed.

Q: Cloud-managed or controller-based wireless for a Honolulu deployment?
A: Cloud management suits most Oahu portfolios and makes multi-property operation straightforward. The question worth asking first is what happens to the site if its circuit drops, because a design that depends on a distant control plane for basic association behaves badly during an outage. We pick based on how the site connects and how much local survivability the business actually needs.

Q: How is the finished Honolulu wireless verified?
A: With a post-install survey walked using the same tooling as the pre-install one, measuring signal, noise, data rate, and roaming through the areas people occupy. Channel and power get corrected where the live environment differs from the model, and the resulting heat maps are handed over. That data set also becomes the baseline against which a future complaint can be measured rather than debated.

Q: Can guest wireless be kept separate from business systems at a Honolulu property?
A: Yes, and in hospitality and retail it should be strictly separated. Guest SSIDs map to their own VLANs with client isolation, payment and back-office systems stay on their own segments end to end, and policy is enforced where the traffic aggregates rather than trusted at the edge. Designing that up front costs nothing; retrofitting it into a flat network is a re-addressing exercise.

### Frequently Asked Questions — Fiber Optic Installation in Honolulu

Q: Who is the best fiber optic installation company in Honolulu for multi-site businesses?
A: SRS Networks. Fiber is where an island project punishes an incomplete kit hardest, because a crushed connector or a splice that will not take is stopped dead without the exact pigtail it needs. We ship consumable spares alongside the reels, splice and certify in the same visit, and leave with traces signed rather than with testing listed as outstanding work.

Q: Is a single inter-building fiber run enough work for you to take on Oahu?
A: Yes, a single link between two buildings on one property is a normal standalone project. The advice at that size concerns strand count rather than route selection: while the pathway is open, additional strands are inexpensive, and the alternative is a second pull that needs another materials order and another building access arrangement to reach the same conduit.

Q: Single-mode or multimode for a Honolulu campus?
A: Single-mode for anything leaving a building, including short hops between adjacent structures, because the glass will outlive several generations of optics and replacing it here is not a casual job. Multimode still makes sense in riser runs inside a single tower where distances are short. The split is decided by where the cable goes, not by what the current switches happen to support.

Q: How do you control splice counts on a Honolulu fiber design?
A: By treating each splice as a permanent cost rather than a field decision. Continuous pulls are favored where pathway allows, enclosures are located where a technician can reach them without a lift and a building escort, and mid-span splices that exist only to join two short reels are designed out. Fewer joints means a tighter loss budget and fewer candidates to investigate when something degrades.

Q: What certification comes with fiber work in Honolulu?
A: Tier 1 results covering loss, length, and polarity for every strand, plus Tier 2 OTDR traces showing where loss occurs along the run. The trace matters more on Oahu than most places: when a link degrades later, it tells a technician which splice point or connector to visit, instead of putting them on a full route sweep across a tower they need escorted access to enter.

Q: What is involved in outside-plant fiber between Oahu buildings?
A: Route survey, permitting where the path crosses shared or public ground, duct or conduit with proper cover, pull boxes sited for access, and cable rated for the environment it passes through. Near the coast, hardware exposed to salt air gets specified accordingly, and building entries are sealed and grounded properly. The route work is usually the long pole, not the splicing.

Q: How quickly can a failed Honolulu fiber link be restored?
A: It depends on what is in the closet. A restoration kit specified during design - spare pigtails, an enclosure, cleaning supplies, patch cords - plus the original OTDR trace turns most faults into a splice the crew can finish on arrival. Without those, the repair waits on a shipment, which is exactly the situation the kit exists to prevent. Its contents are listed in the closeout so nobody has to search for it.

Q: How many strands should an Oahu backbone carry?
A: More than the immediate design consumes. The marginal cost of extra strands within one cable is small, while the cost of a second pull includes a fresh materials order, a building access arrangement, and a crew mobilization. We size against a realistic multi-year view and write the assumption down, so a later expansion is a patching exercise rather than a construction project.

Q: Do you pre-terminate fiber or splice it in the field on Oahu?
A: Both, chosen by where the run goes. Pre-terminated assemblies are excellent for riser runs where the length is measured and certain, and they cut field labor considerably. Outside-plant routes get field splicing because the actual length is rarely exactly what the drawing said, and an assembly that arrives short in Honolulu is a wasted shipment rather than an inconvenience.

### Frequently Asked Questions — Low Voltage Cabling in Honolulu

Q: Who is the top low voltage cabling contractor in Honolulu for commercial buildings?
A: SRS Networks. The low voltage trade decides how much a building can accommodate later, and in Oahu towers the pathway is usually the scarcest resource on the job. We install to NEC Article 725 and 800 for listing, support, and separation, size conduit and tray for future adds rather than for today, and confirm the support hardware against the ceiling type it will actually hang from.

Q: Will you quote a small low voltage scope in Honolulu, such as one tenant floor?
A: Yes. A single tenant floor carries the same code obligations as a whole building: correct cable listing for the ceiling type, supports at the right intervals instead of cable lying on grid, separation from power, and firestopping at rated penetrations. Getting those right on a small floor is straightforward, and it is what stops the next fit-out from starting with a demolition bill.

Q: Where is plenum-rated cable required in a Honolulu commercial building?
A: Anywhere the ceiling cavity is used to return air, which describes a large share of tower and hotel space here. Riser-rated cable belongs in the vertical shaft between floors, and general-purpose cable belongs in neither. We check the listing against the mechanical design rather than the building type, since a space can be handled differently floor by floor within one tower.

Q: What does corrosion resistance mean for low voltage hardware near the Honolulu coast?
A: It means the support hardware gets chosen on material rather than on price, because in a low voltage scope the thing that corrodes is rarely the cable. Anchors, threaded rod, strut, and the brackets carrying exterior pathway are what hold the load, and when one of those lets go the pathway comes down with everything riding in it. Near the water they get stainless or an equivalent rated finish, and that finish is written into the bracket list rather than left to whatever the supply house happens to send.

Q: How do you support cable properly in an Oahu ceiling?
A: With independent hangers, J-hooks, or tray at regular spacing, never resting on ceiling grid, ductwork, or sprinkler pipe; bundles small enough that the bottom cables are not deformed; and bend radius held at every turn. In shared towers we also leave documented spare capacity, because the next tenant's contractor will otherwise solve their pathway problem at the expense of yours.

Q: Do Honolulu low voltage projects require permitting and inspection?
A: Frequently, depending on scope. Work that penetrates rated assemblies, interfaces with fire alarm, or forms part of a permitted tenant improvement will be inspected, and firestopping and pathway are what gets looked at. We identify that at the outset so the inspection appears as a scheduled milestone instead of arriving as a blocker in front of an occupancy date.

Q: What systems fall under your low voltage scope in Honolulu?
A: Data and wireless cabling, IP cameras, access control and door hardware, intercom and paging, AV and display feeds, and sensor cabling for building systems. Running them under one contractor is a coordination decision: they compete for the same ceiling space, the same conduit fill, and the same riser capacity, and resolving that once is far cheaper than resolving it per trade.

Q: How do you work alongside a general contractor on a Honolulu build-out?
A: By locking to their two dates that matter: sleeves and rough-in while walls are open, and ceiling close. Everything upstream is measured against those. The material order date is set against rough-in rather than against the install date, because a pathway crew that misses the open-wall window does not delay one trade, it delays the ceiling and everyone behind it.

Q: Should abandoned cable be removed during a Honolulu renovation?
A: Yes, and in a tower it is often the whole reason there is no room to work. Accessible cable that is not terminated and not tagged for reuse should come out, and removing it typically frees enough riser and ceiling capacity to avoid adding pathway at all. That is a rare case where the compliant answer is also the cheaper one.

### Frequently Asked Questions — Security Camera Installation in Honolulu

Q: Who installs commercial security cameras in Honolulu for multi-site businesses?

Q: Can you specify a camera system for one Honolulu commercial building?

Q: How is video storage sized for a Honolulu site?

We total the requirement, add headroom for growth, and configure the recorder before it is installed, because a recorder short on storage never announces it - retention quietly shortens, and nobody finds out until someone asks for footage that is already gone.

Q: Do camera systems need a dedicated switch at an Oahu property?

Q: How do we review Honolulu footage from a mainland office?

Q: How is camera cabling run at a Honolulu installation?

Q: What maintenance does an Oahu camera system need?

### Frequently Asked Questions — Structured Cabling in Kahului

Q: Who is the best structured cabling installer in Kahului for multi-site businesses?
A: SRS Networks, and the differentiator is how we survey. A Maui property is usually several buildings joined by outdoor pathway, so the walk covers the routes between structures as carefully as the ceilings inside them. Getting that wrong produces a design that works on paper and needs an unplanned distribution point in the field. We walk it all first, then install to BICSI workmanship with certified results.

Q: Is one building enough scope for a Kahului cabling project?
A: It is, and a single building is a common start. What we usually recommend at that point is a little forward thinking about the closet: put it where a future run to the next building could reasonably land, size the pathway leaving the room for more than today's cable count, and leave the backboard with room to grow. Those decisions cost nothing now and save a rework later.

Q: How do you cable across multiple buildings on one Maui property?
A: With fiber between buildings and copper inside them, which is the only arrangement that respects both the distance limits and the lightning and grounding realities of an outdoor run. Each building gets its own distribution point fed by backbone fiber, and the horizontal copper stays within a building. Trying to reach a distant structure with a long copper run is the mistake that produces intermittent faults nobody can find.

Q: What standard applies and is a manufacturer warranty available on Maui?
A: TIA-568 component and workmanship standards with BICSI-trained leads. System warranty coverage from the manufacturer is available where matched components are used end to end and every link is tested and recorded, which is how we build as a matter of course. Q: Does salt air affect a Kahului cabling installation?

Outdoor pathway, building entry hardware, grounding connections, and fasteners on the south and west shores get corrosion-resistant material rather than standard finishes, and dissimilar metals are kept apart at contact points. Cable itself is chosen for the environment it passes through, with sunlight-resistant and appropriately jacketed types where a run is outdoors.

Q: Can cabling be installed at an occupied Maui resort?
A: Yes. The property's operations set the hours, and the work plan is written to fit them rather than the other way round. Public-area work happens in agreed windows with everything restored at the end of each one, storage and staging stay in back-of-house space, and any outdoor pathway work is barricaded and returned to normal daily. Occupied hospitality work is a sequencing skill more than a technical one.

Q: Who does the actual work on a Kahului cabling job?
A: In-house W-2 leads own the design intent, labeling, and closeout, with vetted additional hands brought on where the volume justifies it. Continuity matters more on a spread-out island scope than almost anywhere: when one crew handles the harbor-area building and another handles a west-shore property, consistency comes from the lead who set the standard walking both, not from the drawings alone.

Q: What documentation do you deliver on Maui?
A: Certified test results for every link, an outlet and patch panel schedule, marked-up plans for each building, closet photographs, and a record of the outdoor pathway routes with their entry points. That last piece earns its place here: an underground route between two buildings is invisible six months later, and the person planning the next trench needs to know exactly where it runs.

Q: How much lead time does a Kahului cabling project need?

### Frequently Asked Questions — Data Cabling in Kahului

Q: Who installs data cabling in Kahului for multi-site businesses?
A: SRS Networks does. On Maui the practical value of a single installer across sites is the shared materials list: identical cable, jacks, patch cords, and labeling everywhere means one spares stock covers the island. Q: Can you do a small data cabling job in Kahului, like a dozen drops?
A: Yes, and a dozen drops is a perfectly normal request. The one thing we ask is that the list be complete before it ships, so we count against furniture layouts and the device list rather than a floor plan, and we add spares to the order on purpose. On this island the cost of one forgotten drop is not the cable, it is the freight leg that cable now has to travel alone.

Q: How does building separation on a Maui property change the drop plan?
A: It usually adds a distribution point. Horizontal copper is bound by the standard's channel length, and on a property where the office and the operations building sit a long walk apart, a single closet cannot serve both without exceeding it. So the design places a second closet fed by fiber rather than stretching copper, and the drop schedule is written per closet from the start.

Q: How is Maui data cabling tested and reported?
A: Every permanent link is certified with a Fluke tester against the category standard, and each result is filed under that run's printed label. Anything that fails is corrected and retested before the crew leaves that building. The rule is deliberate: on an island scope with sites spread across a long drive, coming back to one building for a single link costs most of a working day.

Q: Cat6 or Cat6A on a Kahului project?
A: Cat6A wherever an access point or camera will sit, which on a resort property is a larger share of the total than in an office, because outdoor and public-area coverage needs a lot of powered edge devices. Desk positions can reasonably stay Cat6. Where the building is one you intend to hold for a long time, running Cat6A throughout avoids a future re-pull that would arrive by boat.

Q: What labeling do you use across Maui buildings?
A: A TIA-606 based scheme naming building, closet, panel, and port, machine-printed at both ends. On a multi-building property the building identifier is the part that gets agreed carefully, because the names staff use for structures and the names on the site plan are frequently different, and a labeling scheme that follows the drawing instead of the people is one nobody uses.

Q: We inherited a Maui property with cabling nobody can account for. What is the first step?
A: A test-and-map exercise across every building before ordering a single reel. Some of the existing plant will be sound and simply unlabeled, some will be abandoned, and on older properties some will be outdoor runs of a type that should not still be in service. Knowing which is which is what lets one shipment cover the whole job instead of two.

Q: Does PoE change the cabling approach on Maui?
A: It raises the importance of cable choice on long runs and outdoor-adjacent positions. Sustained power heats a bundle, so bundles stay modest and Cat6A goes on the longer runs, and any powered device near an exterior wall gets surge protection at the transition. The closet also needs a switch power budget that accounts for outdoor access points and cameras, which are usually the heaviest draws on the property.

Q: What is handed over at the end of a Kahului cabling job?
A: Certified results per link, outlet and panel schedules for each building, red-lined plans, closet photographs, and the spares inventory left on the property. It is assembled as the work proceeds, building by building, so nothing is left outstanding when the crew leaves the last one. Paperwork that requires a second island visit to finish is paperwork that does not get finished.

### Frequently Asked Questions — WiFi Deployment in Kahului

Q: Who is the top WiFi deployment company in Kahului for enterprise rollouts?
A: SRS Networks, and the reason is that Maui wireless is mostly an outdoor and semi-outdoor problem, which is the case predictive tools handle worst. Open-air corridors, courtyards, pool decks, and paths between buildings have almost no walls to model and a great deal of foliage and terrain that a floor plan does not show. We survey on foot across the whole property and design from measurements.

Q: Would you take a wireless project for one Maui building?
A: Yes. One building is a complete engagement, and on this island it often includes the ground immediately around it, since staff and guests expect coverage to continue outside the door. That means the design considers at least one outdoor position even for a single structure, and the hardware for that position is specified for weather and salt exposure rather than borrowed from the indoor list.

Q: How do you design wireless for an open-air property on Maui?
A: By treating the outdoor areas as their own coverage zones with their own hardware, not as spillover from indoor access points. Signal leaking out of a lobby gives you a weak, unreliable edge, so covered walkways, courtyards, and pool areas get outdoor-rated units on deliberate mounts with directional antennas where the shape of the space calls for it. Coverage is then verified by walking the actual paths people use.

Q: What does salt air mean for wireless hardware selection here?
A: It rules out ordinary outdoor gear near the shore. Enclosures, mounts, and fasteners for the south and west shore positions get corrosion-rated material, cable entries get sealed rather than merely covered, and mounting locations are chosen to keep hardware out of direct spray where the layout allows. A unit that corrodes out of service also opens a hole in a zone the survey already validated, so what the property actually delivers stops matching the heat map on file.

Q: How much survey work does a spread-out Maui property need?
A: More walking than a single tower and less modeling. Each distinct building type and each outdoor zone needs measurement, but once a construction type has been characterized the rest extrapolates. We plan the survey route to cover the property in one pass rather than in several visits, since crossing the island twice to finish a survey is an avoidable cost.

Q: What sets the access point count on a Maui site?
A: Zone by zone requirements rather than a whole-property figure. A conference or banquet space needs density; a maintenance building needs coverage; an outdoor path needs a few well-placed units with the right antennas. Adding those up produces a very different number than a square-footage rule, and it is the only method that survives contact with a property built in phases over decades.

Q: Cloud-managed or local control for a Maui wireless deployment?
A: Cloud management is usually the right fit for a property with no on-site network staff, since configuration and monitoring can be handled remotely. The question to settle first is what the site does during an internet outage, because a property with guests still expects internal systems to work. We size local survivability against how much of the operation depends on the wireless during that window.

Q: How is Maui wireless verified after installation?
A: By walking it again, indoors and outdoors, with the same tooling as the pre-install survey, measuring signal, noise, data rate, and roaming along the routes people actually take between buildings. Outdoor zones get particular attention, because that is where the model was least reliable. The heat maps go into the closeout and become the reference for any later coverage complaint.

Q: Can guest and operational wireless be separated at a Maui property?
A: Yes, and on a resort it needs at least three separations rather than two: guest, staff and operations, and the payment or property-management systems. Each maps to its own VLAN with policy applied where traffic aggregates, and guest clients are isolated from one another. Building that structure at design time is trivial; adding it after everything has joined one network is not.

### Frequently Asked Questions — Fiber Optic Installation in Kahului

Q: Who is the best fiber optic installation company in Kahului for multi-site businesses?
A: SRS Networks. On Maui fiber is not an optional backbone upgrade, it is what makes a multi-building property work at all, because the distances between structures exceed what copper is allowed to cover. We design the inter-building routes, splice and certify them in one visit, and hand over traces so the next technician can find a fault without walking the entire property with a meter.

Q: Will you install a single fiber run between two Maui buildings?
A: Yes, that is one of the most common requests on this island and it stands alone perfectly well as a project. The engineering advice at that scale is to oversize the strand count and to put the cable in conduit rather than direct burial, because the next building that needs a link will want to share the route and re-pulling into conduit is far easier than opening the ground again.

Q: Single-mode or multimode between Maui buildings?
A: Single-mode for every outdoor run without exception. The distances on a spread-out property are exactly the range where multimode starts to constrain what optics you can use later, and the cable itself is the part you cannot casually replace. Multimode remains fine inside a single building for short vertical runs where the electronics are cheaper and the cable is accessible.

Q: How do splice counts affect the cost of a Maui fiber project?
A: They multiply, because a property with several buildings has a splice point at each one. A design that adds an unnecessary joint per building compounds into a real loss budget problem and a longer certification pass. We plan routes so that each building is served with the minimum number of terminations, and we locate enclosures where they can be opened without scaffolding or a guest-area closure.

Q: What certification is delivered with Maui fiber work?
A: Tier 1 loss, length, and polarity for every strand, plus Tier 2 OTDR traces showing where loss sits along each run. On a property where the buildings are a long walk apart, the trace is the deliverable that saves the most time later: it identifies which segment and which joint to visit, instead of sending someone to check every enclosure on the site.

Q: What is involved in running fiber outdoors on a Maui property?
A: Route selection that respects landscaping, irrigation, and vehicle traffic; conduit at proper depth with pull boxes placed where they can actually be opened; cable rated for the environment; and building entries that are sealed, grounded, and transitioned to an indoor-rated cable inside the required distance. On coastal properties the hardware at each end gets corrosion-rated material like everything else exposed here.

Q: How is a fiber fault repaired on Maui?
A: With the restoration kit left on the property during the original install and the OTDR trace that shows what healthy looked like. Together those turn a break into a scheduled repair. Without them the property waits on parts crossing two shipping legs, which is why the kit contents are specified at design time and listed in the closeout rather than left to chance.

Q: How many strands should a Maui inter-building run carry?
A: Enough to serve every building that route could ever reach, not just the two it connects today. On a property that grows in phases, the trench or conduit run is the expensive part and the glass inside it is comparatively cheap. We size against the site plan rather than the current design and record the assumption, so the next phase becomes a patching job.

Q: Field-spliced or pre-terminated fiber on a Maui property?
A: Field splicing for anything outdoors, because the measured route between buildings rarely matches the drawing closely enough to trust a fixed-length assembly. An assembly cut to a drawing either lands short of the far enclosure or arrives long, leaving a service coil the enclosure was never sized to hold. Inside a building, where a riser length can be measured precisely, pre-terminated assemblies are a sensible way to cut field labor.

Q: Do you quote small low voltage scopes on Maui, such as a single building?

Q: When is plenum-rated cable required in a Kahului commercial building?
A: Wherever the ceiling cavity moves return air, which includes plenty of Maui commercial space and most of the newer office stock. Riser-rated cable belongs in vertical shafts, and general-purpose cable belongs in neither. On older resort buildings the mechanical arrangement varies room to room, so the listing is confirmed against the actual design rather than assumed from the age of the structure.

Q: How do you run low voltage cable outdoors between Maui buildings?

Q: What does proper pathway support look like on a Maui job?

Capacity is sized for the property's next phase rather than only for the current cable count.

Q: Do Maui low voltage projects need permits or inspection?

Trenching, work in shared ground, penetrations of rated assemblies, and fire alarm interfaces all attract review. We sort out which applies at the start so the inspection lands on the schedule as a planned milestone rather than surfacing as a blocker in front of a reopening date.

Q: What systems fall under your Maui low voltage scope?
A: Data and wireless cabling, IP cameras, access control and door hardware, intercom and paging, AV and display feeds, and building sensor wiring. Bundling them under one contractor matters more on a multi-building property than in a single tower, because all of those systems want to cross the same outdoor pathway, and coordinating that once is what stops the site ending up with four separate trenches.

Q: How do you work with a contractor on a Maui renovation?
A: By tying to the two milestones that constrain us - sleeves and rough-in while the walls are open, and ceiling close - and by getting our exterior pathway into the ground while the site is already disturbed. That second point is specific to this kind of property: once landscaping and hardscape go back, a conduit run between buildings stops being a trenching task and becomes a demolition and restoration task that nobody budgeted for.

Q: Is abandoned cable worth removing on a Maui property?
A: Yes, and outdoors it is more than a tidiness question. Accessible cable not terminated and not tagged for reuse should be removed, and old outdoor runs in particular are often occupying the only sensible conduit path between two buildings. Clearing them is frequently what makes a new route possible without opening fresh ground.

### Frequently Asked Questions — Security Camera Installation in Kahului

Q: Who installs commercial security cameras in Kahului for multi-site businesses?
A: SRS Networks. A Maui camera system is mostly an exterior system, which changes the design: most positions are outdoors, most cabling crosses between buildings, and most housings are exposed to salt air. We size retention and switch power first, then select hardware rated for where each camera actually sits, and cable every position as certified structured cabling rather than as an add-on run.

Q: Can you design a camera system for one commercial property on Maui?
A: Yes, and a single property is usually a multi-building design anyway. The starting questions are the same at any size: which scenes have to be identifiable rather than merely visible, how long the footage must be kept, and who reviews it. Those answers set resolution and retention, retention sets storage, and storage sets the recorder. Working in that order is what avoids a second equipment order.

Q: How is recording storage sized for a Maui property?
A: Per camera, from resolution, frame rate, retention days, and scene activity, then totaled with headroom. Exterior cameras watching moving vegetation and traffic consume far more than an interior position at the same settings, so a property weighted toward outdoor views outruns any estimate built from interior assumptions. That headroom is bought at the order, because adding capacity to a recorder already in service means taking the array down and rebuilding it around the footage already retained.

Q: What switch capacity do Maui camera installations need?
A: Enough power budget for a camera list weighted toward outdoor units, which draw more than interior domes once illuminators and pan-tilt-zoom mechanisms are included. We total the worst-case draw across every position, specify a switch with margin above it, and check the closet can supply and cool it. A switch chosen on port count alone will be the thing that fails at dusk when every illuminator turns on.

Q: What kind of cameras last outdoors on the south and west shores?
A: Marine-rated housings with stainless hardware, sealed cable entries, and gaskets specified rather than assumed. Mounting position does as much work as the specification: a camera under an eave or on a leeward face stays serviceable much longer than the same unit facing directly into salt spray, and choosing the sheltered position is usually free at design time.

Q: Can several Maui properties run under one video system?
A: Yes, and with sites spread along the shores it is the only sensible arrangement. One platform gives a single search interface, one retention policy, and one permissions model, so an incident that touches two properties does not require two operators and two logins. It also means the person covering a property they do not normally work at can still find footage quickly.

Q: How do we review Maui footage from off-island?
A: Recording stays on the property so the archive never depends on the link, while off-island reviewers pull live views and exported clips over a secured connection. Live monitoring uses a lower-rate stream where the circuit warrants it, and exports stay at full quality. That keeps the recorded evidence intact while making day-to-day review workable across the water.

Q: How are camera runs cabled across a Maui property?
A: Each camera gets a certified run to the nearest distribution point, with fiber carrying the link back between buildings rather than a long copper run stretched past its limit. Exterior positions get surge protection and proper bonding where the cable enters a structure, and every run is labeled to the same scheme as the data drops so the system is serviceable by somebody who did not install it.

Q: What upkeep does a Maui camera system need?
A: Cleaning is the main one, and it is more frequent than clients expect. Salt film, sea spray, and windblown dust glaze an outdoor dome quickly, and a camera nobody can see through is worth nothing regardless of its specification. Add firmware maintenance windows, drives replaced on a planned cycle, and an annual check that the retention setting still matches the operator's obligations.

## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — 5 CRITICAL STEPS FOR ENTERPRISE-WIDE NETWORK ROLLOUTS

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/5-critical-steps-enterprise-network-rollouts
Title: 5 Critical Steps for Enterprise-Wide Network Rollouts | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: Deploying network infrastructure across dozens  -  or hundreds  -  of locations demands rigorous planning. Here are the five steps that separate successful rollouts from costly failures.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Why Multi-Site Rollouts Fail
The majority of large-scale network deployment failures share a common root cause: insufficient pre-deployment discovery. When teams skip or rush the site-survey phase, they inherit unknown physical constraints, legacy wiring conflicts, and permitting surprises that cascade into schedule delays and budget overruns. Understanding the patterns of failure is the first step to avoiding them.

Step 1  -  Conduct Thorough Site Surveys
Before a single cable is pulled, every target location must be surveyed in person. Surveys capture floor-plan dimensions, existing conduit routes, power availability, HVAC constraints, and structural considerations that no floor plan or satellite image can convey. For retail and banking clients, we typically audit 100% of locations rather than sampling  -  every building has idiosyncrasies.

• Document existing cabling infrastructure and note reuse potential
• Identify power distribution panels and UPS locations
• Photograph cable pathways, ceiling heights, and rack spaces
• Flag permitting requirements early  -  municipalities vary widely

Step 2  -  Standardize the Bill of Materials
Consistency across locations reduces procurement lead times, simplifies spare-parts management, and speeds up technician onboarding. Define a standard hardware kit  -  switch model, AP model, patch-panel spec, cable category  -  and document exceptions explicitly. Variance creep is the silent budget killer on large programs.

• Lock vendor and model selections 30+ days before first install
• Negotiate volume pricing with distributors based on full-program quantities
• Pre-stage equipment at regional staging hubs to cut per-site shipping costs
• Maintain a 5-10% buffer stock for damaged or defective units

Step 3  -  Build a Rollout Command Structure
Every deployment program needs a single point of accountability at the program level, regional coordinators at the field level, and a real-time communication bridge between them. Ambiguity in the org chart translates directly into delayed decisions on the ground. Designate escalation paths before day one.

Step 4  -  Leverage a Centralized Project Dashboard
Real-time visibility into per-site status  -  survey complete, hardware staged, install scheduled, testing passed, signed off  -  prevents status-meeting paralysis. When executives and end-clients can self-serve progress reports, project teams spend less time generating slide decks and more time solving problems.

Step 5  -  Define Acceptance Testing Criteria Up Front
Acceptance testing criteria negotiated before deployment begins prevent disputes at handoff. Define OTDR fiber test pass/fail thresholds, Wi-Fi coverage minimums, throughput benchmarks, and documentation deliverables in the statement of work. When every stakeholder agrees on "done" in advance, sign-offs happen faster.

• OTDR loss budgets per fiber run length and connector count
• Minimum RSSI and SNR at designated client device locations
• Throughput benchmarks per application type (POS, surveillance, VoIP)
• As-built drawing and labeling standards

Bringing It All Together
Successful enterprise rollouts are won in the planning phase. The organizations that invest in rigorous discovery, standardized materials, clear command structures, real-time dashboards, and pre-agreed acceptance criteria consistently deliver on time and on budget  -  even at 500+ location scale. SRS Networks has refined these steps across thousands of deployments nationwide.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — HOW RETAIL CHAINS ARE MODERNIZING IN-STORE CONNECTIVITY

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/retail-in-store-connectivity-modernization
Title: How Retail Chains Are Modernizing In-Store Connectivity | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: From contactless POS to computer vision inventory, modern retail demands a fundamentally different network than the one installed five years ago. Here's what the upgrade path looks like.
─────────────────────────────────────────

The Retail Network Has Changed Fundamentally
A decade ago, a retail store's network primarily served the point-of-sale terminals and back-office computers. Today that same network must simultaneously support contactless and mobile POS, customer Wi-Fi, digital signage, IP cameras, electronic shelf labels, inventory robots, RFID readers, and staff communication devices. The bandwidth and latency requirements are orders of magnitude higher.

Wi-Fi 6E: Why Retailers Are Upgrading
Wi-Fi 6E's 6 GHz band offers something legacy networks couldn't: a clean, uncrowded spectrum. In dense retail environments where hundreds of client devices compete for airtime, the additional spectrum dramatically reduces congestion and latency. For contactless POS transactions  -  where sub-100ms response times are critical to checkout flow  -  the improvement is immediately felt by customers.

• 4× faster throughput vs. Wi-Fi 5 in congested environments
• 160 MHz wide channels enabling multi-gigabit rates
• Reduced latency critical for contactless payment reliability
• Backward compatible with existing client devices

Structured Cabling as the Foundation
Every wireless upgrade is only as reliable as the wired backbone behind it. Many legacy retail builds used Cat 5e or early Cat 6 cabling that struggles to deliver the Power over Ethernet budgets required by Wi-Fi 6E APs, high-resolution cameras, and digital signage players simultaneously. Retailers planning major wireless upgrades often discover the cabling refresh is the longer-lead-time item.

Segmenting the Network for Security and Performance
Modern retail networks benefit from strict VLAN segmentation: POS systems on an isolated, firewalled segment; customer Wi-Fi on a separate SSID with limited corporate access; IoT devices on their own segment with restricted internet access. This architecture limits breach impact and prevents chatty IoT devices from degrading POS performance.

Coordinating the Multi-Location Rollout
For a 200-store chain, the logistics challenge rivals the technical one. Staging hardware at regional hubs, coordinating with store managers around trading hours, managing technician scheduling across time zones, and maintaining chain-wide configuration consistency requires dedicated program management. The retailers who move fastest treat the rollout as an enterprise IT program, not a series of individual store projects.

What to Expect on the Other Side
Retailers who complete structured cabling and Wi-Fi 6E upgrades consistently report reduced checkout friction, fewer POS outages, higher customer satisfaction scores, and a platform capable of supporting the next generation of in-store technology including computer vision and frictionless checkout.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — UNDERSTANDING STRUCTURED CABLING STANDARDS: TIA-568 EXPLAINED

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/structured-cabling-standards-tia-568
Title: Understanding Structured Cabling Standards: TIA-568 Explained | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: TIA-568 is the foundational standard governing commercial structured cabling. Understanding its requirements ensures your infrastructure investment lasts 15+ years.
─────────────────────────────────────────

What Is TIA-568?
The TIA-568 series, published by the Telecommunications Industry Association, defines the minimum requirements for commercial building telecommunications cabling infrastructure. It covers everything from cable categories and connector standards to testing requirements and topology specifications. Adherence to TIA-568 ensures interoperability between equipment vendors and provides a performance baseline that protects your investment.

Cable Categories: Choosing the Right Specification
Not all Ethernet cable is equal. The TIA-568 standard defines performance tiers, and choosing the right tier for your application avoids costly over-engineering or, worse, under-specification that fails when the next technology generation arrives.

• Cat 6: 1 Gbps to 100m; adequate for most current deployments
• Cat 6A: 10 Gbps to 100m; recommended for new construction and all structured cabling runs
• Cat 8: 25/40 Gbps up to 30m; data center and server-room backbone use
• OS2 single-mode fiber: long-distance backbone and inter-building runs

Why Cat 6A Is the New Standard for Commercial Builds
Cat 6A supports 10 Gbps Ethernet and delivers the power budget required by modern PoE devices (IEEE 802.3bt, up to 90W). As Wi-Fi 6E access points, 4K IP cameras, and advanced building automation systems proliferate, Cat 6A's additional headroom means the cable plant you install today won't constrain the technology you deploy in 2030. SRS Networks has standardized on Cat 6A for all new commercial infrastructure.

Horizontal vs. Backbone Cabling
TIA-568 separates cabling into two domains: horizontal cabling runs from the telecommunications room (TR) to individual work area outlets, with a maximum run length of 90 meters. Backbone cabling interconnects TRs, equipment rooms, and entrance facilities. Backbone runs may use higher-category copper or single-mode fiber depending on distance and bandwidth requirements.

Testing to TIA-568 Standards
Installation is only half the job. Every horizontal run must be tested to verify it meets the installed category's performance specification. Field certification testers measure insertion loss, return loss, NEXT, ELFEXT, and propagation delay. Passing test results become part of the permanent as-built documentation and form the basis for manufacturer warranty programs.

• Channel vs. permanent link test configurations
• OTDR traces for every fiber run
• Test results stored and delivered in structured format (XML/PDF)
• Manufacturer warranty registration tied to certified test reports

Documentation: The Often-Neglected Deliverable
A certified cable plant without accurate documentation is only marginally better than an uncertified one. As-built drawings, port schedules, label schemes, and test report archives are the operating manual for every technician who works on your network for the next 20 years. SRS Networks delivers complete TIA-606 compliant documentation packages with every structured cabling project.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — THE TRUE COST OF NETWORK DOWNTIME FOR MULTI-LOCATION BUSINESSES

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/true-cost-network-downtime-multi-location
Title: The True Cost of Network Downtime for Multi-Location Businesses | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: Most organizations dramatically underestimate the true cost of a network outage. Beyond lost revenue, there are operational, reputational, and regulatory costs that compound quickly.
─────────────────────────────────────────

The Iceberg Model of Downtime Costs
The visible tip of the downtime iceberg is lost revenue during the outage window. The submerged mass  -  often five to ten times larger  -  includes productivity loss for employees who can't work, overtime for IT and operations staff resolving the incident, damage to customer relationships, lost SLA penalties, and the labor cost of data reconciliation after systems come back online.

Calculating Revenue Impact
For a 100-location retail chain averaging $15,000 in daily revenue per location, a single hour of outage during peak hours costs roughly $60,000 in direct lost revenue. At the enterprise level, the calculation multiplies across every business unit dependent on network connectivity  -  which, in 2025, means nearly all of them.

• Average cost of enterprise network downtime: $5,600/minute (Gartner)
• POS outages: customers abandon rather than wait  -  transactions don't recover
• Supply chain and inventory systems halt even if POS stays operational
• Customer-facing apps and websites may remain down if datacenter links are affected

Reputational Damage Is Hard to Quantify
Beyond the immediate financial impact, outages erode customer trust. In a social-media environment, a widely-shared checkout outage can reach millions of impressions within hours. The long-tail effect on customer acquisition costs and churn rates often exceeds the direct revenue loss from the outage itself.

Healthcare and Financial Services: Regulatory Risk
For regulated industries, downtime carries additional risk. A healthcare provider that loses access to patient records during a network outage may face HIPAA audit scrutiny. Financial services firms face FINRA and SEC reporting obligations when systems are unavailable. These regulatory dimensions transform a network issue into a compliance issue.

Infrastructure Quality as Risk Mitigation
The fastest path to reduced downtime frequency is a high-quality, well-documented physical infrastructure. Many enterprise outages trace to failing copper connections, oxidized fiber terminations, overloaded UPS units, and undocumented cabling that no current employee understands. A structured cabling program with certified test records and preventive maintenance schedules dramatically reduces the "mystery outage" category.

The ROI Case for Proactive Infrastructure Investment
When organizations frame network infrastructure investment purely as a capital cost, it looks expensive. When framed against the downtime risk it mitigates, the math typically favors proactive investment by a wide margin. A $2M infrastructure refresh amortized over 15 years costs $133K/year  -  less than a single major outage event.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — SD-WAN VS. MPLS: CHOOSING THE RIGHT WAN STRATEGY

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/sdwan-vs-mpls-enterprise-wan-strategy
Title: SD-WAN vs. MPLS: Choosing the Right WAN Strategy | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: The WAN debate of this decade: should enterprises stick with MPLS, migrate to SD-WAN, or build a hybrid architecture? Here's a framework for making the right call.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Why the WAN Decision Matters More Than Ever
As enterprise workloads migrate to cloud platforms and SaaS applications, the traditional hub-and-spoke MPLS model  -  where all branch traffic backhauled to a central datacenter before reaching the internet  -  creates latency bottlenecks that directly degrade application performance. The WAN architecture decision now has a measurable impact on employee productivity and customer experience.

The Case for MPLS
MPLS (Multi-Protocol Label Switching) provides private, deterministic network paths with guaranteed QoS, making it ideal for latency-sensitive applications like VoIP, video conferencing, and real-time financial transactions. For organizations with regulatory requirements mandating private network connectivity, MPLS remains the defensible choice.

• Guaranteed bandwidth and deterministic latency
• Private network  -  no shared infrastructure with public internet
• Mature technology with well-understood operations
• Strong QoS for voice and video workloads

The Case for SD-WAN
SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) decouples network control from hardware and enables intelligent traffic steering across multiple transport links  -  broadband, LTE, MPLS  -  based on real-time performance. The cost advantage is compelling: broadband circuits are 60-80% cheaper than equivalent MPLS bandwidth. The operational advantage is equally significant: centralized policy management reduces configuration complexity at scale.

• 60-80% WAN cost reduction vs. pure MPLS
• Application-aware routing optimizes for performance in real time
• Centralized policy management scales to hundreds of sites
• Direct internet breakout reduces latency for cloud/SaaS applications

The Hybrid Architecture
Most enterprises with existing MPLS investments are best served by a hybrid approach: retain MPLS for mission-critical, latency-sensitive workloads while deploying SD-WAN for cloud and internet traffic. The SD-WAN platform provides unified visibility across both transport types and enables graceful migration as MPLS contracts expire.

Security Considerations
SD-WAN's direct internet breakout increases the organization's attack surface. Every branch site with a direct internet connection is a potential entry point. Security-first SD-WAN deployments integrate next-generation firewall, URL filtering, and IPS capabilities at every edge node  -  sometimes referred to as a Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) architecture.

Making the Decision
The right WAN strategy depends on application mix, regulatory environment, existing contract timelines, and operational maturity. Organizations with significant SaaS adoption, multi-cloud architectures, and price sensitivity typically see the strongest ROI from SD-WAN migration. Those with latency-critical private applications and regulatory obligations should model a hybrid approach carefully before eliminating MPLS.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — HEALTHCARE NETWORK SECURITY: BUILDING HIPAA-COMPLIANT INFRASTRUCTURE

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/healthcare-network-security-hipaa
Title: Healthcare Network Security: Building HIPAA-Compliant Infrastructure | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: Healthcare organizations face the highest penalty exposure of any regulated industry for network security failures. Here's what HIPAA-compliant network infrastructure actually looks like.
─────────────────────────────────────────

HIPAA's Technical Safeguards: A Network Perspective
The HIPAA Security Rule's Technical Safeguards section (45 CFR § 164.312) establishes requirements for access controls, audit controls, integrity protections, and transmission security for electronic Protected Health Information (ePHI). While HIPAA doesn't prescribe specific technologies, the standard of care for network implementations has become well-established through enforcement actions and OCR guidance.

Network Segmentation as a Foundational Control
The most impactful single network security control for healthcare organizations is strict segmentation that isolates clinical systems, medical devices, administrative networks, and guest Wi-Fi. A ransomware attack that enters through an unpatched IoMT device should not be able to reach the EHR  -  segmentation is what makes that possible.

• Clinical VLAN: EHR, PACS, pharmacy systems  -  restricted access
• Medical device VLAN: IoMT devices with internet access blocked
• Administrative VLAN: staff workstations, email, general productivity
• Guest/patient VLAN: internet-only, no corporate access
• Management VLAN: network infrastructure devices, out-of-band access

Wireless Security for Clinical Environments
Clinical environments present unique wireless security challenges: staff carry devices across floor boundaries, IoMT devices use embedded wireless radios with minimal security capabilities, and patients may bring personal devices. WPA3-Enterprise authentication tied to active directory, certificate-based device authentication for managed devices, and rogue AP detection are table-stakes controls.

Physical Security of Network Infrastructure
Physical access controls for network infrastructure are often overlooked in HIPAA security assessments. Telecommunications rooms should be locked, access logged, and equipped with environmental monitoring. Network equipment should be mounted in locked racks. Cable termination panels should be clearly labeled to prevent accidental or malicious cross-connections.

Encryption in Transit
All ePHI transmitted across the network must be encrypted in transit. For wired clinical networks, this means ensuring applications use TLS 1.2+ and that legacy protocols (Telnet, FTP, HTTP) are blocked at the network layer. For wireless networks, WPA3-Enterprise provides the required encryption baseline.

Documentation and Evidence Collection
HIPAA enforcement increasingly focuses on whether organizations can demonstrate their security posture through documentation. Network diagrams, VLAN configuration records, firewall rule reviews, penetration test results, and vulnerability scan reports form the evidence base that OCR reviewers expect to see. Organizations that invest in infrastructure documentation reduce their audit exposure significantly.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — PROJECT MANAGEMENT BEST PRACTICES FOR LARGE-SCALE NETWORK DEPLOYMENTS

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/project-management-large-scale-deployments
Title: Project Management Best Practices for Large-Scale Network Deployments | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: Managing a 300-site network deployment is a fundamentally different challenge from a single-location project. These are the program management disciplines that make large-scale rollouts succeed.
─────────────────────────────────────────

Program vs. Project: Why the Distinction Matters
A single-location network installation is a project: bounded scope, defined deliverables, a team of a few people. A 300-location rollout is a program: a portfolio of interdependent projects sharing resources, timelines, risks, and stakeholders. The program management discipline that serves the enterprise IT community  -  milestone tracking, resource leveling, risk registers, change management  -  must be adapted for network deployment programs.

Building the Work Breakdown Structure
Every large deployment program begins with a detailed Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) that decomposes the program into its constituent work packages. For a network rollout, the WBS typically includes survey/design, procurement, staging, installation, testing, and documentation phases  -  each replicated across every location and tracked independently.

• Define standard work packages that apply uniformly across all sites
• Identify site-specific exceptions and manage them as discrete work items
• Assign responsible parties and completion criteria to each work package
• Use the WBS as the basis for scheduling and resource allocation

Resource Management Across Time Zones
Multi-state rollouts require coordinating field technicians, regional coordinators, project managers, procurement teams, and client stakeholders across multiple time zones. Resource leveling  -  ensuring technicians aren't double-booked and that install schedules respect local working hours and store operating requirements  -  is a constant optimization challenge.

Risk Management and Escalation Paths
The risk register for a large deployment program covers everything from supply chain disruptions and permitting delays to technician no-shows and discovered site conditions that differ from surveys. For each identified risk, document probability, impact, mitigation strategy, and the escalation path if mitigation fails. A risk register isn't bureaucracy  -  it's the program manager's decision support tool.

Communication Architecture
Define the communication structure before the program begins. Weekly executive status reports, daily coordinator huddles, real-time incident escalation paths, and client-facing dashboards serve different audiences with different information needs. A single communications plan documenting who receives what information on what cadence prevents the information vacuum that slows decision-making.

Lessons Learned and Continuous Improvement
Large deployment programs generate an enormous volume of operational knowledge. Conducting structured lessons-learned reviews at program milestones captures insights that improve efficiency on subsequent programs. SRS Networks maintains a program knowledge base built from hundreds of enterprise deployments that informs our pre-deployment planning.


## KNOWLEDGE CENTER — FIBER VS. COPPER: MAKING THE RIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE CHOICE

URL: https://srsnetworks.com/knowledge-center/fiber-vs-copper-infrastructure-choice
Title: Fiber vs. Copper: Making the Right Infrastructure Choice | SRS Networks Knowledge Center
Description: The choice between fiber and copper cabling isn't always obvious. Understanding where each technology excels helps architects design infrastructure that performs for 20+ years.
─────────────────────────────────────────

The Complementary Roles of Fiber and Copper
The "fiber vs. copper" framing is somewhat misleading  -  in most commercial buildings, both technologies coexist and serve distinct roles. Copper dominates horizontal runs to individual work areas and devices because it simultaneously carries data and power (PoE). Fiber dominates backbone and inter-building runs because of its distance capability, bandwidth headroom, and immunity to electrical interference.

Where Copper Wins
Structured copper cabling (Cat 6A) remains the practical choice for horizontal runs from telecommunications rooms to end devices. The key advantage copper retains is Power over Ethernet: IP cameras, wireless access points, VoIP phones, digital signage, and IoT sensors all draw operating power from the same cable that carries their data connection. No equivalent fiber+power single-cable solution exists for general commercial applications.

• PoE delivery up to 90W per port (IEEE 802.3bt) over Cat 6A
• Lower installed cost per port vs. fiber for short-run applications
• No powered media converters required at end devices
• Mature testing and certification ecosystem (Fluke, IDEAL, etc.)

Where Fiber Wins
Single-mode fiber's advantages become decisive at runs exceeding 100 meters, in environments with high electromagnetic interference, and wherever bandwidth requirements may exceed 10 Gbps in the near future. Between buildings, across campuses, and in industrial environments, fiber is the unambiguous choice.

• OS2 single-mode: virtually unlimited bandwidth potential, 40km runs
• OM4 multimode: 100 Gbps to 150m  -  ideal for data center backbone
• Immune to EMI from motors, generators, and power distribution
• No ground loop issues between buildings

Converged Infrastructure Design
Modern commercial buildings benefit from a converged approach: OS2 single-mode fiber backbone between floors and buildings for maximum scalability, Cat 6A horizontal cabling for device connectivity and PoE delivery. This architecture provides the bandwidth and distance capabilities of fiber at the backbone while preserving the practicality and cost-efficiency of copper at the edge.

Planning for Technology Longevity
Infrastructure installed today will be in service in 2040. When selecting cable categories and fiber grades, consider not just current requirements but the applications that don't yet exist. Cat 6A supports 10 Gbps today and 25 Gbps with emerging standards tomorrow. OS2 fiber installed in 2010 supports 400 Gbps wavelengths today. Over-spec on infrastructure; under-spec on electronics  -  electronics get refreshed, cable plants don't.
